## **B.1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

## **SUMMARY** 

- Endometriosis is an oestrogen-dependent gynaecological condition, where endometrium-like tissue grows outside the uterus 

- • Endometriosis is estimated to affect approximately 10% of women of reproductive age.[1,2] 

- • The main clinical consequences of endometriosis are chronic pelvic pain (cyclical and non-cyclical), dysmenorrhoea (painful menstruation) and impaired fertility[2] 

- • Symptoms of endometriosis can significantly impact the person’s quality of life (QoL), their physical and psychosocial functioning, including social life, absenteeism from school or work, intimacy and intimate partnerships, as well as mental health and emotional wellbeing[3] 

- • Delays in diagnosis, where UK patients wait on average 9 years for a diagnosis,[4] as well as the ongoing management of this chronic condition, which often involves multiple invasive surgeries, places an additional burden on patients with endometriosis 

- • The economic impact of endometriosis is substantial, and its direct and indirect healthcare costs are comparable to those for other chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease[5] 

- • There is no known way to prevent endometriosis nor guaranteed cure[6] • Treatment options for endometriosis-associated pain (EAP) are diverse and consist of analgesic therapies, hormonal therapies, conservative or minimally invasive surgery, or a combination of these 

- • Treatment decisions are dependent on both the impact of symptoms and patient’s priorities regarding pain management and fertility. As such, a personalised, interdisciplinary treatment approach is required 

- • There is still a significant need for better options for the treatment of endometriosis: approximately 30% of patients with endometriosis develop chronic pelvic pain that is unresponsive to conventional treatments, including surgery[7] 

- • In patients not responding to conventional treatments, effective pharmacological therapies are required to reduce pain and improve QoL 

- • Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists may be used as a second-line treatment option but have numerous limitations, including side effects associated with suppression of oestradiol (E2) to post-menopausal levels and unpredictable reversibility of treatment with injectable depot forms.[8] In addition, currently available GnRH agonists are administered mainly by intramuscular or subcutaneous injections (every 1 to 3 months) that require healthcare professional (HCP) administration 

- • GnRH antagonists, including linzagolix, are an effective new treatment option for symptoms of endometriosis that provide immediate suppression of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH) secretion with rapid reversibility. As GnRH antagonists are administered orally, this can be done at home without HCP supervision 

- • Based on clinical expert opinion in the UK, and in line with European clinical guidelines, GnRH antagonists (including linzagolix) will be used as second-line hormonal treatment options, as an alternative to GnRH agonists[9]

## _**B.1.3 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway**_ 

## **B.1.3.1 Disease overview** 

## **B.1.3.1.1 Description** 

Endometriosis is an oestrogen-dependent gynaecological condition, where endometrium-like tissue grows outside the uterus. It causes a chronic inflammatory reaction that may result in the formation of scar tissue (adhesions, fibrosis) within the pelvis and other parts of the body.[2] Several lesion types have been described: 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 20 -->

- Superficial peritoneal endometriosis: endometrial tissue attachment to the peritoneum. This is the most common type of endometriosis 

- Endometriomas: dark, fluid-filled cysts, also known as chocolate cysts 

- Deeply infiltrating endometriosis: endometrial tissue invasion of organs either within or outside the pelvic cavity 

- Abdominal wall endometriosis: endometrial tissue growth on the abdominal wall 

Establishment and growth of such endometriotic tissue is oestrogen-dependent, thus the condition is predominantly found in women in their reproductive years and usually regresses after menopause, although a small proportion of women (~2–5%) experience post-menopausal endometriosis.[15] 

Whilst several classification systems exist, to date, there is no gold standard for the classification of endometriosis.[16] The revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine (rASRM) classification is the most widely used, and divides endometriosis severity into 4 stages: stage I (mild) to IV (severe) according to the size of the endometriotic lesions in the ovaries, peritoneum, and fallopian tubes, and the severity of adhesion at each of the sites. The staging system is useful for physicians and surgeons to explain the severity of endometriosis in simple terms to the patients, however severity of pain is not correlated with the rASRM stage.[16] 

Endometriosis can cause severe pain in the pelvis and infertility.[2] Patients experience a variety of symptoms including dysmenorrhoea (painful menstrual periods), dyspareunia (painful intercourse), chronic non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP), painful urination and dyschezia (painful or difficult bowel movements).[17,18] 

Symptoms of endometriosis can have a significant impact on the woman’s QoL, her physical and psychosocial functioning, including social life, absenteeism from school or work, intimacy and intimate partnerships, as well as mental health and emotional wellbeing.[3] 

The exact cause of endometriosis is unknown. Reflux of endometrial tissue fragments/cells and protein rich fluid through the fallopian tubes into the pelvis during 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 21 -->

menstruation is considered the most likely explanation for formation of endometriotic lesions within the peritoneal cavity, although this mechanism is not sufficient as nearly all women experience retrograde menstruation.[7] Additional postulated origins include metaplasia and lymphatic and vascular metastasis.[7] It remains unclear how endometriosis causes pain; suggested mechanisms include stimulation of neural pathways and inflammation.[7] 

There is no known way to prevent endometriosis, and there is no guaranteed cure.[6] Current treatments involve a mixture of medical and surgical interventions, with substantial limitations (Section B.1.3.4). 

## **B.1.3.1.2 Epidemiology** 

Globally, endometriosis is estimated to affect approximately 10% of women of reproductive age.[1,2] The number of affected women may be even higher, with a recent survey estimating that 25% will have endometriosis in their lifetime.[19] Most commonly, endometriosis is diagnosed in women between the ages of 25 and 45 years old, and the average age at diagnosis is 28 years old.[20] 

A serious clinical consequence of endometriosis includes infertility; the prevalence of endometriosis among women with infertility is estimated at 50%.[21] 

Data from The Health Improvement Network have been used to estimate the incidence of endometriosis reported by primary care physicians in the UK. The incidence of endometriosis was found to be 1.02 per 1000 person-years, which increased to 1.46 per 1000 person-years after case validation. The incidence of endometriosis increased with age, peaking in the 30–34 years age group. Prevalence was estimated as 2%, with the highest prevalence (3.32%) in women aged 40-44 years.[22] 

## **B.1.3.2 Burden of endometriosis** 

## **B.1.3.2.1 Clinical burden** 

The main clinical consequences of endometriosis are chronic pelvic pain (cyclical and non-cyclical), dysmenorrhoea (painful menstruation) and impaired fertility. 

Dyspareunia (painful intercourse) may affect 30%–50% of patients and, together with infertility, has a tremendous impact on sexual life and reproductive plans.[20] In 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 22 -->

addition to dysmenorrhoea, patients may experience a range of painful cyclical symptoms including dyschezia (painful or difficult defecation), dysuria (painful urination) and shoulder pain, as well as intestinal complaints; haematuria (presence of blood in the urine) and rectal bleeding.[23] 

Symptom severity can range from mild to debilitating. Some patients have no symptoms, others have episodic pelvic pain, and still others experience constant pain in multiple body regions. In a European market research survey,[19] it was estimated that over 50% of women with endometriosis in the UK experience moderate to severe symptoms. Some progress from episodic and localised pain to that which is chronic, complex, and more challenging to treat.[7] It should be noted that patients with a disease that is anatomically “severe” can have minimal symptoms, and patients with “minimal” evidence of endometriosis can have severe, life-affecting symptoms.[7] 

Endometriosis is a multisystem condition, and although pelvic pain is the most common symptom of possible endometriosis, patients with endometriosis also have a high risk of co-occurring or evolving multisite pain such as fibromyalgia and migraines.[7] Patients with endometriosis have a greater risk of presenting with other non-malignant gynaecologic diseases, including uterine fibroids and adenomyosis.[7] They are also at greater risk of a subsequent diagnosis of malignancies, autoimmune diseases, early natural menopause, ovarian cysts, bowel conditions and cerebrovascular and cardiovascular conditions.[6,7] 

While women without endometriosis have a 10%–20% chance of getting pregnant each month, this is reduced to only a 1%–10% chance for patients with endometriosis.[24] Incidence of infertility and the time to conceive have been reported to increase with the stage of disease: reported as 53% and 3.4 years for those with stage 1 (minimal) endometriosis, increasing to 96% and 6.1 years for those with stage 4 (severe) endometriosis, respectively.[25] 

Delays in diagnosis and the ongoing management of this chronic condition place an additional burden on patients with endometriosis. The route to an accurate diagnosis of endometriosis is often circuitous and lengthy. A delay in diagnosis is a significant issue as it can lead to prolonged suffering, ill health and risks to fertility. A study by 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 23 -->

Endometriosis UK that used data from 4,371 UK participants reported that, in 2023, time to diagnosis was nearly 9 years and had increased from 2020 when the delay was 8 years.[4] Reasons for delayed diagnosis included the length of waiting lists and clinicians' lack of awareness and training on endometriosis.[4] The severity of symptoms experienced prior to diagnosis was reflected in patients’s attempts to seek treatment: almost half of all respondents (47%) had visited their general practitioner (GP) 10 or more times, while 52% had visited an accident and emergency department at least once.[4] 

Patients with endometriosis often require multiple invasive surgeries. In the UK, 75% of women with endometriosis will undergo at least one surgery, and over 60% will have multiple surgical procedures.[19,26] In addition, waiting times for surgery can be lengthy: the average time to waiting time for surgery in the UK is estimated to be 19 months.[19] 

## **B.1.3.2.2 Patient burden** 

In addition to endometriosis-specific symptoms, broader effects include depression, feelings of isolation, fatigue and lack of energy, along with an adverse impact on physical, mental and social wellbeing.[27] Endometriosis may have a significant, sometimes devastating impact on all aspects of life, including education, career, relationships, sexual relationships, fertility and QoL.[4] 

In a questionnaire-based study (World Endometriosis Research Foundation [WERF] EndoCost study) with more than 900 respondents, 56% reported problems with pain/discomfort, 29% reported problems with usual activities, 29% reported being unable to work due to endometriosis, 16% of women reported (some or major) problems with mobility and 3% reported problems with self-care.[28] Similarly, in a US study where 40 women with moderate-to-severe endometriosis were interviewed, participants reported significant impacts of their symptoms on daily activities and work or school commitments, as well as social interactions, sleep and emotional well-being:[29] 95% of women described that endometriosis symptoms made it difficult to exercise or complete leisure activities; 92.5% were unable to attend social events or had cancelled pre-existing plans due to endometriosis symptoms; >80% described impairments in sleep; 80% felt they could not cope with signs/symptoms of 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 24 -->

endometriosis; and more than half of women (55.0%) highlighted that endometriosis symptoms had caused them to miss work or school. 

Many women with endometriosis experience depression, the prevalence of which positively correlates with the beginning of dyspareunia and severity of pain.[25] In the WERF EndoCost study 36% of women reported problems with anxiety/depression, and respondents to the UK National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) survey also widely reported being diagnosed with depression (44%) and anxiety (49%).[6] 

Endometriosis impairs work productivity. Women with endometriosis lose an average of 10.8 hours of work weekly, and loss of work productivity was associated with pelvic pain and disease severity.[30] 

Endometriosis has a negative effect on health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The burden of endometriosis is predominantly captured using the generic 36-Item Short Form Survey (SF-36) and disease-specific Endometriosis Health Profile-30 (EHP-30) in addition to the EuroQol 5D (EQ-5D) and Endometriosis Health Profile-5.[27] Routine assessment of HRQoL in women with endometriosis is essential for informing treatment decisions and assessing outcomes following treatment.[6] In the UK additional tools may be used in clinical practice, including the British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy (BSGE) pelvic pain questionnaire and simple numerical rating /visual analogue scales.[9] 

In the WERF Endocost study, endometriosis-associated symptoms generated an average of 0.809 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) per woman annually, representing a QoL reduction of 19% compared with a person with the best possible health state.[28] In a further large study (the Global Study of Women’s Health),[30] the effect of endometriosis on physical (but not mental) HRQoL of women was substantial, with SF-36v2 physical component summary (PCS) scores similar to those reported in women with cancer. The effect was less if women were employed and free of pelvic pain, and worse with severe pelvic pain and advanced disease. PCS scores were significantly reduced in those with moderate/severe compared with minimal/mild disease. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 25 -->

## **B.1.3.2.3 Economic and societal burden** 

The economic impact of endometriosis is substantial. As well as indirect costs encompassing reduced work performance and lost productivity, the condition incurs direct costs which include healthcare expenditures for diagnosis and endometriosis treatment (i.e. expenses associated with consultations, surgeries and hormonal therapies). Taken together, these costs contribute to the overall financial strain on healthcare systems, and its direct and indirect healthcare costs are comparable to those for other chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease.[5] 

There are approximately 1.5 million women in the UK with endometriosis, of which 75% will undergo at least one surgery.[1,19] Endometriosis is estimated to cost the UK economy around £8.2 billion every year in healthcare costs, loss of work and treatment.[4] 

In the WERF EndoCost study, average total annual costs amounted to €9,579 per woman (95% CI: €8,559–€10,599), equating to €12,064 when inflated to the year 2022.[28,31] Total costs were dominated by indirect costs of productivity loss (66% of total costs). Direct costs were made up of healthcare costs (95% of direct costs) and non-healthcare costs (5% of direct costs). The most important healthcare cost components were surgery (29% of healthcare costs), monitoring tests (19%), hospitalisation (18%) and physician visits (16%). Medication accounted for 10% of healthcare costs.[28] 

The economic burden of endometriosis escalates with increasing disease severity. As the frequency of hospitalisations and complexity of surgeries relate to the severity of the condition, the greater the disease severity, the greater the economic burden. Costs are greater with increasing severity of endometriosis, presence of pelvic pain, presence of infertility and a higher number of years since diagnosis.[28] 

## **B.1.3.3 Current treatment pathway** 

The principal objective in treating endometriosis is symptom-relief management. Treatment options for patients with EAP are diverse and consist of analgesic therapies, hormonal therapies, conservative or minimally invasive surgery, or a combination of these (Section B.1.3.4; B.1.3.5).[17] 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 26 -->

Endometriosis-associated symptoms progress and recede over the life course, and EAP affects women in different ways during their lives. As such, a personalised, interdisciplinary treatment approach is required. Treatment decisions are made in consultation with the patient and depend on patient preference, the current impact of their endometriosis-related symptoms on their QoL, and priorities concerning family planning.[9] For example, clinical experts stated that women who wish to conceive immediately would be prioritised for surgical treatment, while those not currently planning a family may try hormonal therapies to manage their symptoms before considering surgery.[9] 

Severe endometriosis should be treated in specialist centres accredited by the BSGE, of which there are 79 in England and Wales.[32–35] The requirements to be an Accredited Endometriosis Centre are: 

- A dedicated consultant-led endometriosis service within a specialist outpatient clinic 

- Sufficient workload to maintain surgical skills for the most complex cases 

- A named colorectal surgeon and other supporting clinicians, including urologists and pain management specialists, (to provide broader specialist support as needed) and an endometriosis specialist nurse 

- Annual submission of an exemplar video of surgery for laparoscopic excision of severe recto-vaginal endometriosis that required dissection of the pararectal space.

## **B.1.3.4.1 Analgesics** 

Both NICE and the ESHRE guidance recommend analgesics for the initial management of EAP. However, there is scarce evidence to support the use of simple analgesics, such as paracetamol and NSAIDs, for this.[37] 

Neuromodulators (e.g. anti-depressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or anticonvulsants), may also be used to manage pain, however, they have not been shown to be superior to placebo and are associated with dose-limiting side effects.[6] 

UK experts advise that the experience of pain is very patient-dependent. For patients with well-managed endometriosis, regular analgesia should not be required but may 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 28 -->

be used as necessary mid-cycle and/or during menstruation. It is unusual for patients to require neuromodulators, with <5% of patients prescribed such treatments.[9] 

## **B.1.3.4.2 Hormonal therapies** 

Hormone therapy can be offered both pre- and post-surgery and often prior to confirmation by laparoscopy where endometriosis is suspected. In the NCEPOD study, 60.5% of patients received hormonal therapy in secondary care, most commonly levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems (40.6%), combined oral contraceptives (COCs); 31.8%), GnRH agonists (30.8%) or oral progestogen (30.5%). In women not receiving hormonal treatments, the most common recorded reason was that they were trying to conceive (40.6%).[6] 

First-line hormonal therapies such as COCs and progestins can be effective for the treatment of EAP.[38] However, in the UK NCEPOD study, only 53% of respondents experienced any improvement in symptoms when their GP first prescribed medications.[6] Over time, many patients on COCs no longer have adequate pain relief and require additional medical therapy.[39] Only one randomised placebocontrolled clinical trial of COCs has been published, demonstrating a statistically significant, though modest, 50% reduction in dysmenorrhoea but no beneficial effect on NMPP or dyspareunia.[40] Progestin monotherapy can be efficacious for the reduction of EAP, but is often associated with breakthrough bleeding, alterations in mood, weight gain and breast tenderness.[41] In addition, progestins are not always effective, and progestin resistance occurs in 30%–50% of patients using progestinbased therapies for endometriosis.[14,42] 

GnRH agonists are reserved as second-line hormonal treatment. Although shown to relieve EAP, their use is often limited due to undesirable side effects.[37] For example, depot GnRH agonists – available only as intramuscular or subcutaneous injections – stimulate the receptor leading to a flare in LH and FSH which increases E2 secretion, causing a temporary worsening of endometriosis symptoms before the therapeutic effect is achieved.[8] In practice, patients are counselled to expect the flare, and this does not affect their treatment.[9] However, eventually, they lead to desensitisation of the GnRH receptor, reduced LH and FSH output and ultimately, suppression of ovulation and a significant reduction in serum oestrogen; thus, their use is associated with hypo-oestrogenic side effects. Short-term side effects include 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 29 -->

menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes, vaginal dryness, loss of libido and emotional lability, and their long-term use is limited by substantial bone mineral density (BMD) reduction.[43] 

To minimise or prevent the hypo-oestrogenic side effects of GnRH agonists, ABT (oestrogen or progestin or a combination of both) is recommended in ESHRE guidelines and frequently used in practice since it prevents loss of BMD without affecting the efficacy of the GnRH agonist treatment.[37] Patients prescribed a shortterm trial of GnRH agonist, i.e. ≤6 months, may not receive concomitant ABT; however, in those on treatment for more extended periods, i.e. >6 months, ABT is universally prescribed.[9] 

GnRH agonists such as leuprorelin, goserelin and triptorelin need to be given via injection, which can be uncomfortable and can result in injection site reactions.[44] Injectable GnRH agonists also need to be given under the supervision of a HCP, increasing the burden on healthcare systems and placing a time burden on patients.[44] Other GnRH agonists are administered via a nasal spray, risking inconsistent absorption, inaccurate dosing, damage to nasal mucosa and local irritation, however their use is minimal in the UK.[45] In addition, reversibility of GnRH agonist treatment is unpredictable, and it can take months for ovarian function to return to normal **.**[46] The following GnRH agonists are indicated for the treatment of endometriosis: goserelin (depot injection), leuprorelin (depot injection), nafarelin (nasal spray), buserelin (nasal spray), and triptorelin (depot injection). Although treatment duration may be extended in clinical practice with concomitant ABT, it should be noted that all available preparations have a licensed maximum treatment duration of 6 months, after which symptoms may return, requiring further alternative treatment.[47–49] 

GnRH antagonists are recommended in the ESHRE guideline as second-line therapies (for example, if hormonal contraceptives or progestogens have been ineffective) due to their side-effect profile. They are effective in relieving EAP and benefit from oral administration.[37] No specific GnRH antagonist is recommended over another in relieving EAP.[37] 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 30 -->

Relugolix in a fixed dose combination with ABT (relugolix combination therapy [relugolix-oestradiol-norethisterone acetate] [relugolix CT]) is a GnRH antagonist indicated for the symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in women with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis, and is also currently undergoing assessment by NICE.[50,51] 

Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are reserved for women with EAP refractory to other medical or surgical treatment, and may be prescribed in combination with other hormone treatments.[37] In practice, the proportion of patients prescribed AIs is negligible compared with the overall population undergoing medical treatment.[9] 

**B.1.3.4.3 Surgical treatment** Surgery is recommended as a treatment option to reduce EAP.[34,37] 

Laparoscopic elimination of endometriosis via excision (most common), ablation/vapourisation or diathermy is central to treatment. Laparoscopic excision and/or ablation of endometrial tissue accounts for 50% of first surgical procedures, and over 60% of women diagnosed with endometriosis undergo multiple surgical procedures.[19,26,52] Where management of endometriosis-associated symptoms has not been successful, more invasive methods may be indicated, involving either partial or complete removal of the uterus. Hysterectomy (with or without oophorectomy) with removal of all visible endometriosis lesions should be reserved for women who no longer wish to conceive and either have coexisting adenomyosis or have not responded to more conservative management.[7,34] 

Surgical treatment during laparoscopy is not always successful; a recent Cochrane review considered that it was uncertain whether laparoscopic surgery reduced overall pain associated with endometriosis.[53] Following surgical treatments, the reported recurrence rate of painful symptoms attributed to endometriosis is high, estimated as 21.5% at two years and 40–50% at 5 years.[7] Surgical treatments are invasive and carry risks of long-term complications. Specifically for deep infiltrating endometriosis, surgery can cause serious lifetime complications including abdominal abscess, rectovaginal or urinary fistulas, intestinal obstruction, or stenosis, all of which can negatively influence patients’ QoL.[54] While hysterectomy can provide symptomatic relief in patients with endometriosis, it can result in a range of short- 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 31 -->

and long-term complications ranging from blood clots and infections to urinary incontinence and early menopause. Nearly 4% of patients undergoing hysterectomy for endometriosis are likely to experience major morbidity.[55] In addition, there is a complete loss of fertility, a severe limitation in pre-menopausal women who wish to preserve fertility. 

## **B.1.3.5 Current treatment guidelines** 

Clinical guidelines from NICE (NG73[34] [Figure 3 and Figure 4] and QS172[35] ) and ESHRE[37] are generally aligned on the diagnosis and management of endometriosis. Both recommend clinical examination and imaging as initial investigations for symptomatic women, although NICE recommends against using pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as the primary investigation for diagnosis.[34] NICE recommends that diagnostic laparoscopy be considered if clinical suspicion remains, even if initial investigations appear normal, although ESHRE acknowledges that the invasiveness of the procedure should be considered and initial hormonal treatment (e.g. COCs or progestogens) may be preferred.[34,37] However, treatment choices must consider whether fertility is a current or upcoming priority. 

Some initial treatment (e.g. excision or ablation) may be given during a diagnostic laparoscopy if appropriate.[34] A short trial (e.g. 3 months) of analgesics such as paracetamol and/or an NSAID should be considered for the first-line management of EAP. However, other forms of pain management and referral for further assessment should be considered where these simple analgesics do not provide adequate pain relief.[34] Women not currently planning a pregnancy may opt for a COC initially, although NICE recommends referral to a gynaecology service if initial hormonal treatment is not effective, not tolerated or is contraindicated.[35] Hormonal treatment may also be used after laparoscopic surgery to further manage symptoms. Patients with suspected or confirmed deep endometriosis involving the bowel, bladder or ureter should be referred to a specialist endometriosis service (Section B.1.3.3).[35] Three months of GnRH agonist treatment should be considered before surgery as an adjunct to surgery for deep endometriosis involving the bowel, bladder or ureter. Ultimately, a hysterectomy (with or without oophorectomy) may be indicated, although the benefits and risks of this surgery need to be considered, taking into account the loss of fertility, possible need for further surgery if endometriosis recurs, 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 32 -->

and the benefits and risks of hormone replacement therapy after hysterectomy with oophorectomy.[34] 

GnRH agonists and antagonists are recommended as second-line treatment options in the ESHRE guidelines, but are not currently included in the NICE guidelines (GnRH agonists are included in the NICE guidelines as adjunct to surgery only).[34,37] NICE does not make a recommendation about AIs; however, due to the severe side effects (vaginal dryness, hot flushes, diminished BMD), the ESHRE guidelines recommend AIs are reserved for women with EAP refractory to other medical or surgical treatment.

## **B.1.3.5.1 Unmet need** 

Endometriosis is a chronic condition with no cure. There is a significant and growing unmet need with regard to timely diagnosis, as well as a need for improvement in ongoing holistic care.[6] Despite available treatment modalities, there is still a major need for better options for the treatment of endometriosis: approximately 30% of women with endometriosis develop chronic pelvic pain that is unresponsive to conventional treatments, including surgery.[7] 

In patients not responding to conventional treatments, effective pharmacological therapies are required to reduce pain and improve QoL. GnRH agonists are effective at treating endometriosis symptoms but have numerous limitations, including a delayed therapeutic impact because of the flare-up effect, suppression of E2 to less than 20 pg/mL, and unpredictable reversibility of treatment when injectable depot forms of GnRH agonists are used.[8] 

In addition, currently available GnRH agonists are mostly administered by intramuscular or subcutaneous injections (every 1 to 3 months) that require HCP administration. The administration of GnRH agonists can be offered as an enhanced service in primary care; practices that provide this service are paid according to a locally agreed-upon price.[56] The use of an orally administered GnRH antagonist would negate the need for HCP administration, vastly reducing the treatment burden for HCPs and patients, and would remove the potential for injection-site reactions. 

Availability of additional effective and well-tolerated hormonal therapies would: 

- 1) provide symptomatic relief whilst patients are waiting for surgery 

- 2) help reduce the risk of symptom recurrence post-surgery, and 

- 3) delay or prevent surgery in patients preferring medical therapy.[19] 

## **B.1.3.5.2 Proposed place of linzagolix in the current treatment pathway** 

GnRH antagonists, including linzagolix, are an effective new treatment option for symptoms of endometriosis that result in immediate suppression of FSH and LH secretion, with no flare-up, rapid reversibility and recovery of hormone secretion after stopping treatment. GnRH antagonists may be administered orally at home without physician supervision:[8] 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 36 -->

Based on clinical expert opinion in the UK, and in line with European clinical guidelines, GnRH antagonists (including linzagolix) will be used as second-line hormonal treatment options, as an alternative to GnRH agonists (Figure 5). Due to the convenience of oral administration, clinicians may initiate treatment earlier than they otherwise would with GnRH agonists.[9,37] 

Clinical experts stated that, based on the administration and adverse effect profiles, GnRH antagonists may be considered preferentially over GnRH agonists in the treatment pathway.[9,37] Unlike linzagolix, relugolix is a fixed dose combination tablet, which, whilst convenient, does not allow for choice of the ABT, if required for management of menopausal symptoms.[9]

## _**B.1.4 Equality considerations**_ 

Although linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is expected to be indicated for the symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in adult women of reproductive age with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis, this should not prevent the use of linzagolix by people with endometriosis who do not identify as a woman.

## **B.2 Clinical effectiveness** 

## **SUMMARY** 

- Results from the Phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 study (N=484) and its extension study EDELWEISS 6 (N=353 for the treatment extension analysis set / 356 in the extension safety analysis set) demonstrated the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for the treatment of moderate-to-severe EAP in women of reproductive age 

- • The daily dose of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT met the primary endpoint of EDELWEISS 3, demonstrating clinically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea (p<0.001) and NMPP (p=0.007) at month 3 versus placebo, with stable or reduced use of analgesics. Significant reductions versus placebo were also observed at month 6 

- • This was accompanied by statistically significant improvements at month 6 in the ranked secondary endpoints of dyschezia (p=0.012), overall pelvic pain (OPP) (p<0.001) and ability to participate in daily activities (based on the EHP-30 pain dimension; p<0.001) for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo 

- • The clinically meaningful improvements observed at month 6 (end of EDELWEISS 3 treatment period) generally improved further at month 12 in the EDELWEISS 6 extension study 

- • Reductions in EAP resulted in a reduced intention for surgery after 6 months in EDELWEISS 3 based on both the Physician Surgery Intention Question (PSIQ) and Subject Surgery Intention (SSIQ) in patients who received linzagolix versus placebo; the reduction from baseline to month 6 on the PSIQ became more pronounced at month 12 in EDELWEISS 6 

- • Reductions in EAP were also accompanied by improved HRQoL as shown by improved scores for the EHP-30 and EuroQoL 5-Dimension 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) Index and visual analogue scale (VAS) 

- • An indirect treatment comparison (ITC) showed that there is no significant difference between linzagolix and leuprorelin in terms of efficacy and safety 

- • The safety profile for linzagolix for women with EAP was consistent with that observed previously for women with uterine fibroids 

- • Linzagolix showed good overall tolerability, with treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) being similar to placebo; the incidence of severe TEAEs was low and comparable between groups, and no fatal or suicide-related TEAEs were reported 

- • The most common TEAEs with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT were headaches (10.5% at month 6 in EDELWEISS 3), hot flushes (6.8%), and fatigue (6.8%) 

- • Serum E2 levels were maintained within a therapeutic range (20–60 pg/mL) throughout the treatment period in patients receiving linzagolix 

- • BMD was largely unaffected by linzagolix treatment at month 6 (EDELWEISS 3) and month 12 (EDELWEISS 6), with most patients having either an increase, no change, or ≤3% decrease in BMD at months 6 and 12 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip. Some BMD increases were noted at 6 months after the end of treatment (EDELWEISS 6, month 6 extension follow-up), indicating partial recovery 

- • Menses resumed within a median time of approximately one month after the end of treatment in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6

## _**B.2.1 Identification and selection of relevant trials**_ 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to identify clinical evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg (the intervention) and other therapies (comparators) for the treatment of endometriosis. Searches for the clinical SLR were conducted in September 2024. Following assessment for eligibility using the population, intervention, comparison, outcomes and study design (PICOS) criteria, four records for two trials were identified for the intervention (the phase 2b dose-ranging EDELWEISS trial[57] [which included a dose of linzagolix 200 mg alone (without ABT) for 12 weeks] and the phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 trial[58–60] [linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT or linzagolix 75 mg versus placebo for up to 24 weeks]) and 18 records for 20 trials were identified for comparators. Full details of the SLR methodology, Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) diagram and included and excluded studies of the SLR are provided in Appendix D. 

. 

## _**B.2.2 List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

The SLR identified one phase 3 study (EDELWEISS 3[58,59] ) (Table 3) that provides evidence of the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200mg plus ABT for treating women of reproductive age with moderate to severe EAP. Data are also included from the EDELWEISS 3 extension study (EDELWEISS 6[61,62] ); data from EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 were reported in the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) submitted to the European Medicines Agency.[13] However, the data from 

EDELWEISS 6 are not yet published. Although the EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 trials evaluated both linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and linzagolix 75 mg versus placebo, the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT dose met the co-primary efficacy endpoints and is the dose for symptomatic treatment of endometriosis stated in the SmPC. This submission, therefore, focuses on the evidence for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT in women with EAP requiring symptomatic treatment. 

Adverse event data from another phase 3 study, EDELWEISS 2, were also included in the SmPC and are presented in this submission. The EDELWEISS 2 trial (NCT03986944; 18-OBE2109-002) and its extension (EDELWEISS 5; NCT04372121;19-OBE2109-005) were planned (to take place in the US and Canada) as replicate pivotal trials to EDELWEISS 3 and 6, but were discontinued

## _**B.2.3 Summary of methodology of the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

## **B.2.3.1 Phase 3 trial design** 

## **B.2.3.1.1 EDELWEISS 3** 

EDELWEISS 3 (NCT03992846; 18-OBE2109-003) was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 trial of linzagolix in women of reproductive age with moderate to severe EAP[58] (Figure 6; Table 4). The trial was conducted in 91 centres (65 in Europe and 26 in the US) and comprised a 3-month screening period, a 6-month treatment period and a 6-month drug-free follow-up period, although patients who completed the 6-month treatment period were invited to enter the EDELWEISS 6 extension study (Section B.2.3.1.2) for a further 6 months of treatment before entering the 6-month off-treatment follow-up period.[58,59] 

The trial included women of reproductive age with surgically confirmed pelvic endometriosis in the past 10 years. Prior to screening, patients had to exhibit moderate-to-severe EAP, defined as scores of ≥2 for both dysmenorrhoea and NMPP over the previous month according to the modified Biberoglu and Behrman scale.[65] During the screening period, patients had to show a mean OPP score of ≥4 (based on a numeric rating scale [NRS] of 0–10) for 5 days over two full menstrual cycles, and ≥2 days of moderate-to-severe pelvic pain (based on a verbal rating 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix for treating pain caused by endometriosis ©Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 42 -->

scale [VRS] of 0–3) on bleeding and non-bleeding days. All participants of childbearing potential were required to use one of the specified birth control methods during the entire study treatment period and for 3 months after the end of treatment.[58,59] 

The main exclusion criteria were liver enzyme anomalies, osteoporosis or other metabolic bone disease, and the use of certain medications (e.g. combined oral contraceptives, GnRH agonists or systemic glucocorticoids) within a specified washout period. 

Patients were randomised 1:1:1 to receive placebo, linzagolix 75 mg alone or linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for a period of 6 months, followed by a 6-month offtreatment follow-up (or entry into the EDELWEISS 6 extension study followed by a 6- month off-treatment follow up [Section B.2.3.1.2]). 

The co-primary efficacy endpoints were a clinically meaningful reduction from baseline of dysmenorrhoea (reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) and NMPP (reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. Ranked secondary endpoints were changes from baseline to month 6 in dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia, overall pelvic pain, interference of pain with the ability to perform daily activities (using the EHP-30 pain dimension) and dyspareunia, and no analgesic / no opiate use for EAP during the preceding 4-week period at month 6. 

Other secondary endpoints included analgesic and opioid use for EAP, number of days in hospital, PSIQ/SSIQ and HRQoL. 

Safety analyses included incidence and severity of TEAEs, changes in laboratory data, change from baseline in BMD at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip, time to post-treatment menses, and pathological alterations in the endometrium. 

## **B.2.3.1.2 EDELWEISS 6** 

Patients who completed the 6-month treatment period in the EDELWEISS 3 study (Section B.2.3.1.1) were invited to enter the EDELWEISS 6 extension study (NCT04335591; 19-OBE2109-006; Figure 6).[61,62] The primary objective of

EDELWEISS 6 was to assess the maintenance of efficacy of linzagolix for up to an additional 6 months (up to 12 months of treatment in total) in women who had already completed 6 months of linzagolix treatment at a dose of 75 mg alone or 200 mg plus ABT in EDELWEISS 3.[61] 

In EDELWEISS 6, patients who received placebo in EDELWEISS 3 were randomised 1:1 to linzagolix 75 mg or linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. Patients who received active treatment in EDELWEISS 3 continued with the same treatment. 

In line with EDELWEISS 3, the co-primary endpoints of EDELWEISS 6 were clinically meaningful reduction of dysmenorrhoea (reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) and NMPP (reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days preceding the month 12 visit, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

Secondary endpoints of EDELWEISS 6 included changes from baseline to month 12 in dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia, OPP, interference of pain with the ability to perform daily activities (using the EHP-30 pain dimension) and dyspareunia. Other secondary endpoints included analgesic and opioid use for EAP, number of days in hospital, PSIQ/SSIQ and HRQoL.

## **B.2.4.3 Patient flow** 

Overall, 484 women were included in the full analysis set (FAS) in EDELWEISS 3; patient disposition up to month 6 is summarised in Figure 7. 

A total of 356 subjects who completed the 6-month treatment period in the EDELWEISS 3 study entered the EDELWEISS 6 extension study and were treated. Three patients discontinued the treatment period prematurely due to discontinuation criteria met at month 6 of BMD loss >8% or Z-score ≤-2.5 (one patient in each of the placebo/linzagolix 75 mg, linzagolix 75 mg and linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT groups). The treatment extension analysis set (TEAS) therefore included 353 patients.[61] Patient disposition in EDELWEISS 6 is summarised in Figure 8.

## **B.2.4.4 Patient baseline characteristics** 

Demographic and baseline characteristics were generally well balanced among treatment groups in both the EDELWEISS 3 (Table 8)[58] and EDELWEISS 6 (Table 9)[61] studies. 

Women in EDELWEISS 3 had an overall mean (standard deviation [SD]) age of 34.9 (6.6) years and were mostly white (98.6%).[59] The mean (SD) weight was 66.42 

(13.77) kg and mean (SD) body mass index (BMI) was 24.27 (4.95) kg/m[2] .[59] 

Women who entered EDELWEISS 6 had a mean (SD) age of 34.8 (6.7) years and most (98.6%) were white. The mean (SD) weight was 66.61 (13.87) kg and mean (SD) BMI was 24.25 (4.94) kg/m[2] .[61]

## _**B.2.6 Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant trials**_ 

## **B.2.6.1 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 | Co-primary endpoints** 

The daily dose of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT met the co-primary endpoint of the EDELWEISS 3 study, demonstrating clinically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP (reductions of ≥1.10 and ≥0.8 points on the verbal rating scale for dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, respectively) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, with stable or reduced use of analgesics[58] (Figure 9). At month 3, the estimated percentage of responders for dysmenorrhoea was 72.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 65.3–79.4) in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group versus 23.5% (95% CI: 17.5–30.7) in the placebo group (odds ratio [OR] 8.80 [97.5% CI: 4.86–15.91]; p<0.001). Respective proportions for NMPP were 47.3% (95% CI: 39.5–55.3) with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus 30.9% (95% CI: 24.1–38.6) with placebo (OR 2.01 [97.5% CI: 1.18– 3.42]; p=0.007). 

The linzagolix 75 mg alone dose demonstrated a clinically meaningful and statistically significant reduction in dysmenorrhoea versus placebo at month 3, but the reduction in NMPP at month 3 versus placebo was not statistically significant. Linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is, therefore, the dose for EAP stated in the SmPC, and this submission focuses on the evidence for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT.

Ranked secondary endpoints showing statistically significant and clinically 

meaningful improvements from baseline to month 6 with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo were dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia, OPP and ability to participate in daily activities (based on pain dimensions listed in the EHP-30) (Table 12). The statistical analysis hierarchy was interrupted as the change from baseline to month 6 in dyspareunia with linzagolix did not differ significantly from that observed with placebo. Therefore, statistical significance cannot be confirmed for the numerically higher proportions of patients reporting no use of analgesia in the 4 weeks to month 6 with linzagolix versus placebo (Table 12). The proportion of 

patients reporting opiate use in the 4 weeks before month 6 was minimal (<10%) for all groups (Table 12).

Responders were defined as patients who met the clinically meaningful reduction thresholds of a reduction of ≥1.10 and ≥0.8 points on the VRS for dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, respectively, from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 12 (month 12 analysis) or 28 days prior to month 6 post-treatment follow-up (month 6 extension follow-up analysis), along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for endometriosisassociated pain. 

Source: EDELWEISS 6 CSR (data on file)[61] 

## **B.2.6.2.2 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 | Secondary endpoints | Number of days in hospital** 

Hospitalisations were infrequent throughout the EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 studies, with <2% of patients hospitalised at any measured time point (and most time points having 0% hospitalisation). For this reason, it was not deemed necessary to incorporate into the economic modelling.

Improvements from baseline in the EHP-30 dimensions of pain, control and powerlessness, emotional wellbeing, social support, self-image and sexual relationship and EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS scores continued to be observed with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT up to month 12 in EDELWEISS 6.[61] 

## **B.2.6.3 Efficacy conclusions** 

The efficacy of up to 12 months of treatment with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for moderate-to-severe EAP in women of reproductive age was confirmed in the Phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 study and its extension study EDELWEISS 6. 

The daily dose of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT met the primary endpoint of EDELWEISS 3, demonstrating clinically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP at month 3 versus placebo, with stable or reduced use of analgesics. At month 3, the estimated percentage of responders for dysmenorrhoea was 72.9% (95% CI: 65.3–79.4) in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group versus 23.5% (95% CI: 17.5–30.7) in the placebo group (OR 8.80 [97.5% CI: 4.86–15.91]; p<0.001). Respective proportions for NMPP were 47.3% (95% CI: 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 73 -->

39.5–55.3) with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus 30.9% (95% CI: 24.1–38.6) with placebo (OR 2.01 [97.5% CI: 1.18–3.42]; p=0.007). 

Significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP were observed at month 6 for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo. This was accompanied by statistically significant improvements in the ranked secondary endpoints of dyschezia, OPP and ability to participate in daily activities (based on pain dimensions listed in the EHP30). 

The clinically meaningful improvements observed at month 6 (end of EDELWEISS 3 treatment period) generally improved further at month 12 in the EDELWEISS 6 extension study. Reductions in EAP resulted in a reduced intention for surgery after 6 months in EDELWEISS 3 based on both the PSIQ and SSIQ in patients who received linzagolix versus placebo; the reduction from baseline to month 6 on the PSIQ became more pronounced at month 12 in EDELWEISS 6. 

Reductions in EAP were also accompanied by improved HRQoL as shown by improved scores for the EHP-30 and EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS. 

## _**B.2.7 Subgroup analyses**_ 

Pre-planned subgroup analyses for EDELWEISS 3 are listed in Section B.2.3 (Table 4), although some planned analyses (based on race, ethnicity, history of pregnancy) were not performed due to small patient numbers.[59] Subgroup analyses for the coprimary endpoints for EDELWEISS 3 showed consistent results across analysed pre-planned subgroups.[59] Forest plots for subgroup analyses of the co-primary endpoints are presented in Appendix E. 

Dyspareunia for patients with a mean dyspareunia score >1 at baseline was the only pre-planned subgroup analysis for EDELWEISS 6. Data for dyspareunia for patients with a mean dyspareunia score >1 at baseline were consistent with those in the main analyses for both EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6.

EDELWEISS 3 subgroup analyses for BMD showed more bone loss in all sites in patients aged ≥35 years, those weighing <63 kg and those with a BMI <23 kg/m[2 ] (Appendix E).[58,59] 

## _**B.2.8 Meta-analysis**_ 

A network meta-analysis was not performed as there was only one randomised controlled trial for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT (EDELWEISS 3[58,59] and its extension study EDELWEISS 6[61] ). 

## _**B.2.9 Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons**_ 

In the absence of head-to-head data, an ITC was performed using the Bucher analysis method to compare the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT with leuprorelin, the pharmacological comparator of relevance to the decision problem using published evidence from the clinical SLR (see Section B.2.1 and Appendix D). The efficacy outcomes analysed in the ITC were based on those specified in the final scope issued by NICE and the availability of data reported in the literature.

Various surgical techniques are recommended in guidelines for the treatment of EAP, however due to the invasiveness of these procedures they may be considered following initial hormonal treatment (see Section B.1.3.4).[34,37] An SLR was 

conducted to identify relevant evidence and assess the feasibility of a comparison of 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 75 -->

efficacy and safety of minimally invasive surgical procedures versus linzagolix in combination with ABT. Full details of the SLR and feasibility assessment are provided in Appendix M. 

Four relevant publications reporting outcomes following surgical procedures were identified for further comprehensive analysis (Table 19). The studies are highly heterogeneous, with considerable differences that precluded an ITC with linzagolix plus ABT: 

- definitions of endometriosis severity varied in the trials, with some studies lacking the specific severity measure altogether; 

- the diagnostic processes in the studies on surgeries were inconsistent with the diagnostic process in the EDELWEISS 3 trial; 

- limited baseline characteristics suitable for comparison were available in the publications of interest; 

- the publications identified for surgery were published ≥20 years ago. Since then, multiple improvements and modifications have been made regarding the training of professionals and the approach to the perioperative care; 

- in some cases, a lack of a common comparator was a considerable limitation; 

- outcomes were defined and measured differently. Adjusting of the identified results for surgeries to match the results for linzagolix is unfeasible or highly limited. 

Considering the aforementioned factors, conducting an ITC between linzagolix and the currently recommended minimally invasive surgical treatments for endometriosis is not feasible.

## **B.2.9.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies from the clinical SLR** 

As described in Section B.2.1 and Appendix D, an SLR was conducted in September 2024. Of the 22 studies identified for the intervention (n=2) and comparators (n=20), only two studies relating to linzagolix and leuprorelin were eligible according to the scope for this submission. The PICOS criteria used for the ITC are presented in Appendix D. 

## **B.2.9.2 Risk of bias** 

The methodological quality of each trial was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Collaboration’s revised risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2).[73] Disagreements were resolved by consensus. The risk of bias was defined as low for all the trials included in the Bucher analysis. Further details can be found in Appendix D. 

## **B.2.9.3 Overview of the selected studies** 

The SLR identified the EDELWEISS[57] and EDELWEISS 3[58] studies for linzagolix in EAP and 20 comparator trials (described in 18 publications) The studies considered to be suitable for inclusion in the ITC Bucher analysis are presented in (Table 20). 

The SLR for the comparators searched for trials that could be compared with the trials found in the review for the intervention (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT). Therefore, only studies with 12 or 24 weeks of follow-up were included in the ITC for the efficacy analysis. Safety was assessed using the longest available follow-up period of 24 weeks. 

Although two linzagolix studies (EDELWEISS 3, EDELWEISS) were identified from the SLR, only the EDELWEISS 3 trial was included in the ITC. The EDELWEISS study was a dose-ranging phase 2b study that included a dose of linzagolix 200 mg alone (without ABT) and was not included in the ITC for the efficacy analysis due to a lack of alignment of clinically relevant endpoints for inclusion in the treatment 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 78 -->

comparison. In addition, safety in the EDELWEISS study was only assessed for 12 weeks, so this study could not be included in the ITC for the safety analysis. 

Reasons for exclusion of other studies from the ITC included: comparator therapy not relevant to the scope of this submission; no placebo group for comparison with the intervention arm; data displayed only graphically, without detailed breakdown for analysis; outcomes data did not include standard deviation/standard error; lack of clarity of scale used. Further details regarding the rationale for inclusion/exclusion of individual comparator trials on the basis of heterogeneity can be found in Appendix D.

## **B.2.9.4 Heterogeneity assessment of trials included** 

Consistently reported inclusion/exclusion criteria were age, diagnosis of endometriosis, menstrual cycle, presence of dysmenorrhoea and pelvic pain, history of surgery, and need for treatment. 

No trials were excluded from the Bucher analysis because of their inclusion/exclusion criteria. The effect of different inclusion/exclusion criteria was assessed by reviewing the baseline characteristics. The included trials used similar inclusion criteria for age, endometriosis diagnosis and interval between menstrual cycles. Although the trials all included adult premenopausal women with moderate to severe EAP as measured by dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, the scales used to measure dysmenorrhoea and NMPP scores differed between trials. The 

heterogeneity assessment confirmed the feasibility of an ITC between linzagolix

<!-- page 79 -->

versus leuprorelin. Further details regarding heterogeneity are presented in Appendix D. 

## **B.2.9.5 Methods** 

An ITC was conducted using the Bucher method performed in R version 4.3.2. The Bucher method can only be applied to two-arm trials. The main assumption is that the relative efficacy of a treatment is the same in all trials included in the ITC to allow the indirect comparison of A versus C when direct evidence of A versus B and B versus C is available. 

The results of the included trials were analysed to determine whether it was possible to construct a network of relationships between the different arms of the trials. The methodology of each study and patient baseline characteristics were also analysed to identify differences between the trials that might have an impact on the health outcomes. Non-inferiority was defined based on p-values of >0.05 for the ITC, indicating no statistically significant difference between the treatments. 

Detailed methods for the ITC are presented in Appendix D.

## **B.2.9.6.2 Safety of linzagolix versus leuprorelin** 

The safety of linzagolix was comparable to leuprorelin (Table 22), although some statistically significant differences between these treatments are discussed in this section. 

Linzagolix demonstrated a statistically significantly reduced impact on lumbar spine BMD (possibly due to the use of ABT with linzagolix) and lower incidence of hot flushes versus leuprorelin, although the incidence of serious TEAEs was statistically significantly higher with linzagolix versus leuprorelin (Table 22). However, the incidence of serious TEAEs was similar for both treatments (1.2% for linzagolix[58] , 0.0% for leuprorelin[74] ) and the significant difference was likely driven by the relatively high incidence of serious TEAEs in the placebo group of the Osuga et al study (5.2%) versus the EDELWEISS 3 study (0.0%).

## **B.2.9.7 ITC conclusions** 

The ITC using the Bucher method, suggests that there is no significant difference in terms of efficacy between linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and leuprorelin at both week 12 and week 24. Furthermore, linzagolix appeared to have comparable safety to leuprorelin at week 24 in terms of any TEAE, severe TEAE, TEAE leading to permanent discontinuation of study drug and headache. In addition, linzagolix showed significantly lower incidence of hot flushes than leuprorelin monotherapy.

## _**B.2.10 Adverse reactions**_ 

Key safety evidence from EDELWEISS 3 and 6 is presented in this section; this is supported by adverse event data from the terminated EDELWEISS 2 study (see Section B.2.2). The safety profile for linzagolix in women with EAP was consistent with that observed previously for women with uterine fibroids.[10,76] Linzagolix showed good overall tolerability, with TEAEs similar to placebo.

## **B.2.10.2.1 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 2 | Summary of treatment-emergent adverse events up to month 6** 

Linzagolix was well tolerated, with similar percentages of patients reporting TEAEs in the linzagolix 75 mg and placebo groups (46.9% in each group) during the 6-month treatment period in EDELWEISS 3; slightly higher rates of TEAEs were observed in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group (56.8%; Table 25). ## _**B.2.10.4.1.2 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 2 | Most common ABT-related adverse events up to month 6**_ 

Overall, 22.9% of patients in the EDELWEISS 3 safety analysis set reported TEAEs considered related to ABT.[59] The percentage of patients reporting TEAEs related to ABT was similar in the placebo (20.4%) and linzagolix 75mg (20.6%) groups and slightly higher in the linzagolix 200 mg ABT group (27.8%). The most common ABTrelated TEAEs included headache (5.8%), fatigue (2.9%), nausea (2.9%), and hot flushes (2.7%). Nausea was observed with similar frequency in the placebo and linzagolix groups. Headache, fatigue and hot flushes were reported more frequently in the linzagolix groups compared with placebo. 

In EDELWEISS 2, the number of patients reporting ABT-related TEAEs was similar between the placebo (n=4 patients), linzagolix 75 mg (n=4) and linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT (n=5) groups. In the placebo group, nausea, headache, chest discomfort, anxiety, and pain in extremities were reported by one patient each. In the linzagolix 75 mg group, nausea, abdominal distension, vomiting, headache, breast tenderness and non-cardiac chest pain were reported by one patient each. In the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, two patients reported dizziness; nausea, upper abdominal pain, diarrhoea, headache, menstrual disorder, vaginal haemorrhage, nervousness and dyspnoea were reported by one patient each.

## _**B.2.10.7.1.1 EDELWEISS 3 | Serum E2 levels**_ 

In EDELWEISS 3, E2 levels were maintained within a therapeutic range (between 20 and 60 pg/mL), similar to that naturally observed during the early follicular phase, throughout the treatment period in both linzagolix treatment groups (Figure 13).[58] This is considered the ideal range to manage endometriosis symptoms while reducing oestrogen-deprivation side effects such as hot flushes and BMD loss,[77] although the optimal E2 level may vary from patient to patient. E2 levels of >60 pg/mL were observed for most patients in the placebo group.

## _**B.2.10.7.1.2 EDELWEISS 3 | liver enzymes and triglycerides**_ 

Elevated liver enzyme parameters that were considered clinically significant by the investigator were reported for 12 patients during treatment (placebo: n=3, 1.9%; linzagolix 75 mg: n=6, 3.2%; linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: n=3, 1.9%, including one patient with alanine transaminase [ALT]/aspartate aminotransferase [AST] ≥3 times upper limit of normal [ULN]).[58] Elevated liver enzymes were transient and reversible. One patient had an isolated AST increase with concomitant creatine kinase increase due to excessive physical training, which was rapidly reversed, and one patient in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group showed gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) ≥3xULN. All other transaminase increases were <3xULN. 

Two patients had clinically significantly elevated triglyceride levels.[58] In the placebo group, a patient with grade 1 elevation (187 mg/dL) at baseline had high triglyceride levels at month 4 (428 mg/dL; grade 2), month 5 (392 mg/dL; Grade 2) and month 6 (327 mg/dL; grade 2), but values normalised when she switched to linzagolix 75 mg during the extension study. In the linzagolix 75 mg group, one patient had a single increased triglyceride level at month 3 (637 mg/dL; grade 3) that returned to normal under continued treatment.

## **B.2.10.7.2 EDELWEISS 6 | Clinical laboratory evaluations up to month 12** 

Clinically significant changes in laboratory values, including increases in liver enzymes, were infrequent in all groups. There were no patterns or trends in any other laboratory parameters in any treatment group. 

## _**B.2.10.7.2.1 EDELWEISS 6 | Serum E2 levels**_ 

Median E2 levels were comparable across treatment groups at baseline. In the linzagolix groups, there was a trend towards a decrease in E2 levels from baseline up to month 12, with median E2 levels of 39.50–58.10 pg/mL in the linzagolix 75 mg group and 28.05–35.30 pg/mL in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group. 

In the placebo/linzagolix groups, an increase in E2 levels was observed from baseline to month 6, followed by a decrease after the first administration of linzagolix and stabilisation until the end of treatment period at month 12. In the placebo/linzagolix 75 mg group, median E2 levels were 56.20–98.10 pg/mL from day 1 to month 6 and 38.90–80.90 pg/mL from month 6 to month 12. In the placebo/linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, median E2 levels were 63.40–105.00 pg/mL from day 1 to month 6 and 29.90–80.70 pg/mL from month 6 to month 12. 

Most patients in the linzagolix groups had an E2 level <60 pg/mL throughout the treatment period, with a higher percentage of patients in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group. In the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, approximately 17%–28% of patients maintained an E2 level <20 pg/mL, while approximately 56%–64% maintained E2 ≥20 and <60 pg/mL throughout the treatment period. In the linzagolix 75 mg group, E2 levels were suppressed to <20 pg/mL in approximately 15%–27% of patients, while approximately 30%–43% maintained E2 ≥20 and <60 pg/mL throughout the 12-month treatment period. Similar trends were observed for the placebo/linzagolix groups from month 6 to month 12. 

Rapid reversibility of E2 suppression was observed after the end of treatment with linzagolix. In the post-treatment extension follow-up (ExFU) period, median E2 levels were 96.00–113.00 pg/mL in the placebo/linzagolix 75 mg group, 44.70–84.00 pg/mL in the placebo/linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, 93.85–98.90 pg/mL in the linzagolix 75 mg group and 58.35–62.30 pg/mL in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT

Similar trends were observed for the placebo/linzagolix groups at the ExFU period.

## **B.2.10.9 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 | Time to first post-treatment menses** 

Menses resumed within a median time of approximately 1 month after the end of treatment across groups in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6. 

In EDELWEISS 3, menses resumed after cessation of therapy for all of the 51 patients (placebo n=15, linzagolix 75 mg n=15, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, n=21) who did not continue into the extension study. The estimated time to recovery of menses was 4–5 weeks due to rapid recovery of ovarian function (based on blood test results).[58] In the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, post-treatment menses data were recorded for 19 patients (90.5%) and 2 patients (9.5%) were considered censored.[59] The median Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimate was 33.0 days (95% CI: 30.0– 58.0 days). In the linzagolix 75 mg group, all 15 patients had events (menses). The median KM estimate was 24.0 days (95% CI: 4.0–26.0 days). The KM probability estimates were 0.929 (95% CI: 0.735–0.995) at 196 days for the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group and 0.933 (95% CI: 0.740–0.996) at 56 days for the linzagolix 75 mg group.[59]

<!-- page 99 -->

In EDELWEISS 6, post-treatment menses data were recorded as follows.[61] For the placebo/linzagolix 75 mg group, data were available for 53 patients (98.1%) and one patient (1.9%) was considered censored; the median KM estimate was 24.0 days (95% CI: 21.0–26.0 days). In the placebo/linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, data were recorded for 49 patients (98.0%) and 1 patient (2.0%) was considered 

censored; the median KM estimate was 30.5 days (95% CI: 29.0–33.0 days). In the linzagolix 75 mg group, data were recorded for 108 patients (96.4%) and 4 patients (3.6%) were considered censored; the median KM estimate was 22.0 days (95% CI: 19.0–24.0 days). In the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, data were recorded for 107 patients (94.7%) and 6 patients (5.3%) were considered censored; the median KM estimate was 32.0 days (95% CI: 31.0–33.0 days). 

The KM probability estimates were 0.981 (95% CI: 0.912–0.998) at 140 days for placebo/linzagolix 75 mg, 0.960 (95% CI: 0.879–0.993) at 140 days for placebo/ linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, 0.967 (95% CI: 0.919–0.990) at 196 days for linzagolix 75 mg and 0.954 (95% CI: 0.902–0.983) at 168 days for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT.[61] 

## **B.2.10.10 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 | Pathological changes in the endometrium** 

There were no clinically meaningful changes from baseline in gynaecological examinations or endometrial biopsies in any group during the EDELWEISS 3 or EDELWEISS 6 treatment periods.[59,61] 

Endometrial biopsies were performed on 99.4% of patients (n=481/162) at EDELWEISS 3 screening, most of whom (n=455/481) had assessable results. One patient (0.6%) in the placebo group had an abnormal finding of endometritis on the endometrial biopsy at screening, which was considered as not clinically significant. At month 6, endometrial biopsies were performed on 20.5% of patients (n=99/484). All 95 assessable endometrial biopsies were normal. All endometrial biopsies were classified as benign endometrium without hyperplasia or atypia at both screening and month 6 of the EDELWEISS 3 treatment period. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 100 -->

Endometrial biopsies were performed at month 6 and month 12 of EDELWEISS 6. At month 6, biopsies were performed on 22.8% of patients (n=81/356), most of whom (n=78/81) had assessable results; there were no abnormal findings. Biopsies were performed on 19.4% of patients (n=69/356) at month 12. All 63 assessable biopsies were normal. All endometrial biopsies were classified as benign endometrium without hyperplasia or atypia at both month 6 and month 12 of the EDELWEISS 6 treatment period. 

During the EDELWEISS 6 ExFU period (after the end of treatment), endometrial biopsies were performed at ExFU months 1 (17.9% of patients [n=59/329], 54 assessable), 3 (20.1% of patients [n=66/329], 60 assessable) and 6 (12.5% patients [n=41/329], 35 assessable). All endometrial biopsies were classified as being benign endometrium without hyperplasia or atypia. At month 6 ExFU, one patient in the placebo/linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group had an abnormal finding of benign (weakly) proliferative endometrium with breakdown change, which was considered as not clinically significant, and one patient in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group had an abnormal finding (unspecified), which was considered to be clinically significant. However the biopsy for the patient with ‘abnormal finding (unspecified)’ had been assessed in a local laboratory, and additional information was not available. As this patient had an endometrial biopsy at Month 1 ExFU, which had been classified as being benign endometrium without hyperplasia or atypia, the unknown abnormality at Month 6 ExFU was not followed up further. 

## **B.2.10.11 Safety conclusions** 

Linzagolix showed good overall tolerability in the EDELWEISS 3, EDELWEISS 2, and EDELWEISS 6 trials, with TEAEs similar to placebo. The incidence of severe TEAEs was low and comparable between groups, and no fatal or suicide-related TEAEs were reported. The safety profile for linzagolix for women with EAP was consistent with that observed previously for women with uterine fibroids. 

The most common TEAEs with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT were headaches (10.5% at month 6 in EDELWEISS 3), hot flushes (6.8%) and fatigue (6.8%). 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 101 -->

In patients receiving linzagolix, serum E2 levels were maintained within a therapeutic range (20–60 pg/mL)[77] throughout the treatment period. 

BMD was largely unaffected by linzagolix treatment at month 6 (EDELWEISS 3) and month 12 (EDELWEISS 6), with most patients having either an increase, no change or ≤3% decrease in BMD at months 6 and 12 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip; some BMD increases were noted at 6 months after the end of treatment (EDELWEISS 6 month 6 extension follow-up), indicating partial recovery. Menses also resumed within a median time of approximately 1 month after the end of treatment in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6.

The trial is expected to recruit a total of 540 patients (n=180 per group). The primary completion date is June 2024 and the final study completion date is March 2025.[78] 

## _**B.2.12 Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence**_ 

## **B.2.12.1 Principal findings from the clinical evidence base** 

## **B.2.12.1.1 Comparative efficacy and safety of linzagolix versus placebo in the EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 studies** 

The efficacy and safety of up to 12 months of treatment with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for moderate-to-severe EAP in women of reproductive age were confirmed in the phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 study[58,59] and its extension study EDELWEISS 6.[61] 

The daily dose of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT met the primary endpoint of EDELWEISS 3, demonstrating clinically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP at month 3 versus placebo, with stable or reduced use of analgesics. At month 3, the estimated percentage of responders for dysmenorrhoea was 72.9% (95% CI: 65.3–79.4) in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group versus 23.5% (95% CI: 17.5–30.7) in the placebo group (OR 8.80 [97.5% CI: 4.86–15.91]; p<0.001). Respective proportions for NMPP were 47.3% (95% CI: 39.5–55.3) with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus 30.9% (95% CI: 24.1–38.6) with placebo (OR 2.01 [97.5% CI: 1.18–3.42]; p=0.007). 

Significant reductions versus placebo were also observed at month 6. This was accompanied by statistically significant improvements in the ranked secondary 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 103 -->

endpoints of dyschezia, overall pelvic pain and ability to participate in daily activities (based on pain dimensions listed in the EHP-30). 

The clinically meaningful improvements observed at month 6 (end of EDELWEISS 3 treatment period) generally increased at month 12 in the EDELWEISS 6 extension study. Reductions in EAP resulted in a reduced intention for surgery after 6 months in EDELWEISS 3 based on both the PSIQ and SSIQ in patients who received linzagolix versus placebo; least squares mean (LSM) differences for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo were −0.7 (97.5% CI: −1.3, −0.1; p=0.017) for the PSIQ and −0.9 (97.5% CI: −1.6, −0.2; p=0.005) for the SSIQ. The reduction in the PSIQ from baseline to month 6 in EDELWEISS 3 (LSM change −1.5 [97.5% CI: −1.9, −1.2]) became more pronounced at month 12 in EDELWEISS 6 (mean [SD] change from baseline −2.7 [2.8]). 

Reductions in EAP were also accompanied by improved HRQoL as shown by improved scores for the EHP-30 and EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS. 

The safety profile for linzagolix in women with EAP was consistent with that observed previously for women with uterine fibroids.[10,76] Linzagolix showed good overall tolerability in the EDELWEISS 3,[58,59] EDELWEISS 2[63] and EDELWEISS 6[61] trials, with TEAEs being similar to placebo. The incidence of severe TEAEs was low and comparable between groups, and no fatal or suicide-related TEAEs were reported. The most common TEAEs with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT in women with EAP were headaches (10.5% at month 6 in EDELWEISS 3), hot flushes (6.8%) and fatigue (6.8%). Serum E2 levels were maintained within a therapeutic range (20–60 pg/mL) throughout the treatment period in patients receiving linzagolix. 

BMD was largely unaffected by linzagolix treatment at month 6 (EDELWEISS 3) and month 12 (EDELWEISS 6), with most patients having either an increase, no change or ≤3% decrease in BMD at Months 6 and 12 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip; some BMD increases were noted at 6 months after end of treatment (EDELWEISS 6 month 6 extension follow-up), indicating partial recovery. Menses also resumed within a median time of approximately 1 month after end of treatment in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6.
