## **B.2.12.1.2 Comparative efficacy of linzagolix versus other treatments based on an ITC** 

ITC data indicate that the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT are comparable to leuprorelin. 

Linzagolix was associated with a statistically significantly lower incidence of hot flushes versus leuprorelin. 

## **B.2.12.2 Strengths and limitations of the clinical evidence base for linzagolix in the treatment of EAP** 

**B.2.12.2.1 Strengths of the evidence base** 

Data from the Phase 3 EDELWEISS 3[58,59] and EDELWEISS 6[61,62] trials demonstrated the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo for women with EAP. The linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT dose met the primary endpoint of EDELWEISS 3, demonstrating clinically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP at month 3 versus placebo, with stable or reduced use of analgesics. Efficacy was observed across all pre-specified subgroups in EDELWEISS 3 and improved at month 12 in the EDELWEISS 6 extension study. 

In addition to the compelling results from EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6, the mechanism of action of linzagolix and other GnRH antagonists in endometriosis is well understood and documented (i.e. reducing the release of LH and FSH, leading to decreased serum concentrations of oestradiol, depriving the endometriosis lesion of its major growth stimulant).[79] For linzagolix, this mechanism of action is fully supported by previously assessed data in the pathophysiologically-related condition of uterine fibroids.[12,13] 

The approvals of other GnRH antagonists (relugolix and elagolix) in the EU and US, and recently in the UK for relugolix, for the treatment of symptoms of endometriosis provides strong and consistent evidence for the effectiveness of the GnRH antagonist class in the treatment of EAP and the need for alternative medicines for the management of endometriosis symptoms.[50,80–83] . 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 105 -->

## **B.2.12.2.2 Potential limitations of the evidence base** 

The EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 trials showed clear evidence for the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for women with EAP,[58,59,61,62] compared with placebo, but do not provide a head-to-head comparison between linzagolix plus ABT and other potential active treatments. Therefore, an ITC was performed and indicated that the efficacy and safety of linzagolix are comparable to leuprorelin. 

The EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 trials comprised mostly white women (98.6% in both studies).[59,61] Patients from other ethnic groups were therefore not well represented in these trials.

## **B.3 Cost effectiveness** 

## **SUMMARY** 

- An SLR was undertaken to identify previous cost-effectiveness evidence relevant to the decision problem, with a total of 16 records identified, including seven full articles and nine conference abstracts. The evidence identified was used to inform the model structure and some of the inputs used in the analysis 

- A _de novo_ economic model was developed to assess the cost-effectiveness of linzagolix 200mg plus ABT versus GnRH agonists and conservative surgery, as a treatment for patients with moderate to severe EAP, and a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis 

- The economic model simulates the complex treatment pathway for women with endometriosis at the point of treatment initiation with a GnRH analogue, including initial response to treatment and subsequent treatment with other medical therapies and/or surgical interventions. The model structure was aligned to established treatment guidelines and validated by clinical expert opinion[10, 19, 35, 104] 

- Model development was also informed by the NICE draft guidance issued for the ongoing relugolix CT STA, with steps taken to address key feedback provided by NICE and the evidence assessment group (EAG) 

- The main comparator in the model is GnRH agonists (represented by leuprorelin), as linzagolix is most likely to be prescribed in situations where GnRH agonists are currently prescribed. It was assumed that GnRH agonists would be used in combination with ABT from the start of therapy for a duration of 1.5 years, based on expert clinical opinion.[10, 104] Laparoscopic surgery was also included as an additional comparator in the model 

- Response data based on the co-primary endpoints (clinically meaningful reduction from baseline in dysmenorrhea and NMPP, with no increase in use of analgesics) in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 were used to determine efficacy of initial medical treatment in the model. Based on the results of an ITC, it was assumed that response rates for the GnRH agonists are equal to those for linzagolix 

- It was deemed unfeasible to do an ITC comparing linzagolix to surgery (see Appendix M), therefore, response rates for laparoscopic surgery and pain recurrence following surgery were established with studies identified in the SLR 

- Utility values for model health states were calculated from EQ-5D data collected within EDELWEISS 3 (health states related to treatment response and pain levels) and from relevant literature (disutilities for AEs and surgical complications). Alternative utility values based on different regression models and literature were tested in scenario analyses 

- Costs were sourced from UK national resources in line with an NHS perspective and the literature. In the absence of published healthcare resource use (HRU) data specific to the target population, expert opinion informed HRU frequencies for disease management and regular monitoring 

- In the base case analysis, linzagolix compared with leuprorelin was associated with incremental costs of £2,252 and incremental QALYs of 0.41, resulting in an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of £5,554 per QALY; below the UK costeffectiveness threshold of £20,000-£30,000 

- Linzagolix was also cost-effective versus surgery, with an incremental cost of £421 and an incremental QALY of 0.61, resulting in an ICER of £693 

- Linzagolix remained cost-effective across sensitivity analyses performed, including deterministic, probabilistic and scenario analyses

## _**B.3.1 Published cost-effectiveness studies**_ 

## **B.3.1.1 Summary of characteristics and results of the included costeffectiveness evidence** 

Systematic database searches for this review were conducted on 11 July, 2024. Details are presented in Appendix G. 

The cost-effectiveness review identified 3,583 records, of which 16 were included in the systematic review. Nine studies were conference abstracts, and the remaining seven full articles were accessed. However, two studies were irrelevant to the technology evaluation, and only five were discussed in detail. Table 33 presents a summary and outcomes of the seven full-text studies; noting that the first five studies were most relevant. The last two studies – Wu et.al (2018[84] ) and Sanghera et.al (2016[85] ) were of secondary interest as they focused on time to recurrence after treatment. Table 34 includes nine conference abstracts, where analyses of surgical treatment were of use due to the model construction (health states, transitions, health effects). 

Among the 16 identified studies, there were two cost-utility studies, four costminimisation studies and ten cost-effectiveness studies. They analysed various treatment options for endometriosis such as: dienogest, (combined) oral contraceptives, goserelin, elagolix, leuprolide acetate, NSAIDs, short-acting reversible contraception (SARC) or long-acting reversible contraception (LARC). 

Seven studies employed a simple Markov model; in four studies a decision tree was developed. In five studies, no specific model employed was clearly stated. Time horizons varied between 1 year in one of the basic scenarios in Wang et al. (2019[86] ), Marmarali et al. (2012[87] ), Ferracini et al. (2013[88] ) and Choi et al. (2011[89] ) and 18 years in cases of Wu et al. (2017[84] ) and Grand et al. (2019). Cycle lengths were of 1 month in Wu et al. (2017[84] ), Grand et al. (2019[90] ) and Sanghera et al. (2016[85] ) and of 3 months in Wang et al. (2019[86] ). Inputs were based on sources such as published literature, key opinion leader elicitations, and author’s assumptions. Because of limited data availability and lack of evidence in several areas, authors broadly discussed uncertainties surrounding the results provided by their analyses.

## **B.3.2.1 Patient population**

## **B.3.2.2 Model structure** 

The model simulates a cohort of premenopausal women diagnosed with symptomatic endometriosis who are eligible for treatment with linzagolix 200 plus ABT, over time. It encompasses 17[*] distinct health states that reflect the varied responses to both medical therapies and surgical interventions. This framework enables a comparative analysis of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT against alternative treatment options currently available in the NHS, evaluated from a healthcare perspective over a 16-year time horizon extending until the average age of menopause, established at 50 years in the UK. The costeffectiveness analysis utilises a semi-Markov cohort model, particularly suited for capturing the complexities of endometriosis management (see section B.1.3.3). This structure aligns with the clinical pathways experienced by patients, enhancing its 

> * Including one tunnel state with three sub-states. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 119 -->

applicability and relevance in real-world contexts. Markov chain models (MCMs) are effective for health conditions characterised by ongoing risks and recurrent health events, such as endometriosis. In this model, patients transition between defined states, each associated with specific health utilities and costs. This approach is appropriate for endometriosis due to the extended time horizon required to assess treatment impacts on outcomes and costs, as well as the complexity of interrelated health states that must be represented to accurately reflect the management of symptomatic endometriosis. 

To capture clinically and economically significant aspects of managing symptomatic endometriosis, the model is divided into two main components. The first component employs a decision tree, wherein health states are determined by treatment response, defined as a meaningful reduction in pain levels. This segment consists of two, threemonth cycles, culminating in a six-month period during which the decision to continue treatment is made. The three-month cycle aligns with the EDELWEISS 3 primary endpoints, which include a clinically meaningful reduction of dysmenorrhoea and NMPP to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3. The six-month period is consistent with clinical practice, where specialist consultations for treatment continuation typically occur biannually and allowed flexibility to build the tunnel-state pregnancy. Additionally, the Markov transitions during initial treatment at month 6 were based on EDELWEISS 6 data. Due to the relatively long cycle length, a half-cycle correction has been applied. 

The second component focuses on health states contingent upon the level of pain experienced by the patient. The model structure is based on reviews of the study designs for EDELWEISS 3, as well as prior economic models for the treatment of symptomatic endometriosis identified through a targeted literature review [section B.3.1 and Appendix G] and established clinical practice guidelines.[19,36] Additionally, the model structure and patient pathway have undergone validation by clinical experts.[9,100] The various conditions or stages through which the model can transition over time are presented in Table 36.

<!-- page 122 -->

The initial two cycles of the model last three months each. During this time, patients are categorised into one of three health-states based on their treatment responses (treatment response definitions are described in section B.3.3): 

- **No response** : in this state, patients show no improvement, with pain levels remaining unchanged from the baseline 

- **Partial response** : in this state, patients experience a reduction in pain, particularly in NMPP or dysmenorrhoea, indicating a partial therapeutic effect 

- **Complete response** : in this state, patients exhibit a dual response, with significant reductions in both NMPP and dysmenorrhoea, reflecting an optimal treatment outcome 

Following the two initial cycles, a new phase in the model starts (Markov model), where treatment cycles extend to six months. Patients responding to the treatment (Complete Response and Partial Response) are categorised into three pain-related health states based on OPP: **No pain/mild** , **Moderate** , or **Severe**[†] **.** Patients can transition between pain states until they transition into the Severe state (dependent on treatment waning assumption applied), until the maximal duration of therapy is reached (in the case of GnRH agonists) or until moving to the **Pregnancy** tunnel state. 

- Patients entering the Severe pain state are transitioned to **Other Medical Treatment** or **Laparoscopy #1 Waiting** . 

- When the maximum therapy time is reached, patients remaining in No pain/mild are transitioned to **Off-treatment no pain/mild,** and those remaining in the Moderate pain state transition to Other Medical Treatment or Laparoscopy #1 Waiting. 

- Patients can enter the Pregnancy state from No pain/mild pain state (fixed probability per model cycle). 

> † No patient responding to the treatment according to the EDELWEISS 3 study criteria qualified to Severe state. However to remain the completeness of the model and remain its flexibility this state was included in the model structure. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 123 -->

After each of the two three-month cycles of initial treatment, patients who do not respond to treatment (No Response) are transitioned to subsequent treatment options, which may include the Other Medical Treatment health state or the Laparoscopy #1 Waiting health state. Patients remain in the Laparoscopy #1 Waiting state for one cycle of the model (six months[‡] ) before progressing to the **Laparoscopy #1** state. 

If symptoms recur whilst in the Other Medical Treatment state, patients transition to the Laparoscopy #1 Waiting state and subsequently to the Laparoscopy #1 state. Laparoscopy #1 is a temporary state, and patients remain in it for one cycle of the model. This pathway assumes timely surgical intervention for patients experiencing symptom resurgence. 

After conservative surgery is performed in Laparoscopy #1, patients enter a postoperative care phase in the **Post-Laparoscopy #1** state, aimed at maintaining the benefits of the surgical procedure. From this state, they may proceed to another surgical intervention, either conservative surgery **Laparoscopy #2** or a radical procedure - 

**Radical surgery #1** . Notably, patients who experience a recurrence of symptoms within three months of their initial surgery bypass the Post-Laparoscopy #1 state and move directly to the second surgical procedure. Following Laparoscopy #2, patients may enter the **Post-Laparoscopy #2** state, analogous to the Post-Laparoscopy #1 state, or proceed to a radical surgical intervention, specifically Radical surgery #1. After this intervention, patients transition to the **Post-Radical surgery** state. Alternatively, if they still have disease symptoms, they undergo a second radical surgery, **Radical surgery #2** . Post Radical surgery #2 they will also transition to the Post-Radical surgery state (for a description of the treatment applied in this health-state see section B.3.5.7). 

Similar to Laparoscopy #1, the states Laparoscopy #2, Radical surgery #1, and Radical surgery #2 are temporary. Patients remain in these states for one model cycle, subsequently transitioning either to the next surgical intervention state or post-surgical intervention state. 

> ‡ Based on EMRS 2024 the average waiting time is around 18 months, however it was conservatively assumed this period would last only 6 months, which is equal to one model cycle in order to simplify already complex model. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 124 -->

Patients can only enter the Pregnancy state from the No pain/mild pain state (fixed probability per model cycle). Pregnancy is a tunnel state with three sub-states, each with one cycle duration. It was assumed that 18 months would be the minimum time for conception, pregnancy and breastfeeding. After three cycles (18 months) spent in this health state, patients move back to the No pain/mild pain state (with active initial treatment) or to the Off-treatment, no pain/mild state if the maximal therapy time of the initial treatment has been reached. 

It is important to note that patients may transition to the "Dead" state from any health state within the model and the same mortality rate is applied across all states. 

The analysis was performed from an NHS perspective, adhering to the existing NICE guidelines. Consequently, the base-case analysis considers all expenses associated with the healthcare sector. Both costs and outcomes are discounted at an annual rate of 3.5%, consistent with the NICE reference case.

**B.3.2.3.1 Modified surgery model – differences vs base model for medical therapies** Laparoscopic surgery is an additional comparator included in the analysis, at the request of NICE and the EAG, expressed during the decision problem meeting for linzagolix. Compared with medical therapy, there are differences in the expected course of disease after surgery is performed. Surgery is a one-time event, after which a patient can either be a responder or a non-responder. Patients who respond remain in such a state until the recurrence of symptoms. This is a major difference compared to medical therapy, where a patient’s level of response can be maintained or change over time as they receive ongoing treatment. To reflect these differences some changes were incorporated into the model structure for this comparator. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 126 -->

Based on UK clinical expert opinion, it is assumed that a patient waits an average of 18 months for surgical treatment on the NHS.[19,100] This is reflected in the model where patients spend four cycles (two 3-month-cycles and two 6-month-cycles) in the Laparoscopy #1 waiting state before surgery is performed. Once surgery is performed, the patient is categorised as a responder (successful surgery) or a non-responder (unsuccessful surgery). 

Patients responding to the treatment are subsequently categorised into three painrelated health states as in the base model (i.e., model for medical therapies), however the patient cannot transition between the three pain cycles (i.e., transitions based on data for medical therapies where patients can get better or worse). In the surgery model, the transition to a subsequent treatment is due to symptom recurrence (based on the literature), whereas for medical therapies, it is based on treatment discontinuation or waning assumptions. 

In the surgery model, a non-responder or patient with symptom recurrence transitions to the next treatment, following the same subsequent model structure as a patient on medical therapy who experiences severe symptoms. 

The part of the surgery model that is different to the base model is visualised in Figure 17. This replaces the initial decision tree part of the model that is used for medical therapies.

## **B.3.2.4 Intervention and comparators** 

The intervention evaluated in the model is linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, administered orally once daily. Linzagolix 200 mg is designed to address endometriosis symptoms, through the reduction of EAP, while the addition of ABT preserves BMD. As a result, this regimen can be used continuously without a predefined treatment duration, except for cessation at the onset of menopause. 

The comparators in the model are: 

1. GnRH agonists; with the licensed agents in the UK of leuprorelin acetate, goserelin, and triptorelin. All are administered via intramuscular or subcutaneous injection, available in both monthly and three-monthly formulations. All GnRH agonists were assumed to have equal efficacy and safety [see section B.2.9.7] 

2. Laparoscopic surgery (see the description at the end of this section for more details) 

To inform the model assumptions, the Endometriosis Market Research Survey (2024) and Expert Elicitation Reports (August and October 2024) were conducted among UKbased healthcare professionals to gather input on the use of GnRH agonists for managing endometriosis symptoms.[9,19,100] 

The Expert Elicitation Reports (2024) indicated considerable variability in prescribing practices, with no clear consensus on the most frequently used agent. Intranasal GnRH agonists (nafarelin and buserelin) were rarely prescribed, with all surveyed clinical experts reporting a preference for intramuscular or subcutaneous formulations.[9,100] Consequently, only leuprorelin acetate, goserelin, and triptorelin were considered comparators in the model, while intranasal formulations were excluded due to their limited clinical use. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 128 -->

In the base case analysis, leuprorelin acetate was selected as the GnRH agonist due to the assumption that all GnRH agonists have equivalent efficacy in this population. This approach is aligned to the submission for relugolix CT in this indication.[51] The GnRH agonists have the same mechanism of action, specifically aimed at downregulating pituitary GnRH receptors. Evidence indicates that all GnRH agonists effectively inhibit endometriosis through this shared mechanism.[101] In ESHRE recommendations, GnRH agonists are listed among the recommended hormonal treatments to reduce EAP pain, with no preference for specific agonists.[36] Furthermore, a Cochrane systematic review collectively reported for the entire group of GnRH agonists, and conclusions were derived without differentiating between specific pharmacological agents.[102] Leuprorelin acetate was chosen as the base case comparator due to having the largest UK market share, according to clinical experts.[100] Goserelin and triptorelin, also commonly used in clinical practice, were evaluated in scenario analyses. 

Based on input from UK gynaecologists, the model assumes that all patients treated with GnRH agonists receive ABT, initiated upon starting treatment.[19,100] No differences are noted between the efficacy of GnRH agonists with or without ABT. A meta-analysis evaluating pain outcomes, including relief of dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and NMPP, indicated that results were comparable across both treatment groups, irrespective of the ABT use.[102] Furthermore, no statistically significant differences were observed in most safety outcomes, except side effects of prolonged hypoestrogenism, such as climacteric symptoms (hot flashes, sweating, and vaginal dryness) and bone loss. Side effects of prolonged hypoestrogenism are expected for GnRH agonist treatment without ABT.[102] 

ESHRE treatment guidelines recommend limiting the use of GnRH agonists to 12 months when combined with ABT, emphasising the limited evidence for extended use, particularly in adolescents where there are concerns about long-term consequences.[36] To align with clinical expert opinion, the treatment duration of leuprorelin acetate in the model was extended to 18 months.[19] NICE and EAG feedback during the relugolix CT single technology appraisal also indicated that the treatment duration with GnRH agonists should align with clinical practice and extend beyond one year.[103] Clinical experts also highlighted that problems with adherence to long-term treatment with GnRH 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 129 -->

agonists are related to the inconvenient route of administration for patients and can lead to discontinuation. Overall, they concluded that it was very unlikely that treatment would be continued for more than 24–36 months. In scenario analyses, a six-month treatment duration with leuprorelin acetate in line with the standard clinical indication, was also evaluated. 

The treatment duration for linzagolix is consistent with the model used for the relugolix CT STA, where it is assumed that GnRH antagonists can be administered continuously until menopause, reflecting their long-term use in managing endometriosis symptoms.[51] 

Laparoscopic surgery was included as an additional comparator only, as it is more likely to be used as a complementary treatment to pharmacotherapy.[9] According to clinical experts, whether or not surgery could be considered a direct comparator to medical therapies is dependent on the type of endometriosis. As GnRH agonists are already available and widely used in patients with endometriosis, it is assumed that the decision to prescribe linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT would primarily be in situations where gynaecologists are currently prescribing GnRH agonists. Due to the wide variety of surgery types, laparoscopic excision and ablation were chosen to be the most representative surgeries as they are used most frequently in the relevant treatment setting.[19,36] 

## _**B.3.3 Clinical parameters and variables**_ 

The principal source of data used to inform the effectiveness of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is EDELWEISS 3, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 study conducted in women of reproductive age with moderate to severe EAP (B.2.6). 

Clinical input encompasses the entire treatment pathway within the model, including key parameters such as treatment efficacy, probabilities of various events occurring, and decisions related to disease management. This includes patient withdrawal from treatment, selection of surgical interventions, instances of repeat surgeries and the scheduling of treatment regimens, all of which are essential for accurately simulating clinical outcomes. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 130 -->

## **B.3.3.1 Treatment response** 

Two sets of health states are used in the model to address patient response to treatment. The first set, applied during the initial decision tree, includes three possible response states: no response, partial response and complete response. The second set, based on EAP levels, is used after the first six months of treatment and consists of three OPP states (no pain/mild, moderate, and severe). Both sets are derived from patient responses to treatment and individual patient-level data from EDELWEISS 3. 

## **B.3.3.2 Treatment response in the initial decision tree** 

The definition of treatment response in the model is fixed and based on the co-primary endpoints from EDELWEISS 3. This includes a clinically meaningful reduction in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

The model allows for the selection of three different definitions of partial response: 

1. **Dysmenorrhoea-based definition:** A clinically meaningful reduction in dysmenorrhoea (i.e., a reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

2. **NMPP-based definition:** A clinically meaningful reduction in NMPP (i.e., a reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

3. **Dysmenorrhoea- or NMPP-based definition:** A clinically meaningful reduction in either dysmenorrhoea (as above) or NMPP (as above) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

Patients with no response at the month 3 switch to a different treatment, while those with partial response may either lose their response, maintain a partial response or achieve a complete response (by month 6). A decision to continue treatment is made after the

## **B.3.3.5 Treatment discontinuation** 

During each model cycle in which patients receive either the intervention or the comparator, there is a probability that they will discontinue treatment. In the model, treatment discontinuation is interpreted as a loss of efficacy (i.e., patients shifting into the severe health-state, OPP >2.0 on the VRS), intolerability to treatment, a break in the state of no pain/mild symptoms, or due to pregnancy and breastfeeding. The discontinuation rates for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT were derived from different sources, depending on the cause and timing of discontinuation. The rate of patients who discontinue due to loss of efficacy was estimated based on EDELWEISS 3 and 6. The percentage of women discontinuing treatment due to pregnancy was estimated from the live birth rate in the UK.[104] 

In the EDELWEISS 3 and 6 studies, discontinuation was primarily attributed to factors such as COVID-19, political reasons, or the withdrawal of patient consent from the study. Such instances of discontinuation, which were clearly unrelated to the medical intervention, were excluded from the analysis. Following the exclusion of these cases, discontinuation rates were assessed at three and six months of treatment using individual patient-level data, and the resulting discontinuation coefficients were determined and are presented in Table 46.

## **B.3.3.6 Clinical parameters for additional comparator: laparoscopic surgery** 

Response rate for laparoscopic surgery and pain recurrence following surgery were established with studies found in the SLR described in Appendix M. 

Response rate for laparoscopic surgery was set to 50% based on Johnson et al. 2004.[70] The response definition provided in this study (at least 50% reduction of pain on the VAS) was considered most consistent with the response definition applied for the pharmacological treatments. As different definitions of pain response and timepoints were available in this study, conservatively (in favour of surgery vs linzagolix), the highest response rate was selected. The response rate for surgical treatment was validated with clinical expert opinion.[19,100] The split between complete and partial responders was assumed similar to the one adopted for pharmacological treatments. 

Pain recurrence following surgery was established based on the KM curve for the recurrence of moderate to severe pain based on the Vercellini et al. 2003 (Figure 18).[105]

## **B.3.3.7 Adverse events and surgical complications** 

Adverse events (AEs) were incorporated into the cost-effectiveness model within the scenario analysis, based on the absence of significant (grade 3 or 4) adverse events, such as depression, headache, hot flushes or increased blood pressure in the EDELWEISS 3 study. These events, along with surgical complications and their influence on HRQoL, are detailed in Section B.3.4; data informing their impact on HRQoL and their frequency were sourced from the literature. 

## **B.3.4 Measurement and valuation of health effects** 

Health effects in the cost-effectiveness model were based on evidence collected in a clinical trial and systematically sourced from the literature (see Appendix H), in line with the NICE hierarchy of preferred HRQoL evidence.[107] The methods for measurement and valuation of health effects are described in the following subsections, outlining how HRQoL data were collected, processed and incorporated into the model. These subsections provide a detailed overview of both trial-based and literature-sourced data integration. 

## **B.3.4.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

In EDELWEISS 3 and 6, two instruments were used to collect HRQoL data: the diseasespecific EHP-30 and the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire.[58,62] However, only EQ-5D data were utilised in the model due to their consistency with the NICE reference case and suitability for cost-effectiveness analysis. 

The EQ-5D is a self-administered, generic utility instrument developed by the EuroQoL Group in 1990. The EQ-5D consists of 2 parts: a descriptive system of 5 dimensions and a 20-cm vertical VAS with endpoints 0 and 100. It was collected by the subjects in the EDELWEISS 3 study at day 1, month 1, month 3 and month 6. The descriptive system includes five single-item dimensions: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression. Subjects choose between five levels of difficulty (from 1 to 5) in accomplishing tasks in each dimension. The health states were described in as five-digit numbers based on the answers to each of the five questions. The states were then 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 143 -->

converted into a single index score using the Time Trade-Off method. An index score based on the individual dimensions was calculated using a scoring algorithm and the US Index from Crosswalk value set downloaded from the EuroQoL website.[108] 

Baseline mean EQ-5D-5L index resulting from EDELWEISS 3 was similar across treatment groups (Section B.2.6.2.4). During treatment, substantial improvements in the EQ-5D-5L index value versus placebo were observed at month 6 in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, as indicated by 95% CIs in Table 17. 

Since the cost-effectiveness model utilised HRQoL from EDELWEISS 3 rather than EDELWEISS 6 (due to the possible attrition bias), the values obtained from the latter study have not been detailed in this description. 

**B.3.4.1.1 Clinical trial based HRQoL regression models** The EQ-5D-5L five-digit health states were sourced from individual patient data from EDELWEISS 3 and mapped using the NICE DSU mapping function according to the ‐ algorithm presented in Hernández Alava and Pudney et al. (2017).[109] The mapping algorithm facilitates the conversion of EQ-5D-5L health states into EQ-5D-3L utility scores through a joint statistical model that employs a multi-equation ordinal regression framework. This approach utilises EQ-5D-5L dimension data alongside demographic factors such as age and gender. Utilities were then derived using the UK value set. 

For the base analysis, the mapped values were used to develop two separate regression models: response model and pain model aimed to estimate the HRQoL for patients with endometriosis in different pain-related health states as specified in the cost-effectiveness model (No response, Partial response, Complete response—defined by dysmenorrhea and NMPP reduction and No pain/mild, Moderate, Severe – based on overall pelvic pain measured on the VRS scale as described in section B.3.2). 

Additionally, to enhance the accuracy of the regression model, a comprehensive grey literature search was conducted alongside references identified in a SLR. This approach aimed to identify quality of life predictors relevant to the patient population to build the adjusted regression model. The predictors identified through this search, which matched 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved.

For this purpose, multiple binary variables were created with groups defined by the median value. Variables found to be statistically significant (p-value ≤ 0.05), were then incorporated into the linear mixed-effects regression model. Linear mixed-effects regression models were utilised if more than one measurement was available (baseline, month 3, month 6). ## **B.3.4.1.2 Response-based regression model for utility values** 

In the regression model developed to assess the HRQoL of patients in EDELWEISS 3, the same response criteria used for the co-primary endpoints of EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 were applied (see section B.2.6). 

- Complete response was defined as a patient meeting the response criteria for both dysmenorrhoea and NMPP endpoints, indicating a comprehensive improvement in pain management and overall well-being 

- Partial response was characterised by a patient achieving a response in either dysmenorrhoea or NMPP but not both, potentially reflecting a more limited benefit from the treatment 

- Non-responders were those who did not meet the criteria for any of the endpoints, indicating a lack of therapeutic effect. 

Table 51 summarises EQ-5D-3L data from all the treatment arms in the EDELWEISS 3 study in the context of the patient’s response. 

Baseline observations were excluded from the response regression model. However, baseline utility values were incorporated into the cost-effectiveness model, assigned to patients at the model's initial stage (1[st] model cycle). The regression model predicting health states related to treatment response utilised data from the 3- and 6-month assessments of EDELWEISS 3. This is because patients in the no-response health state showed higher utility values at the 3-month mark compared with baseline (Table 51), suggesting some improvement in overall health and a reduction in EAP despite the lack of a response. Since utility values in the cost-effectiveness model apply to health states after the first three-month treatment cycle, it was important to account for this observed improvement and exclude baseline data from the regression model. This approach ensured that the model accurately reflects patient-reported outcomes while appropriately utilising baseline utility values at the initial stage of the analysis.

## _**B.3.4.1.3**_ **Pain-based regression model for utility values** 

The levels of pain associated with dysmenorrhoea and NMPP significantly impact the quality of life of patients suffering from endometriosis. To capture both types of pain, a single outcome of OPP was employed in the second HRQoL analysis.[9,100] In EDELWEISS 3, pain was measured on VRS (dysmenorrhoea and NMPP) and NRS (OPP) scales using an electronic diary (eDiary). Given the profound influence of pain on quality of life, the decision was made to develop a regression model that incorporates pain severity in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP combined into OPP as key predictors of HRQoL. By linking pain to HRQoL metrics the model aims to elucidate the relationship between pain experiences and overall patient outcomes. 

The regression model for health states defined by pain intensity represented as a single OPP value in the VRS scale was constructed similarly to the regression model based on response categories. Pain intensity was categorised into three distinct levels based on OPP: no pain/mild, moderate pain and severe pain (see section B.3.3.3 for criteria definitions). Initially, two models were developed based on different patient populations. The first model was constructed exclusively from the dataset comprising only partial and complete responders at the six-month follow-up. The justification for this was that only patients demonstrating partial or complete response continue treatment within the costeffectiveness framework. As a result, these patients were categorised according to health states associated with pain, to which utilities derived from this model were assigned. However, the decision to consider only month six observations of responders (either partially or completely) was ultimately reconsidered, because only one patient was available for the severe pain state, rendering the estimate highly unreliable. Consequently, the second model was developed using the 6-month observations of all patients and employed in the base analysis. 

All variables in the base case model are statistically significant (p-value ≤0.05). Specifically, Moderate and No/mild pain states are associated with an average increase in HRQoL of 0.264 and 0.399, respectively, when compared to the severe pain state. Since the optimal pain model included only pain levels, there was no necessity to adjust the results for other predictors. The utility values derived from the pain-based model for the health states of No pain/mild, Moderate, and Severe are presented in Table 56.

## **B.3.4.3 Health-related quality-of-life studies** 

Utility data were obtained from published studies identified through an SLR conducted in July 2024 (see Section B.2.1) and EDELWEISS 3. For the base case scenario, utility values were primarily derived from EDELWEISS 3, except for disutility values associated with infertility and surgical complications, which were sourced from the existing literature. Detailed methodologies and an overview of the studies and results are provided in Section B.2.1 and Appendix H. 

## **B.3.4.3.1 Health states utility values from the literature** 

The SLR identified 11 studies potentially relevant to the decision problem. Upon further evaluation, two studies were of special interest based on the model population and structure (they included health states with similar definitions to the model). 

Aubry et al., 2017 reported EQ-5D scores for a cohort of patients experiencing symptoms not captured by the clinical trial data, specifically focusing on infertility.[110] The utility values derived from this study informed the disutility associated with the posthysterectomy/bilateral oophorectomy health state within the model. A discrepancy was noticed regarding the utility decrement reported for patients with infertility in this study, and the authors were contacted to clarify. However, no response was received by the date of submission. The utility value reported for patients with infertility was higher than the utility value reported for patients without infertility – these numbers were swapped for the analysis. Due to this uncertainty, results from this study were included in scenario analysis only. 

Kent et al., 2016[111] provided utility values for patients with severe endometriosis undergoing various treatments, including GnRH agonists, laparoscopy, and conservative surgery/pelvic clearance. Data extracted from this study were employed in the scenario analysis to inform utility values for the following health states: laparoscopy (#1 and #2), post-laparoscopy (#1 and #2), hysterectomy/bilateral oophorectomy (#1 and #2), and post-hysterectomy/bilateral oophorectomy.

## **B.3.4.5 Health-related quality-of-life data used in the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

HRQoL data have been systematically categorised into two primary groups corresponding to distinct health states within the model. The first group is related to the initial decision tree and includes the initial patient response to treatment and subsequent intensity of NMPP and dysmenorrhea (collectively defined as OPP). 

The second group includes health states related to various interventions, such as other medical treatment, waiting for laparoscopic surgery, the surgical procedures themselves (Laparoscopy #1 and #2), post-laparoscopic care (Post-laparoscopy #1 and #2), Radical surgery (#1 and #2), and subsequent post-surgical treatment. Additionally, this group incorporates the off-treatment state, which reflects the quality of life experienced by patients following the cessation of treatment. 

## **B.3.4.5.1 Pain-related health-states utility values** 

The utility values assigned to pain-related health states (no response, partial response, complete response, no pain/mild, moderate-, and severe- pain) were derived from the proportion of patients occupying each health state during each cycle of the model. These utility values were informed by a regression model developed from individual patient-level data collected in EDELWEISS 3 (see section B.3.4). In the model base case, no disutilities (infertility, AEs) were applied to these health states, as it was assumed that they were already captured within EDELWEISS 3 EQ-5D data measurements. Additionally, no infertility disutilities were assumed during linzagolix treatment (and conservatively, any other medical therapy) as the half-life of linzagolix is approximately 15 hours and ovarian activity may recover within days of treatment cessation.[46] As indicated by clinical expert opinion, patients wanting to conceive can stop medical therapy at any time, therefore no infertility disutility would apply whilst on therapy.[9] 

The regression model’s foundation on individual patient data collected directly from the clinical trial and its subsequent mapping to the EQ-5D-3L instrument lend credibility to the derived utility values. Consequently, these values accurately represent the realworld quality of life experienced by patients undergoing treatment for EAP. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 161 -->

## **B.3.4.5.2 Other health-states utility values** 

The HRQoL for additional health states within the model was developed by leveraging the utility values associated with pain-related states, utilising the regression model from EDELWEISS 3 data. To effectively capture quality-of-life implications for patients undergoing specific medical interventions, the following algorithm was employed: 

1. Health states to which patients transition from the No pain/mild health state (including off-treatment, no pain/mild, off-treatment during the washing period, and the initial stages of conception) were assigned the HRQoL values corresponding to the No pain/mild state as it is assumed that they experience the same level of pain. The assumption regarding the maintenance of treatment effects is derived from EDELWEISS 6. 

2. For health states associated with other medical treatments, including patients categorised as No response, No pain/mild, Moderate, and Severe: the mean HRQoL value of these states was assigned in line with the algorithm presented in Wang et al., 2019.[86] The HRQoL for the waiting period for laparoscopy was calculated similarly, excluding the No pain/mild state from the average, as patients with No/mild pain typically do not require surgical intervention. As these patients were already heavily pretreated (with surgery and a multitude of pharmacological therapies, including GnRH analogues), the approach was deemed to be conservative. Most patients are assumed to continue sub-optimal therapy whilst waiting for the next surgical treatment. 

3. For Laparoscopy #1 and #2, weighted averages were computed, incorporating the utility loss associated with undergoing surgery (177 days) and a designated period (3 days) during which utility was set to zero, due to the invasive nature of surgery. A similar methodology was applied to the radical surgery (#1 and #2) states, with an extension to the ‘zero’ period (7 days). Number of days with zero utility was based on assumptions in Wang et al. 2019.[86] Disutilities for complications were applied only to the proportion of patients experiencing respective complications 

4. Utilities for post-laparoscopy health states (#1 and #2) were derived from the HRQoL values assigned to other medical treatments and the off-treatment state. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 162 -->

This allocation was proportionately based on the transitions of patients from these states to the post-laparoscopy state (see section B.3.3.4). 

5. The HRQoL for post-radical surgery was assumed to align with the No pain/mild health state, with an additional infertility-related disutility applied only to the proportion of patients who wish to preserve fertility.[19,100] The value estimated for this health-state is higher than Post-laparoscopy #1 and #2, which is in line with the literature.[111] This could be because most patients are assumed to be cured from endometriosis symptoms after radical surgery (especially after bilateral oophorectomy), whereas some patients would still experience EAP after laparoscopic surgery. 

This comprehensive approach to defining HRQoL across various health states reflects the complexities of patient experiences and outcomes associated with endometriosis treatment. The summary of utility values for the cost-effectiveness analysis can be found in Table 64. 

A conservative approach was taken for some of the utility assumptions related to surgical procedures. It was assumed that the HRQoL of patients during and after successive conservative surgeries remained the same (Laparoscopy #1 HRQoL is equal to Laparoscopy #2 HRQoL; Post-laparoscopy #1 HRQoL is equal to Post-laparoscopy #2 HRQoL). According to clinical experts, subsequent surgical procedures tend to be more invasive, leading to more complications.[100] Additionally, patients waiting for surgery were associated with a higher HRQoL than those entering the model. It was assumed that some patients receive pharmacological treatment to manage symptoms during this period.

## _**B.3.5 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation**_ 

A cost and resources SLR was conducted to identify any relevant cost or healthcare resource use data relevant to the model. Full details of the SLR and results are presented in Appendix I. 

The model includes several cost categories to reflect the key cost components related to drug therapies, surgical procedures, disease management, the natural course of pregnancy, and management of fertility issues in patients with endometriosis. 

## **B.3.5.1 Intervention and comparators’ costs and resource use** 

## **B.3.5.2 Drug acquisition costs** 

The costs of medical therapy (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and GnRH agonists) were applied in model cycles relating to patients on treatment i.e., within a decision tree in the initial response states and whilst in No pain/mild or Moderate pain states thereafter. The duration of therapy for the intervention and comparator was assumed to be fixed (1.5 years for GnRH agonists) or without restriction (linzagolix). Drug acquisition costs were not applied for treatment breaks (in the Off-treatment, No pain/mild and Pregnancy health-states). 

A 50:50 split was assumed between patients treated with the short- (1-month) and long(3-month) acting GnRH agonists - leuprorelin acetate, goserelin and triptorelin. This assumption was based on the equivalent parameter in the NICE STA for relugolix and indicated by expert opinion.[51,100] 

No wastage or compliance was considered in the base case analysis. However, compliance for linzagolix and ABT was used in the scenario analysis, based on data from the EDELWEISS 6 study and relugolix CT long-term study.[61,118] 

The calculation of drug costs is shown in Table 65.

## **B.3.5.3 Add-back therapy** 

Market research and expert opinion indicate that the majority of patients treated with GnRH agonists use ABT, which is prescribed upon initiating treatment with the GnRH agonist.[19,100] Therefore, ABT was included for all patients on GnRH agonists and linzagolix 200 mg for the entire treatment duration. ## **B.3.5.7 Health-state unit costs and resource use** 

Ongoing management and resource use (e.g., visits to healthcare professionals or performance of certain tests) are required to monitor patients undergoing medical therapy, follow up patients during treatment breaks, and undergo medical procedures. 

At therapy initiation and evaluation of response, it was assumed that patients would need one visit to the gynaecologist per event. Patients continuing initial therapy after response assessment were subject to regular monitoring by a nurse at a frequency of 4 visits per year. Long-term management of therapy was based on the NICE STA for relugolix.[51] 

Additionally, it was assumed that patients on a treatment break with No/mild pain would still require monitoring by a nurse. However, the frequency was reduced to one visit per year. It was assumed that patients on an Off-treatment break in the first pregnancy state (Pregnancy #1) would require a visit to the gynaecologist or fertility specialist; 0.67 gynaecologist visits and 0.33 fertility specialist visits per year, were included respectively based on clinical expert opinion.[100] 

All patients switching to another therapy (i.e., entering the next line of treatment) required one consultation, which was included as the cost of a gynaecologist visit.[100] 

For the Other medical treatment health-state, monitoring by a nurse was applied at the same frequency as initial therapy (i.e., four visits per year). Additionally, it was assumed that the proportion of patients who would be treated pharmacologically whilst waiting for (50%), during (57%) and after (100%) laparoscopic surgery, would require the same monitoring frequency, i.e. 1.99, 2.28 and four visits per year for the respective healthstates.[19,100] 

It was assumed that ultrasound and MRI would be performed before surgery (conservative or radical) and ultrasound would be performed once per year after 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved.

## _**B.3.6 Severity**_ 

In assessing the proportional and absolute QALY shortfall, it is not anticipated that the treatment of linzagolix 200mg plus ABT for endometriosis will be applicable for any form of severity weighting. 

## _**B.3.7 Uncertainty**_ 

The EDELWEISS studies provide robust clinical evidence for the benefit of linzagolix 200mg plus ABT in the treatment of symptomatic endometriosis. However, due to the range of surgical interventions, evolving surgical techniques, difficulty assessing surgery via an RCT, and inconsistency of outcomes assessed for surgery (see Appendix M), there is a lack of high-quality evidence for surgical interventions and consequently, it is challenging to compare medical therapy (i.e., linzagolix plus ABT) to surgery.

Not applicable.

## **B.3.10.1 Base-case incremental cost-effectiveness analysis results**

## _**B.3.11 Exploring uncertainty**_ 

A range of sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore the underlying uncertainty in the base-case cost-effectiveness results. These include deterministic sensitivity analyses, probabilistic sensitivity analyses, and scenario analyses. The results for net marginal benefit are presented only for the base-case scenario, but are available within the cost-effectiveness model. For comparison with laparoscopic surgery, no probabilistic or deterministic cost effectiveness analyses were conducted as this is additional comparator only, however, two alternative scenarios on surgery efficacy were performed. 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 182 -->

**B.3.11.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** A probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to explore the uncertainty around key model parameters. PSA was conducted by varying these parameters using their upper and lower bound values based on an assigned distribution. 1,000 simulations were run for the PSA, by which time the ICERs had converged to a stable mean, represented by the probabilistic ICERs. The probabilistic ICER vs leuprorelin (£5,810) lies closely to the base-case ICER (£5,554) indicating that the cost-effectiveness results are robust (See Table 85 and Table 86). 

Output from the PSA iterations is presented as scatter points on the cost-effectiveness plane in Figure 19 for linzagolix vs. leuprorelin. All scatter points, which represent the simulated incremental costs and QALYs, are in the northeast quadrant for linzagolix vs. leuprorelin. This indicates that linzagolix plus ABT is associated with both higher costs and QALYs compared to leuprorelin, that is, linzagolix plus ABT is both more effective and more costly. 

The PSA results were also plotted in the form of a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC), as shown in Abbreviations: ABT, add-back therapy; PSA, probabilistic sensitivity analysis; QALYs, quality-adjusted life years 

Figure 20 for linzagolix vs. leuprorelin. The CEAC shows the probability of cost effectiveness for linzagolix vs. leuprorelin given varying willingness to pay thresholds for a QALY. According to the CEAC, the probability of linzagolix vs. leuprorelin being costeffective is 63% at a willingness to pay of £5,000/QALY. The probability is close to 100% at £10,000/QALY.

## **B.3.11.3 Scenario analysis** 

The sensitivity of the model results to changes in key assumptions or parameters was explored through several scenario analyses. The scenario analyses results are presented below, with pairwise ICERs presented (Table 87). The most impactful scenarios are related to the time horizon parameters: different time horizons, or alternative starting or maximum age of patients with the disease. Other significant scenarios included an alternative probability algorithm for health state transitions, alternative rules for continuing initial treatment (i.e., minimum health benefit required to continue therapy), assumptions applied to the Pregnancy health-state, and infertility disutility and utility values utilised in surgery-related health-states (e.g. Laparoscopy #1, Post-laparoscopy #1, Radical surgery #2 etc.).

Two alternative scenarios were tested in the comparison of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT with laparoscopic surgery. These scenarios used alternative values for the response rate to surgical treatment and the recurrence rate following successful surgery. These values were explored in the scenario analyses because they were both sourced from the literature in the base case analysis, whereas values informing the efficacy of GnRH analogues were sourced from the EDELWEISS trials and the ITC. 

To assess the robustness of this assumption, more conservative values (i.e., less favourable for linzagolix plus ABT vs surgery) were tested in the scenario analysis. The response rate presented in Sutton et al. 1994[71] was used because the definition of response was less strict (any pain improvement on VAS scale, 0-10) compared to the response rate for pharmacological therapies (see section B.3.3.2). Similarly, the recurrence rates based on Shakiba et al. 2008 were used because the definition was less strict (reoperation free survival) in this study compared to Vercellini et at. 2003[105] (recurrence of moderate or severe DYS). According to the Shakiba et al. 2008[123] definition of recurrence, patients could use pharmacological treatment if pain recurred, and they would not be qualified as a recurrent patient. 

The overall conclusions did not change in either of the scenarios tested. When the response rate based on Sutton et al. 1994[71] was applied, treatment with linzagolix plus ABT was more expensive (£771) and generated an additional 0.55 QALYs compared to laparoscopic surgery, resulting in an ICER of £1,394 per QALY. Similarly, when the recurrence rate was based on Shakiba et al. 2008, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT was more expensive (£244) and generated an additional 0.62 QALYs compared with laparoscopic surgery, resulting in an ICER of £392 per QALY. The results of the scenario analysis confirmed the robustness of the base case analysis.

## _**B.3.13 Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation**_ 

Prescribing linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for the treatment of endometriosis offers non-quantifiable savings that could have a significant benefit to public payers. Effective symptom management can lead to increased productivity and reduced absenteeism from work. Whilst not directly measurable in healthcare costs or captured in the cost-effectiveness model, this can have a substantial positive impact on the economy and society. 

Further benefits of linzagolix plus ABT vs GnRH agonists not captured in the model include: oral administration at home, removing the need to arrange and attend monthly/3-monthly appointments in primary care for a GnRH agonist depot injection; rapid return of periods/fertility after stopping treatment; and the ability to discontinue treatment immediately in the event of intolerable adverse events (as opposed to depot GnRH injections). 

## _**B.3.14 Validation**_ 

## **B.3.14.1 Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis** 

The model has undergone thorough internal validation to reveal possible errors and incorrect operation of individual model modules. The Drummond and Jefferson checklist was used in the validation process. Internal validation included testing the values of key parameters entered into the model. This included checking that zero or extreme values had the expected impact on model results. For instance, setting drug acquisition costs for linzagolix to zero only affects cost reduction in the linzagolix arm; setting utility value in the _no response on initial treatment_ state to 0 (1) decreases (increases) the number of QALYs; using a shorter time horizon decreases the number of QALYs and reduces total costs, etc. In each cycle, the sum of 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 193 -->

proportions across health states, including cumulative mortality, is equal to 100% in each modelled arm. 

As part of the convergence validation, the model was compared with other models for the same health problem, identified based on the literature search conducted by two independent reviewers (section B.3.1). The individual cost-effectiveness studies were shown to validate the model design, the defined health states, and the choice of cost categories. Nevertheless, most of the compared studies were performed over a much shorter time horizon than included in this economic analysis, which affects the results obtained. 

As a part of external validation, the clinical experts verified the most impactful assumptions used in the model, and its structure[9,100] . In particular, clinical experts validated model health-states, assumptions regarding initial and long-term treatment continuation (pain endpoints used in clinical trials utilised in the model), resource use, comparators, and the treatment pathway. 

## _**B.3.15 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence**_ 

Compared with the current standard second-line medical treatment (GnRH agonists), linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is highly cost-effective when assessed against the NICE cost-effectiveness threshold of £20,000 to £30,000 per QALY. Linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is associated with increased QALYs and an acceptable increase in costs. 

The tangible benefits of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT include the potential for it to be prescribed for a longer duration than GnRH agonists, ease of administration, rapid onset of therapeutic effect, and quick reversibility of its effects. Additionally, it is expected that using linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT will help avoid more radical laparoscopic and abdominal surgeries, which could impair patient HRQoL, particularly in patients requiring multiple surgeries due to early onset of the disease and/or symptom recurrence over time. 

The cost-effectiveness analysis has some limitations. The treatment pathway is individualised with a variety of possible treatment options. Therefore, an economic model cannot fully capture the complexities of endometriosis management. To address uncertainties, a broad range of scenario analyses was performed to confirm the robustness of the results. Another limitation relates to the health utility inputs; for 

Company evidence submission for linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 194 -->

some health states, utilities were derived directly from the EDELWEISS 3 study (for initial pharmacological treatment). However, for health states related to surgical procedures, some assumptions were necessary, and a conservative approach was applied to avoid overestimating the treatment benefit of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. Furthermore, the long-term maintenance of the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT treatment effect was based on only a six-month period from the EDELWEISS 3 study. This assumption was validated by clinical experts, who do not expect any treatmentwaning effect for GnRH antagonist therapy. The treatment waning effect was also tested in scenario analyses. 

The economic analysis supports the expectation that linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT provides a cost-effective treatment option in NHS England practice for patients with symptoms of endometriosis.

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

Endometriosis is a condition where cells similar to the ones in the lining of the womb (uterus) are found elsewhere in the body. These cells react to the menstrual cycle each month and also bleed. However, there is no way for this blood to leave the body. This can cause inflammation, pain and the formation of scar tissue.[1] 

Some patients with endometriosis may have no or mild symptoms, whilst at the other end of the spectrum, symptoms can be severe and debilitating. Symptoms vary for each individual depending on where their endometriosis is, with severe, chronic pelvic pain being the most common symptom. Women with endometriosis may experience fatigue, depression, an inability to conceive, problems in working and social life, and relationship or sexual issues. There is no definitive cure for endometriosis, and it can severely impact quality of life and wellbeing.[1] 

Endometriosis is a condition which usually affects those assigned female at birth between puberty and menopause. Globally, endometriosis is estimated to affect approximately 10% of women of reproductive age, however a study based on data from a UK population estimated a lower prevalence of 2% in women of reproductive age.[1,2] 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

The process of getting a diagnosis can take some time because the symptoms are often similar to other conditions. The only definitive way to diagnose endometriosis is laparoscopy, an operation in which a camera (a laparoscope) is inserted into the pelvis via a small cut near the navel. The surgeon uses the camera to see the pelvic organs and look for any signs of endometriosis.[3,4] 

In the UK, patients with endometriosis wait, on average, 9 years for a diagnosis, which is a significant issue as it can lead to prolonged suffering, ill health and risks to fertility.[5] 

## **2c) Current treatment options:** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

- What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines. It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 



<!-- page 208 -->

`o` are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

There is no cure for endometriosis and current treatment options aim to manage the symptoms of endometriosis. Treatment options are diverse and consist of analgesic therapies, hormonal therapies, surgery, or a combination of these.[4] The type of treatment a patient receives for endometriosis depends on the individual case, needs and priorities and should be decided in partnership with a healthcare professional; age, severity of symptoms and family planning are key considerations.[1] 

Hormonal contraceptives, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and long-acting reversible contraception, are generally the first kind of hormone treatment tried.[4] Another type of hormonal treatment, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, are reserved as secondline hormonal treatment. To minimise or prevent some of the side effects of GnRH agonists, these are often prescribed in combination with hormone-based therapy, known as add-back therapy (ABT; oestrogen or progestin or a combination of both).[6] 

If approved for use in the UK, it is anticipated that linzagolix plus ABT will be used as a second-line hormonal treatment option, as an alternative to GnRH agonists, after surgery, hormonal treatments, and analgesics (painkillers) have been considered and have failed to adequately control symptoms (Figure 1).

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

**Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

All-party parliamentary group report on the burden of endometriosis (2020):[7] 

- A survey of 10,000 people living in the UK who were diagnosed with endometriosis 

- In the survey, 95% and 81% of respondents said that endometriosis had had a negative, or very negative, impact on their wellbeing and mental health, respectively, and 89% felt isolated due to their condition 

- The following symptoms had a negative or very negative impact: pelvic pain (95%); fatigue (93%); heavy menstrual bleeding (86%); painful bowel movements (84%); pain during or after sex (83%); urinary symptoms (60%); difficulty getting pregnant (for those for whom this was relevant) (83%) 

- In respect of treatment options, the prominent concerns were around pain and a lack of pain management support, lack of information, access to, and availability of treatments, and concern around treatment effectiveness 

Endometriosis UK, “Dismissed, ignored and belittled” The long road to endometriosis diagnosis in the UK Diagnosis (2024)[5] 

- An online survey to determine the average length of time to secure a diagnosis of endometriosis, which included 4,371 UK participants diagnosed with endometriosis 

- Revealed a lengthy route to diagnosis; diagnosis times in the UK increased to an average of 8 years and 10 months in 2023, up from 8 years in 2020 

UK National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death survey (2024):[8] 

- A study on the pathway and quality of care in endometriosis, part of which was an online survey on the views of 941 patients 

- The study highlighted deficiencies in pathways of care, holistic and medical management, and follow-up of patients with endometriosis 

- 43% of respondents experienced no improvement with medication. Despite this, most (82%) had no further investigation by their GP. 

World Endometriosis Research Foundation EndoCost study:[9] 

- A cross-sectional questionnaire-based survey among 931 women with endometriosis treated in 12 tertiary care centres in 10 countries 

- In this survey, 56% reported problems with pain/discomfort, 29% reported problems with usual activities, 29% reported being unable to work due to endometriosis, and 16% of women reported (some or major) problems with mobility. In addition, 36% of women reported problems with anxiety/depression.

## **SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work?** 

What are the important features of this treatment? 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body. Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

Linzagolix blocks the action of a hormone, GnRH, that helps to regulate the release of female sex hormones oestradiol and progesterone. These hormones trigger women’s periods (menstruation). When blocked, the levels of the hormones oestrogen and progesterone circulating in the body are reduced.[10] By decreasing their levels, linzagolix stops or reduces menstrual bleeding and decreases pain and pelvic discomfort and other symptoms associated with endometriosis. 

## **3b) Combinations with other medicines** 

Is the medicine intended to be used in combination with any other medicines? 

• No 

If yes, please explain why and how the medicines work together. Please outline the mechanism of action of those other medicines so it is clear to patients why they are used together. If yes, please also provide information on the availability of the other medicine(s) as well as the main side effects. 

**If this submission is for a combination treatment, please ensure the sections on efficacy (3e), quality of life (3f) and safety/side effects (3g) focus on data that relate to the combination, rather than the individual treatments.** 

Linzagolix, for the treatment of symptomatic endometriosis, is taken once daily together with ABT. The ABT is important as it helps to reduce side effects including the risk and extent of bone mineral density loss.[10] 

Linzagolix is therefore not suitable for women who are not able to, or prefer not to, take hormone-based therapies, including those wishing to conceive. 

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

The recommended dose for the treatment of symptoms of endometriosis is 200 mg once daily (single tablet) with concomitant ABT.[10] 

There is no fixed treatment duration. Treatment continuation depends on the risk of bone mineral density loss. Bone mineral density is determined by a scan after the first 12 months of treatment to see if treatment can continue. If treatment is continued beyond one year, bone mineral density should be checked at regular intervals.[10] 

Both linzagolix and the ABT are orally administered and do not require administration by a healthcare professional, unlike, for example, the injectable forms of GnRH agonists.
