## **3d) Current clinical trials** 

Please provide a list of completed or ongoing clinical trials for the treatment. Please provide a brief top-level summary for each trial, such as title/name, location, population, patient group size, comparators, key inclusion and exclusion criteria and completion dates etc. Please provide references to further information about the trials or publications from the trials. 

## **Completed main clinical trials (Phase 3)** 

The efficacy (how well a treatment works) and safety of linzagolix with or without ABT were evaluated in a phase 3 clinical trial (EDELWEISS 3) over 6 months. This was immediately followed by its extension study (EDELWEISS 6) for a further 6 months.[11–14] Although the EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 trials evaluated two doses of linzagolix (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and linzagolix 75 mg alone) versus placebo, the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT dose met the co-primary efficacy endpoints (i.e. achieved the main assessment criteria as explained below) and is the dose for symptomatic treatment of endometriosis stated in the Summary of Product Characteristics. This submission, therefore, focuses on the evidence for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT in women with endometriosis-associated pain (EAP) requiring symptomatic treatment. 

## **EDELWEISS 3** 

EDELWEISS 3 (NCT03992846) was a phase 3 placebo-controlled trial that assessed the efficacy and safety of linzagolix (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and linzagolix 75 mg alone) in women of reproductive age with moderate to severe EAP. The trial was classed as ‘double-blind’, meaning that neither the doctors nor the patients knew who was taking linzagolix or placebo. A doubleblind approach is often used in clinical trials so that knowledge of which treatment (or placebo) is being received doesn’t affect (bias) the drug assessment. 

Patients were randomised (split randomly) into three groups. One group of patients were given placebo (a substance with no medicinal activity that is given in an identical way to the medicine under investigation), one group was given linzagolix alone at a dose of 75 mg; the third group was given linzagolix at a dose of 200 mg along with ABT (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT). 

The co-primary (main) endpoint (assessment) of the EDELWEISS 3 trial was how good linzagolix was at reducing dysmenorrhoea (period pain) and non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP; pain experienced in between periods) along with stable or decreased use of analgesics (painkillers) after 3 months of treatment. The study also looked at the effect of linzagolix on dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia (difficulty emptying the bowel), overall pelvic pain (OPP), interference of pain with the ability to perform daily activities (based on the Endometriosis Health Profile-30 [EHP-30] questionnaire), and dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse), and no analgesic / no opiate (a type of strong painkiller) use for EAP during the preceding 4-week period at month 6. 

To enter the study, patients had to be women of reproductive age with surgically confirmed pelvic endometriosis in the past 10 years. Prior to screening, patients had to exhibit moderate-to-severe EAP, based on dysmenorrhoea and NMPP over the previous month. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are published.[11] 

## **EDELWEISS 6** 

Patients who completed the 6-month treatment period in the EDELWEISS 3 study were invited to enter the EDELWEISS 6 extension study (NCT04335591), which aimed to assess the maintenance of efficacy of linzagolix with or without ABT for up to an additional 6 months (up to 12 months of treatment in total) in women who had already completed 6 months of linzagolix treatment in EDELWEISS 3. 



<!-- page 212 -->

In EDELWEISS 6, patients who received placebo in EDELWEISS 3 were randomised 1:1 to linzagolix 75 mg or linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. Patients who received active treatment (linzagolix 75 mg or linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT) in EDELWEISS 3 continued the same treatment. 

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

As outlined in Section 3d, the efficacy of linzagolix plus ABT was evaluated in the EDELWEISS 3 trial over 6 months, followed by its extension study EDELWEISS 6 for a further 6 months.[11–14] 

## **Endometriosis-associated pain** 

Linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT met (achieved) the co-primary endpoint of the EDELWEISS 3 study, demonstrating ~~clin~~ ically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP (reductions of ≥1.10 and ≥0.8 points on the verbal rating scale for dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, respectively) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, with stable or reduced use of analgesics. At month 3, the estimated percentage of responders (people with reduced pain and stable or reduced use of analgesics [painkillers]) for dysmenorrhoea was 72.9% in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group versus 23.5% in the placebo group. Respective proportions for NMPP were 47.3% with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus 30.9% with placebo. 

Further improvements were observed at month 12 in EDELWEISS 6 in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group. At month 12, the estimated percentage of responders in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group was 91.0% for dysmenorrhoea and 67.6% for NMPP. 

In EDELWEISS 3, statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements from baseline to month 6 with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo were also observed at month 6 for dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia, OPP and ability to participate in daily activities. Steady improvements in these measures were observed throughout the treatment period in EDELWEISS 6. 

## **3f) Quality of life impact of the medicine and patient preference information** 

What is the clinical evidence for a potential impact of this medicine on the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers? What quality of life instrument was used? If the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) was used does it sufficiently capture quality of life for this condition? Are there other disease specific quality of life measures that should also be considered as supplementary information?

Please include all references as required. 

Along with the observed reductions in EAP and the ability to perform daily activities based on EHP-30 pain scores with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo in EDELWEISS 3, there were improvements in broader health-related quality of life aspects.[13] The EHP-30 dimensions of 



<!-- page 213 -->

‘control and powerlessness’, ‘emotional wellbeing’, ‘social support’ and ‘self-image’ also showed statistically significant improvements (score reductions) from baseline to month 6 in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group versus placebo, although improvement in the ‘modular sexual relationship’ dimension was not statistically significant versus placebo. The improvement (increase) in EuroQoL 5-Dimension 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) scores from baseline to month 6 was also significantly greater with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo. 

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

The safety profile for linzagolix in women with EAP in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 was consistent with that observed previously for women with uterine fibroids.[15,16] Linzagolix showed good overall tolerability, with side effects similar to placebo.[11,13,14] Most side effects (approximately 99% overall) were mild or moderate in intensity. The incidence of severe side effects was low and comparable between groups, and no fatal or suicide-related side effects were reported. The proportion of patients who discontinued treatment in EDELWEISS 3 due to side effects in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group (3.1%) was similar to that for the placebo group (2.5%), although the rate was slightly higher for the linzagolix 75 mg group (5.6%). 

The most common side effects (regardless of whether or not they were related to the treatment) were headaches, which were reported for similar proportions of patients in each group (EDELWEISS 3: 10.5% of patients in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, 8.1% in the linzagolix 75 mg group, 8.0% in the placebo group). Hot flushes were more common in the linzagolix groups (6.8% in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group, 7.5% in the linzagolix 75 mg group) than the placebo group (2.5%) in EDELWEISS 3. 

Headaches (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: 6.2%, linzagolix 75 mg: 7.5%, placebo, 3.7%) and hot flushes (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: 6.8%, linzagolix 75 mg: 7.5%, placebo, 2.5%) were also the most common side effects considered to be related to linzagolix treatment in EDELWEISS 3. 

Bone mineral density was largely unaffected by linzagolix treatment at month 6 (EDELWEISS 3) and month 12 (EDELWEISS 6).[11,13,14] Some bone mineral density increases were noted at 6 months after the end of treatment (EDELWEISS 6 follow-up), indicating partial recovery. The average (least squares mean) percentage change from baseline to month 6 in EDELWEISS 3 was <1% in all three treatment groups at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip. 

Periods resumed within a median time of approximately 1 month after the end of treatment across groups in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6.

## **3j) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g. whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g. travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

**Cost-effectiveness/cost-comparison assessment of new medicines** 



<!-- page 215 -->

In assessing whether a medicine represents a cost-effective use of NHS resources, NICE refers to a measure called the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER).[17] This looks at the costeffectiveness of the product in question – in this case, linzagolix plus ABT – against other treatments currently used to treat the condition. 

The ICER is measured in terms of what needs to be spent to gain one quality-adjusted life year (QALY). The QALY is a measure of disease burden and includes both the quality and quantity of life lived. A treatment can increase the number of QALYs a patient experiences by extending life, increasing the quality of life, or both. 

## **How the economic assessment of linzagolix was conducted** 

The cost-effectiveness analysis took into account the various treatments available on the NHS for treating the symptoms of endometriosis. This included other medicines and different types of surgery. 

A new model was created to show how a patient with a confirmed diagnosis of endometriosis and previous medical or surgical treatment would be treated in the NHS, and estimate both the benefits (in terms of QALYs) and costs of different treatment options. The relative effectiveness of the different treatments, in terms of treating pain, and their impact on the quality of life of patients was informed by clinical studies, and an indirect treatment comparison. Literature and expert opinion were also used to provide data unavailable from the EDELWEISS 3 and 6 clinical studies, including data needed to compare linzagolix versus surgery. The costs captured within the analysis include drug, administration, healthcare resource use, surgery, and adverse event-related costs. 

The model structure captures both the initial response to treatment and patient health status over a period of time extending until menopause. The model includes health states that reflect the varied responses to medical therapies, pain symptoms and surgical interventions that can be experienced by this population. The model includes a scenario comparing linzagolix against laparoscopic surgery. This required a modified initial structure of the model, to account for surgery as a ‘one-time’ event with potential disease recurrence, versus ongoing treatment with medical therapy that is assumed for the base model. 

## **The value proposition for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT** 

Based on the modelling approach summarised above linzagolix 200mg plus ABT shows the following: 

- Linzagolix 200mg plus ABT is cost-effective versus leuprorelin plus ABT: linzagolix is associated with higher costs and higher QALYs, resulting in an ICER below the UK threshold of £20,000 per QALY (the threshold below which NICE generally consider a treatment to be cost-effective) 

- Linzagolix is also cost-effective versus laparoscopic surgery as patients initially treated with linzagolix are associated with higher QALYs, and only slightly higher costs 

## **3k) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

There is a significant unmet need in patients with endometriosis who do not have adequate pain relief despite use of conventional hormonal therapies or surgical treatment. Use of GnRH agonists is often limited due to undesirable side effects.[6] In addition, administration of injectable GnRH 



<!-- page 216 -->

agonists can be uncomfortable, may result in injection site reactions and need to be given under the supervision of a healthcare professional, increasing the burden on healthcare systems and placing a time burden on patients.[18] 

GnRH antagonists, including linzagolix, with ABT, are an effective and innovative new treatment option for symptoms of endometriosis that may be administered orally at home without physician supervision.[19] 

Due to its mechanism of action, linzagolix has a rapid onset of therapeutic effects, as well as rapid recovery of hormone secretion, meaning periods return quickly after stopping treatment.[20] In addition, as opposed to depot GnRH injections, treatment can be discontinued immediately if needed, e.g. due to intolerable adverse events. 

## **3l) Equalities** 

Are there any potential equality issues that should be taken into account when considering this condition and this treatment? Please explain if you think any groups of people with this condition are particularly disadvantaged. 

Equality legislation includes people of a particular age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation or people with any other shared characteristics 

More information on how NICE deals with equalities issues can be found in the NICE equality scheme Find more general information about the Equality Act and equalities issues here 

Although linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is expected to be indicated for the symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in adult women of reproductive age with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis, this should not prevent the use of linzagolix by people with endometriosis who do not identify as a woman.

## **4b) Glossary of terms** 

**Hormonal add-back therapy (ABT):** an hormonal treatment (oestrogen or progestin or a combination of both) given alongside linzagolix 200 mg and some other gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogue treatments to prevent the loss of bone mineral density without affecting the efficacy of the GnRH analogue treatment.[6] 

**Adverse event:** an unintended medical event that occurs while you are taking a medicine, although it may not necessarily be caused by that medicine. 

**Analgesics:** painkillers. 

**Baseline:** the start of a clinical trial. Trials often assess changes from baseline to a certain timepoint, e.g. 3 months, to assess the effect of taking a drug for 3 months. 

**Bone mineral density:** a measure of how dense bones are; bones that are less dense may be weaker and more prone to fractures in the future. 

**Double-blind:** a design often used in clinical trials meaning that neither the doctors nor the patients knew which treatment group (e.g. a particular drug or placebo) a patient was assigned to. A double-blind approach is used so that knowledge of which treatment (or placebo) is being received doesn’t affect (bias) the drug assessment. 

**Dyschezia:** difficulty emptying the bowel. 

## **Dysmenorrhoea:** period pain. 

**Dyspareunia:** painful sexual intercourse. 

**Efficacy:** how well a treatment works (this term is usually used when reporting clinical trial data). 

**Endometriosis Health Profile-30 (EHP-30):** a patient-reported outcome (PRO) questionnaire that asks patients about the effects of endometriosis on various aspects of their quality of life. 



<!-- page 218 -->

**EuroQoL 5-Dimension 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L):** a patient-reported outcome (PRO) questionnaire that asks patients about their health-related quality of life or ‘health state’.[21] It is used in patients with many different health conditions, so it is often termed a ‘generic PRO’. 

**Femoral neck:** part of the hip. 

**Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogue:** a drug that targets gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptors to reduce the amount of oestrogen produced. There are two types of GnRH analogues, GnRH agonists and GnRH antagonists (such as linzagolix), that work in slightly different ways to reduce oestrogen levels.[22] 

**ICER:** incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. A measure of the cost-effectiveness of a medicine against other treatments currently used to treat the condition. In the UK, NICE generally consider an ICER below the threshold of £20,000 per QALY to be cost-effective, although this can vary for some conditions. 

**Indirect treatment comparison:** A statistical approach used to compare two different treatments in cases where those treatments have not been directly compared in the same study (e.g. a clinical trial). 

**Laparoscopic surgery:** a type of keyhole surgical procedure that can be used for people with endometriosis, where small cuts are used to perform surgery inside the abdomen and pelvis. 

**Lumbar spine:** lower backbone. 

**Marketing authorisation:** approval from a regulatory body to market a medicine in a specified country (e.g. Great Britain, United Kingdom) or region (e.g. European Union). 

**NCT number:** the number assigned to a clinical trial when registered on https://clinicaltrials.gov, a database that lists clinical trials and provides details of their status (e.g. ‘recruiting’, ‘completed’), methods and results. 

**Non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP):** pain experienced in between periods. 

**Opiate:** a type of strong painkiller. 

**Patient reported outcomes (PROs):** information regarding health conditions and their effects on quality of life that are reported directly by patients (often using a questionnaire) without any interpretation from doctors. 

**Placebo:** a ‘dummy drug’ given to patients in the control group of a clinical trial. A placebo is designed to look the same as the drug being investigated so that people do not know if they received the actual drug or the placebo. A placebo is given to compare the effects of receiving the drug being investigated versus no drug (over and above any ‘placebo effect’). 

**Phase 3 trial:** a late-stage clinical trial that usually involves large numbers of patients and is often used as the primary source of data for applications for marketing authorisation of a drug. 

**QALY:** quality-adjusted life year. A measure of disease burden, including both the quality and quantity of life lived, used for the economic assessment of medicines. 



<!-- page 219 -->

**Randomised:** when patients in a clinical study are randomly assigned (split randomly) to a group in the trial (e.g. the group being given the medicine, or the group being given a placebo). 

**Responder:** the term ‘responder’ was used in the EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 trials to refer to people with reduced pain (dysmenorrhoea and NMPP) and stable or reduced use of analgesics (painkillers). 

**Second-line:** the second treatment used for a particular disease/condition. 

**Single technology appraisal (STA):** technology appraisal guidance from NICE covering a single drug or treatment for a single indication (e.g. a particular disease or a specified group of people with a particular disease).

## Response A1f 

In the systematic literature review on cost-effectiveness, Medical Subject Heading (MeSH) terms in PubMed and Emtree terms in Ovid were not used. This approach was chosen to avoid potential limitations associated with controlled vocabulary indexing, for example, the variability in how scientific publications are indexed. The use of natural language keywords allowed a broader and more inclusive retrieval of studies by capturing variations in terminology used by authors, that may appear in titles or abstracts but are not reflected in MeSH or Emtree terms. While this method may reduce the precision of search results, as indexing terms can refine searches to highly relevant papers, it minimises the risk of omitting important articles that might otherwise be overlooked due to incomplete or inconsistent indexing. As a result of not using MeSH terms and Emtree terms, more results were obtained by the 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 229 -->

systematic literature search, many of which proved to be irrelevant to the topic. However, this approach ensured that no significant evidence was missed, as the broader search captured all potentially relevant studies. According to NICE’s manual: when identifying subject headings, variations in thesaurus and indexing terms for each database should be considered, for example MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) in MEDLINE and Emtree in Embase. Not all databases have indexing terms, and some contain records that have not yet been indexed. It was decided that a search strategy based on free-terms and synonyms would be sufficient to cover relevant publications.

## Response A1i 

In the SLR on HRQoL in patients with endometriosis, MeSH terms in PubMed and Emtree terms in Ovid were not used. This approach was chosen to avoid potential limitations associated with controlled vocabulary indexing, for example, the variablility in how scientific publications are indexed. The use of natural language keywords allowed a broader and more inclusive retrieval of studies by capturing variations in terminology used by authors, that may appear in titles or abstracts but are not reflected in MeSH or Emtree terms. While this method may reduce the precision of search results, as indexing terms can refine searches to highly relevant papers, it minimises the risk of omitting important articles that might otherwise be overlooked due to incomplete or inconsistent indexing. As a result of not using MeSH terms and Emtree terms, more results were obtained by the systematic literature search, many of which proved irrelevant to the topic. However, this approach ensured that no significant evidence was missed, as the broader search captured all potentially relevant studies. According to NICE’s manual: when identifying subject headings, variations in thesaurus and indexing terms for each database should be considered, for example MeSH in MEDLINE and Emtree in Embase. Not all databases have indexing terms, and some contain records that have not yet been indexed. It was decided that a search strategy based on free-terms and synonyms would be sufficient to cover relevant publications.

## _**Decision problem**_ 

- **A 2.  Priority question. Surgery is included as a comparator in the Decision Problem and the cost-effectiveness analysis. However, it is not included in the clinical effectiveness evidence. The only other comparator is leuprorelin.** 

   - **a) Please provide adequate justification for the comparators that have been included.** 

   - **b) Please include clinical and cost-effectiveness evidence for a comparison with all comparators that are might be used in clinical practice in the NHS regardless of market share.** 

## Response A2a 

Linzagolix is anticipated to be indicated for xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx[1] Based on clinical expert 

opinion in the UK, and in line with European clinical guidelines, gonadotropinreleasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists (including linzagolix) will be used as secondline hormonal treatment options, as an alternative to GnRH agonists (see Figure 5 in Company Submission Document B, Section B1.3.5.2). The comparators included in the submission are based on those treatments used at the same point of the treatment pathway. 

As such the following treatments are not considered to be comparators: 

- Analgesics, which are recommended for the initial management of endometriosis-associated pain (EAP), and may be used alone or in combination with other treatments. 

- Neuromodulators, which are reserved for patients with exceptionally difficultto-manage pain secondary to endometriosis, and are prescribed after referral to a specialist pain service rather than as part of routine supportive care. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 240 -->

Clinical experts advised that it is unusual for patients to require neuromodulators, with <5% of patients prescribed such treatments.[2] 

- Combined hormonal contraception, oral progestogens and intrauterine devices which are used as first-line hormonal therapies. 

GnRH agonists are reserved as second-line hormonal treatment, and are therefore considered to be appropriate comparators. The following GnRH agonists are indicated for the treatment of endometriosis: goserelin (depot injection), leuprorelin (depot injection), nafarelin (nasal spray), buserelin (nasal spray), and triptorelin (depot injection). Intranasal GnRH agonists (nafarelin and buserelin) are rarely prescribed, with all surveyed clinical experts reporting a preference for intramuscular or subcutaneous formulations, therefore only leuprorelin acetate, goserelin, and triptorelin were considered comparators in the model.[2,3] Leuprorelin, as a representative of all GnRH agonists, is included in the base case (see response to question A5 for further discussion). 

While surgery is an important part of the treatment pathway for women with endometriosis, the clinical decision to perform surgery is based on individual circumstances independent of the choice to prescribe a GnRH analogue. Women who wish to conceive immediately would be prioritised for surgical treatment, while those not currently planning a family may try hormonal therapies to manage their symptoms before considering surgery.[2] Surgery is not considered to be a direct comparator to linzagolix because: 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 241 -->

- 1) Linzagolix would be used in situations where GnRH agonists are currently prescribed, and where medical therapy is preferred over surgical intervention. 

- 2) Treatment decisions are guided by the need to balance treatment priorities regarding fertility and pain management. Women who do not wish to take hormonal therapy due to priorities regarding fertility would not be suitable for linzagolix treatment and would be prioritised for surgical treatment. 

- 3) Clinical experts suggest that when included in the overall pathway, GnRH analogues impact when and how surgery might be used. GnRH analogues may be used as a complementary treatment to reduce the risk of symptom recurrence post-surgery or to provide symptom relief whilst women are waiting for surgery, and in this case, do not directly replace surgical treatment. 

The feasibility of an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) versus surgery was explored; however, there are considerable methodological challenges in comparing medical therapy with surgery due to differences in study objectives, study design and endpoints. Adding complexity, a range of different surgical interventions may be used to treat endometriosis. As described in the CS (Document B section B2.9, page 72 and Appendix M) an indirect treatment comparison with surgical treatments was not feasible. Therefore, outcomes following surgical treatment (laparoscopy) were modelled using data identified in the published literature and validated with clinical experts, as described in the Company Submission (section B3.3.6). 

Relugolix combination therapy (relugolix-oestradiol-norethisterone acetate, relugolixCT) has not yet been received positive guidance by NICE for use in England and Wales and therefore was not included as a comparator in the original submission, however at NICE’s request we are now able to provide comparative data, **see addendum to clarification response – comparison with relugolix** . 

## Response A2b 

As described in the response to A2a, it is not appropriate to include analgesics  and first-line hormonal therapies as comparators. These would be used before linzagolix 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 242 -->

in clinical practice, whilst neuromodulators are used in special circumstances in a small minority of patients. The submission, therefore focussed on the main treatment expected to be replaced by linzagolix, i.e., GnRH agonists. While surgery was also not considered to be a direct comparator to linzagolix for the reasons described above, the company has undertaken a thorough review of the available evidence. Limitations in the data available for surgical treatments precluded an ITC, however results from published studies were used to inform the economic analysis, as described in the CS Document B Section B3.3.6. 

Whilst relugolix is not yet “approved” by NICE, an indirect treatment comparison comparing linzagolix with relugolix has been provided, with results incorporated into the economic analysis ( **see addendum to clarification response – comparison with relugolix** ). 

- **A 3.  Priority question. The Decision Problem population is described as requiring a: “…history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis” (Table 1).** 

   - **a) Please provide details of the precise nature of these medical and surgical treatments.** 

   - **b) Please indicate if there is a different treatment history for those patients where the comparator is leuprorelin as opposed to those where the comparator is surgery or for any of the other comparators (see question A4).** 

   - **c) If there are systematic differences in treatment history (see question b) the please confirm that these differences would imply different subgroups.** 

## Response A3a 

Table 1 of the CS Document A refers to the intended indication specified in the summary of product characteristics (SmPC). The SmPC (section 5.1) also states "The majority of the study population of EDELWEISS 3 reported having undergone previous surgeries/procedures for endometriosis treatment before inclusion into the 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 243 -->

EDELWEISS studies. Previous medical treatments consisted of analgesics for pelvic pain, including opioids. The most frequently reported other pharmacotherapies for endometriosis treatment included dienogest, hormonal oral contraceptives and GnRH agonists." 

Most patients (93.8%) in the EDELWEISS 3 safety analysis set (SAF) had undergone prior surgeries or procedures to treat endometriosis. The most commonly performed procedures involved laparoscopies. 

Prior medications were taken by 69.6% of patients in the EDELWEISS 3 SAF; the use of prior medications was similar across treatment groups (66.3% to 73.5%). The most commonly used (by ≥5% of the SAF) prior medications were in the following Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classes: genito-urinary system and sex hormones (43.8%), musculoskeletal system (38.2%), nervous system (10.5%), alimentary tract and metabolism (8.9%), antineoplastic and immunomodulating agents (8.3%), and systemic hormonal preparations excluding sex hormones and insulins (7.0%). The most commonly used (i.e., at least 2% of the SAF) prior medications were: ibuprofen (33.1%), dienogest (25.8%), dienogest/ethinyloestradiol (10.3%), levothyroxine sodium (5.2%), goserelin (4.1%), paracetamol (3.7%), drotaverine hydrochloride (2.3%) and diclofenac (2.1%). 

The treatments received prior to linzagolix in EDELWEISS 3 are reflective of the treatments that would be received in UK clinical practice before treating with linzagolix (as outlined in Response 2a and according to clinical expert opinion and NICE/ESHRE guidelines). 

## Response A3b 

As described in the response to Question A2a, clinical expert opinion in the UK suggests that linzagolix would be used as a second-line hormonal treatment option, most likely as an alternative to GnRH agonists, which is in line with European clinical guidelines. The comparators included in the submission are based on those treatments used at the same point of the treatment pathway. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 244 -->

For patients treated with leuprorelin, other GnRH agonists or conservative surgery at this point in the treatment pathway, a similar mix of previous treatments to linzagolix would be expected. The choice of treatment (medical therapy or surgery) is largely driven by patient circumstances relating to pregnancy and family planning, therefore many women receive medical therapies before surgery. Clinical expert opinion indicated that while waiting for surgery, patients may receive combined oral contraceptives, progestogens and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which is in line with medications that would be tried prior to GnRH agonists, as well as those expected to be used prior to linzagolix (and as reflected in EDELWEISS 3). Most women diagnosed with endometriosis will undergo multiple surgical procedures. Therefore women receiving surgery at this point in the treatment 

pathway may have undergone previous surgery; this is in line with the EDELWEISS 3 study population, and the population expected to be treated with linzagolix and GnRH agonists in UK clinical practice. 

## Response A3c 

No systematic differences in treatment history across comparators are expected for the population considered within the decision problem. 

**A 4.  Priority question. **A 5.  Priority question. The DP (see Table 1, CS) states that leuprorelin was chosen specifically as a representative of all GnRH agonists. However, the company seems to believe that other GnRH agonists are used in clinical practice, as shown by them being included in the costing (see Table 65, CS). Table 65 also refers to short- (1-month) and long- (3- month) acting** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 251 -->

**GnRH agonists, but no such distinction was made in the indirect treatment comparison (ITC).** 

- **a) Please provide justification for the use of leuprorelin specifically as a representative of all GnRH agonists.** 

- **a) Why was another GnRH agonist approved by NICE for this indication (e.g. goserelin, triptorelin or histrelin) not selected?** 

- **b) Why was no distinction made between short- and long-acting forms of leuprorelin in the ITC?** 

- **c) Please include all GnHR that might be used in clinical practice, differentiating between short- and long- acting forms of leuprorelin as required, as comparators in both analysis of clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness.** 

## Response A5a 

As noted in the response to question A2a, only leuprorelin acetate, goserelin and triptorelin were considered comparators in the model. 

Only one study investigating a GnRH agonist for the treatment of EAP was identified that could be used in an ITC with the EDELWEISS 3 study. This was a placebocontrolled randomised controlled trial (RCT) and its long-term extension study that investigated the efficacy and safety of leuporelin and relugolix for the treatment of EAP, reported by Osuga et al (Osuga et al 2021a/2021b[4,5] ). As outlined in Company Submission Appendix D (Section D3.2.1), this study included outcome data that could be compared with the results of the co-primary endpoints of EDELWEISS 3 in a Bucher analysis. 

In the base case analysis, leuprorelin acetate was used as the representative GnRH agonist based on the assumption that all GnRH agonists have equivalent efficacy in this population. As noted in the CS (Document B, page 126), this approach was deemed appropriate since all GnRH agonists effectively inhibit endometriosis through a shared mechanism of action, and is aligned to the submission for relugolix 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 252 -->

CT in this indication, as well as NICE and ESHRE guidelines which do not distinguish between the different agonists.[6–8] As also noted in the CS, leuprorelin acetate is the GnRH agonist most commonly used for the treatment of endometriosis in the UK.[3] 

## Response A5b 

None of the GnRH agonists are specifically “approved” by NICE for the treatment of endometriosis: there are no technology appraisals available in this indication, and the recently updated NICE endometriosis guidelines do not recommend specific GnRH agonists for use in the treatment of endometriosis.[9] In addition, it should be noted that histrelin is not indicated for the treatment of symptoms of endometriosis and is no longer available in the UK.[10] 

As described in A5a, no studies investigating goserelin and triptorelin for the treatment of EAP were identified that could be included in an indirect comparison with linzagolix. Goserelin and triptorelin were evaluated in scenario analyses of the cost-effectiveness analysis. 

## Response A5c 

To clarify, the formulation of GnRH agonists is not specifically ‘short’ or ‘long’ acting; this notation applies to the length of coverage of the depot injection. Clinicians and patients can choose the one-month depot or three-month depot and expect no difference in clinical efficacy or safety of the active drug. This is why there is no distinction made between the two formulations in the ITC. 

In practice, prescribing clinicians advised that a one-month depot is most often prescribed at treatment initiation.[3] This allows for a review within four weeks to determine if there has been a clinical effect and/or if any adverse events have been reported. A three-month depot may be chosen for convenience when a patient is keen to continue treatment. However, this would not change any outcomes for the patient versus the administration of three one-month depot injections as an alternative.[3] In some centres, patients remain on a one-month depot, given every 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 253 -->

four weeks until treatment cessation; in others, patients are offered the opportunity to switch to the three-month depot. 

The search strategy was broad, and no distinction was made between “short- and long-acting” forms of leuprorelin. The approach identified all evidence available, regardless of the form of leuprorelin. While reviewing the evidence, the criteria were established to include studies on both forms of leuprorelin. Only one trial was found in the process (Osuga et al 2021a/2021b[4,5] ), in which patients received leuprorelin once a month. 

## Response A5d 

The following GnRH agonists are indicated for the treatment of endometriosis in the UK: goserelin (depot injection), leuprorelin (depot injection), nafarelin (nasal spray), buserelin (nasal spray), and triptorelin (depot injection). In clinical practice in the UK, however, none of the prescribers consulted during expert elicitation reported prescribing nasal formulations. With reference to A5c (above) and the Budget Impact Analysis, Section 4.2 Table 2, in clinical practice, both one-month and three-month depot formulations of leuprorelin, goserelin and triptorelin are prescribed in the UK. The budget impact analysis assumes a 50:50 split between these two formulations based on the NICE single technology appraisal (STA) for relugolix and expert opinion.[3] 

**A 6.  Priority question. The Decision Problem includes a broad set of comparators representing established clinical management without linzagolix. However, the company’s SLR appears to limit the scope of comparators in several areas. Please provide a detailed justification when comparators deviate from the NICE scope e.g. are listed in the NICE scope but were not used in the company submission and provide clarification on the following points:** 

- **a) The scope includes a variety of hormone-based treatments, such as combined hormonal contraception and oral progestogens, as potential comparators. Please clarify why these additional hormonal treatments were not included in the GnRH analogue SLR.** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 254 -->

- **b) The scope specifies surgical comparators as “excision/ablation with or without hysterectomy.” Please explain the rationale for limiting surgical comparators in the surgical SLR to minimally invasive procedures only, excluding hysterectomy.** 

- **c) The scope lists analgesics, NSAIDs, and neuromodulators as part of established clinical management without linzagolix. Please clarify why these treatments were not included as comparators in the SLRs.** 

## Response A6a 

As described in response to question A2a, combined hormonal contraception and oral progestogens are used as first line hormonal therapies in UK practice and were therefore not considered to be comparators in the submission. 

## Response A6b 

In the NICE endometriosis guideline (published in 2017 and updated in 2024[9] ) the suggested surgical approaches involve laparoscopic excision or ablation plus adhesiolysis and laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy, depending on the location of the lesions. Hysterectomy is advised only if other surgical options have been offered, failed or are inappropriate, and research with clinical experts indicated that hysterectomy tends to be a last resort rather than considered early in the treatment pathway.[2] Additionally, hysterectomy is indicated if treatment-resistant adenomyosis or heavy menstrual bleeding is present. Linzagolix is a treatment indicated for the treatment of adult women of reproductive age - in this population it might be a priority to maintain fertility. When performing a hysterectomy the fertility is not maintained. Therefore, it was decided not to include it in the feasibility analysis. 

## Response A6c 

Analgesics and NSAIDs are routinely prescribed as first-line therapies in endometriosis (often before a formal diagnosis has been made). Expert elicitation revealed an expectation that once GnRH agonists (or antagonists) are introduced, there is a clinical expectation that the need for such treatments should reduce or cease.[2] Neuromodulators are reserved for patients with exceptionally difficult-to- 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 255 -->

manage pain secondary to endometriosis. Prescription would be started after referral to a specialist pain service rather than as part of routine supportive care. As such, the proportion of patients prescribed neuromodulators is limited and not part of routine practice. 

**A 7.  Priority question. The NICE technical team notes that relugolix CT has not been included as a potential comparator in the company’s submission. ## _**Systematic review**_ 

- **A 8.  Please describe the process used for data extraction and risk of bias** 

## **assessment of the included studies (for intervention and comparator data).** 

Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and quality-checked by the other reviewer. The extraction was performed in tables. Additionally, if available in the identified publications, graphs were provided. Data from graphs was not extracted if specific values were not provided, due to the possibility of introducing bias to the analysis . 

The process of risk of bias assessment is described in Appendix D (Section D.3.7). The methodological quality of each trial was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Collaboration’s revised risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2). Disagreements were resolved by consensus. The risk of bias was defined as low for all the trials included in the Bucher analysis. This demonstrates the high quality of the studies. The specific results of the risk of bias analysis were provided in Table 31.

## Response A13a 

Based on the clinical SLR performed (including studies limited to placebo as a common comparator) and analysing other published SLRs (Veth et al., 2023[11] ), we discovered significant variability in the studies reporting the efficacy and safety of different interventions. The heterogeneity is not limited to differing inclusion and exclusion criteria but extends to variability in the reported endpoints and scales used to measure the outcomes. Furthermore, many studies are outdated, methodology and population descriptions are not provided in certain instances and are unclear when reported, with some results only presented graphically (with no numerical values provided) and/or without variability measures (like standard deviation) – see Responses A13b and A13c. 

Based on the results of the SLRs, we concluded that it is appropriate to compare linzagolix with other GnRH agonists based on the simple pairwise indirect comparison, provided that it was possible to evaluate and minimise the risk of bias. 

In the base case analysis, we provided a pairwise comparison based on the two studies (EDELWEISS 3 and Osuga 2021a/b). While we consider it the most credible approach, it requires numerous assumptions and has limitations, even with just two trials included. Introducing any additional studies would result in further limitations, making conclusions more difficult to interpret and results more prone to bias. 

We believe that including studies comparing GnRH agonists versus other medical technologies into the ITC and building more complex networks might bring additional uncertainties (i.e., risk of bias, difficult or impossible to measure) and certainly would 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 260 -->

not address remaining uncertainties (after conducting the pairwise comparison) regarding effectiveness of linzagolix vs GnRH agonists. 

Finally, as we were only able to link linzagolix with leuprorelin (EDELWEISS 3 and Osuga studies), it can be assumed that including trials comparing GnRH agonists vs active treatments would not offer any benefits to the ITC. To address this, studies comparing different GnRH agonists with placebo, and studies linking different GnRH agonists vs other GnRH agonists, directly or indirectly, are required. We have only one GnRH agonist which we can compare with linzagolix via placebo. 

Building an NMA would not be credible in this therapeutic area for the reasons already mentioned above.

## **B 2.  Priority question:** 

**a) Please clarify whether the population demographics in the economic model (i.e., the EDELWEISS 3 trial population) can be generalised to the patient population in England and Wales, given that the trial did not include any patients from the UK.** 

Clarification questions

- **b) Also, the decision problem described “Adults with symptoms of endometriosis” while in Table 1 of the CS it is stated that the population considered are “women with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis”. Please resolve that discrepancy.** 

- **c) Please explain the difference in the population as defined by the NICE scope and the population considered by the company.** 

- **d) Please clarify what exactly the “previous history” can entail. Please explain if that means that linzagolix can only be administered as 2[nd] or 3[rd] line of treatment.** 

## Response B2a 

The EDELWEISS 3 trial population is considered to be generalisable to the patient population in England and Wales. Patients in EDELWEISS 3 were enrolled across Europe (65 centres in Austria, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, France, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Spain and Ukraine) and the US (26 centres). We have no reason to believe that there would be clinically relevant differences between overall patient populations in Europe, the US and UK, but acknowledge in Section B.2.12.2.2 that the patient population in EDELWEISS 3 was mostly white, so patients from other ethnic groups were not well represented. The mean age of patients in 

EDELWEISS 3 was 35 years, which is similar to the mean age of women in the UK with endometriosis.[12] 

## Response B2b 

The wording on the population in the decision problem Table 1 “Symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in women with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis” was added to reflect the wording of the expected indication for linzagolix in the UK and the position of linzagolix in the treatment pathway. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 265 -->

## Response B2c 

The only difference is that, according to the expected indication, linzagolix would not be used as a 1[st] line therapy in adults with symptoms of endometriosis, and would only be indicated when other treatments (either medical, surgical or both) have been tried. This positioning aligns with expert clinical opinion and the patient population in clinical studies of linzagolix (see response to B2d), and is identical to the relugolix indication in endometriosis.[2,13] 

## Response B2d 

It is correct that linzagolix is intended for 2nd or later-line therapy after conventional hormone therapy (see response to question A3a). As stated in section 5.1 of the SmPC, "The majority of the study population of EDELWEISS 3 reported having undergone previous surgeries/procedures for endometriosis treatment before inclusion into the EDELWEISS studies. Previous medical treatments consisted of analgesics for pelvic pain, including opioids. The most frequently reported other pharmacotherapies for endometriosis treatment included dienogest, hormonal oral contraceptives and GnRH agonists." 

## _**Model Structure**_ 

## **B 3.  Priority question: Regarding Figure 1 that presents the model structure:** 

- **a) Please confirm if patients can stay on linzagolix treatment for as long they remain in the no pain or moderate pain health states.** 

## **b) Please define explicitly the conditions in the model under which patients can continue receiving linzagolix treatment.** 

## Response B3a 

In the initial decision tree, patients continue linzagolix treatment if they achieve either a full or partial response to therapy, defined by improvements in dysmenorrhoea or non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP) symptoms as specified in the EDELWEISS 3 study. After completing the six-month decision tree (comprising two, three-month 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 266 -->

cycles), patients transition into pain-related health states. Patients can remain on linzagolix treatment while in the no pain/mild pain or moderate pain health states, as these conditions meet the criteria for continued therapy (specified in Response B3b). In the no pain/mild pain health-state, pain severity is reported as <1 on the verbal rating scale (VRS), while in the moderate pain health-state, pain does not exceed two on the VRS. However, it is important to note that there is a probability of discontinuation from these health states for reasons other than pain severity. This probability, set at 3.03%, represents the six-month discontinuation rate after the initial six months of treatment as determined in the EDELWEISS 6 study. The reasons for discontinuation comprised adverse events and the request of patients to discontinue treatment. Patients in the no pain/mild health-state can also transition to the pregnancy state and thus discontinue treatment with linzagolix. 

## Response B3b 

In the model, patients continue linzagolix treatment under specific conditions tied to their response and pain states. During the initial six-month decision tree phase, comprising two three-month cycles, patients remain on treatment if they demonstrate a full or partial response. These responses are defined based on improvements in dysmenorrhoea or NMPP pain levels, as specified in the EDELWEISS 3 study. After the initial decision tree, patients can stay on linzagolix while in the no pain/mild pain or moderate pain health states. The no pain/mild pain health state corresponds to a pain level of <1 on the VRS, whereas the moderate pain health state is defined by a pain level of 2 or less on the VRS. The assumption is in line with clinical expert opinion presented in the expert elicitation reports (2024[2,3] ), stating that patients will continue therapy as long as pain symptoms are managed. 

**B 4.  Priority question: On page 121 of the CS, it is mentioned that “patients who experience a recurrence of symptoms within three months of their initial surgery bypass the Post-Laparoscopy #1 state and move directly to the second surgical procedure.” Please explain how this input is informed in the model. Please clarify if that implies that the 6-month cycle-length may also be too long for the economic model. Please explain why a 3-** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 267 -->

## **month cycle was not considered for the total structure of the model instead of switching from 3- to 6-months in different parts of the model.** 

The assumption that patients experiencing a recurrence of symptoms within three months of their initial surgery bypass the Post-laparoscopy #1 state and move directly to the second surgical procedure is informed by expert opinion, which indicates that a subset of patients (16.28%) may still experience symptoms directly after unsuccessful surgical intervention within this timeframe.[14] Therefore, it is less relevant to focus on three or six months recurrence and more appropriate to consider a lack of response (i.e. captured as a proportion of patients with recurrence at three months assumed to be non-responders). In such cases, it is assumed that patients are referred for a subsequent surgical procedure (e.g., a second laparoscopy or radical surgery) as soon as possible, taking into account waiting time. It was also assumed that a six-month cycle length would adequately capture the waiting time for subsequent laparoscopic surgery (in line with Response B8). This reflects clinical practice (in line with the opinion of clinical experts, who indicated that some patients do not respond to laparoscopic surgical treatment, which is separate from the initial response and annual recurrence[3] ). This does not imply that the six-month cycle length is too long for the economic model. 

The three-month cycle is used selectively in the model during the initial decision tree to align with the EDELWEISS 3 co-primary endpoints, which evaluate the significant reduction in dysmenorrhoea and NMPP up to month 3. Conversely, the six-month cycle length corresponds to standard clinical practice, where treatment reviews or continuation typically occur biannually. This longer cycle length also provides flexibility to incorporate tunnel states (like pregnancy health-state) without a need to implement too many sub-states and further increase model complexity. Markov transitions at every six months are informed by the EDELWEISS 6 data, reporting results of six months of treatment, ensuring alignment of probabilities with the time of reported clinical evidence. It is worth noting that a half-cycle correction has been applied to address potential biases introduced by the longer model cycle. The combination of three- and six-month cycles reflects the need to capture both shortterm clinical outcomes and long-term treatment pathways while maintaining consistency with real-world practices and the requirements of economic modelling. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 268 -->

This hybrid approach balances accuracy and practicality in representing treatment pathways and patient outcomes. 

- **B 5.  Priority question: On page 116 of the CS, it is mentioned that a 16-year time horizon is used to extend “until the average age of menopause, established at 50 years in the UK.”** 

   - **a) Please provide the source used to inform the average age of menopause in the UK.** 

   - **b) Please justify why the current time horizon used by the company in the base-case analysis (i.e., 15.1-year time horizon) is not a lifetime time horizon.** 

   - **c) In section B.1.3.1.1 it is mentioned that a small proportion of women (~2–5%) experience post-menopausal endometriosis. Please discuss if these women should be considered in the analysis by extending the time horizon of the model. Please explain the potential impact of linzagolix on these women.** 

   - **d) Please adjust the model to allow for a lifetime time horizon or, if the company declines this request, please discuss the expected impact on the cost-effectiveness results of using a lifetime time horizon.** 

## Response B5a 

The source for the average age of menopause in the UK is the National Health Service website: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/menopause/ 

## Response B5b 

The development of endometriotic tissue depends on oestrogen levels and is linked to the period between menarche and menopause. Consequently, the initial submission set the time horizon at 15.1 years, representing the difference between the expected age at initiation of linzagolix treatment and the age at which patients typically reach menopause in the UK. This duration was sufficient to capture all significant differences in costs and outcomes between the compared technologies. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 269 -->

## Response B5c 

It was estimated that with a very small proportion of women who experience postmenopausal endometriosis and a high discount rate after 15 years, the impact of extending the time horizon would be marginal and not affect the overall conclusions. 

## Response B5d 

As indicated in B.5.c the expected impact on the cost-effectiveness results using a lifetime time horizon should be marginal. Most patients would complete linzagolix treatment at menopause (incurring no further costs) and, on average, experience higher utility values over the longer term compared to the comparator arm (due to fewer surgical interventions with long-term complications). 

**B 6.  Priority question: Patients in the model are assumed to enter the pregnancy health state from the ‘No pain/mild pain’ health state using a fixed probability per model cycle. Please provide evidence supporting this assumption. Furthermore, please justify why patients following surgeries such as post-laparoscopic patients (with no or moderate pain due to endometriosis) are not allowed to enter the pregnancy health state. If transitions from more health states to the pregnancy health state are allowed within the economic model, please update Figure 16 with arrows indicating all possible transitions.** 

The assumption that patients in the model transition to the pregnancy health-state from the no pain/mild state with a fixed probability (estimated from the live birth rate in the UK) per cycle is based on population norms. It assumes that women with endometriosis have similar desires and probability of pursuing pregnancy as the general UK population, as there is no evidence to suggest otherwise. This approach ensures that the model reflects real-world reproductive intentions without introducing unnecessary bias. 

The inclusion of a pregnancy health state was motivated by NICE's feedback on the Relugolix STA, which questioned the handling of infertility-related disutility. This state was introduced to capture future reproductive aspirations of women undergoing GnRH analogue therapy and to ensure that infertility disutility was not inappropriately 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 270 -->

applied to this group. Hormonal treatment is intended for women who wish to preserve their fertility for the future (according to NICE guidelines and expert clinical opnion[2,9] ) and do not wish to conceive immediately. Women can stop treatment at any time if they wish to conceive. Therefore, pregnancy was not intended to be the central element of the cost-effectiveness model, as this would require further detailed modelling beyond the scope of this submission. The aim was to demonstrate that for women treated with GnRH analogues, it is possible to temporarily withdraw therapy and conceive. The model and health-states concentrate on pain symptoms and related utility values, in line with primary endpoints of the EDELWEISS clinical trials. 

The decision to exclude the transition to the pregnancy state from other health-states (e.g., the post-laparoscopy health-state) was primarily made to maintain model simplicity. A scenario analysis has been provided to assess the impact of the pregnancy health state on the base case results, which excludes this health state from the model (Table 7). It is important to note that, as with initial treatment, no infertility disutility is applied to other health states in the model except those representing radical surgical interventions where infertility would be permanent.

- **B 7.  Priority question: The model assumes that patients once pregnant spend 3 cycles (in total 18 months) in the pregnancy health state and then move back to the no pain/mild pain state (with active initial treatment or to the Off treatment). Please provide evidence supporting this assumption.** 

The assumption of three cycles (in total 18 months) in the pregnancy health state was made to align with the six-month cycle length and the tunnel state structure of the model. This duration was chosen as the optimal balance: two cycles (12 months) would be too short to account for conception, pregnancy, and breastfeeding, while more cycles would further complicate the already very complex cost-effectiveness model. Eighteen months effectively captures the necessary timeline while keeping the model focused on its primary objectives.

It is correct that the model assumed a waiting time of 18 months for surgeries when comparing linzagolix with laparoscopic surgeries but only six months for laparoscopic surgeries performed in subsequent treatment lines. This approach was taken to maintain model simplicity and not introduce additional tunnel states within the cost-effectiveness model. The results of sensitivity analyses were provided below. 

## **Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

A probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to explore the uncertainty around key model parameters. PSA was performed by varying these parameters using their upper and lower bound values based on an assigned distribution. 1,000 simulations were run for the PSA, by which time the ICERs had converged to a stable mean, represented by the probabilistic ICERs. The probabilistic ICER vs laparoscopic surgery (£804) lies closely to the base-case ICER (£693) indicating that the cost-effectiveness results are robust (Table 9). According to the costeffectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC), the probability of linzagolix versus. laparoscopic surgery being cost-effective is already 100% at a willingness to pay of £2,000/quality-adjusted life year (QALY; Figure 2).

## _**Comparator**_ 

- **B 14.  Priority question: According to the NICE scope, the relevant comparators should include ‘surgery such as excision/ablation with or without hysterectomy’. In the CE analysis, the company includes laparoscopic surgery as an additional comparator to GnRH agonists.** 

   - **a) Please explain what the alternative surgery options for the population of interest are.** 

   - **b) Please justify why radical surgeries such as hysterectomy or oophorectomy are not relevant comparators.** 

   - **c) Please explain if subgroup analysis would be relevant for patients requiring radical surgeries such as hysterectomy or oophorectomy versus linzagolix.** 

## Response B14a 

The patient population considered in the analysis comprises adult pre-menopausal women with moderate to severe endometriosis-associated pain and a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis. It was assumed that for this population, the alternative surgical options to linzagolix are limited to conservative procedures. GnRH antagonists are a treatment of choice for patients wishing to preserve fertility, as radical surgeries such as hysterectomy or oophorectomy do not align with this goal. This is especially true once patients still have alternative treatments to use. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 279 -->

## Response B14b 

In clinical practice, radical surgeries are typically reserved for heavily pretreated patients with recurrent disease, where both pharmacological treatments and conservative surgeries have proven ineffective. Furthermore, patients who are offered radical surgeries in the earlier stage of their treatment pathway are generally not candidates for pharmacological therapy (unlike patients who want to preserve their fertility for the future). Radical surgeries, unlike pharmacological options, close the path to pregnancy for those patients. 

We understand that radical surgery is used in the management of endometriosis, but not at the time a patient would initiate treatment with GnRH analogues, where there is an aim to preserve fertility for the future. 

## Response B14c 

Subgroup analysis comparing patients requiring radical surgeries, such as hysterectomy or oophorectomy, with patients eligible for linzagolix treatment would not be relevant for several reasons based on clinical practice and patients' characteristics. 

Radical surgeries are typically considered for patients who have exhausted all other treatment options, including pharmacological therapies and conservative surgeries, and for whom these approaches have proven ineffective or sub-optimal. This subgroup represents a clinical population distinct from patients earlier in their treatment pathway, where linzagolix may be considered a treatment option. For patients who are offered radical surgeries in the early stages of their treatment pathway, pharmacological treatment is usually considered as less, or not, effective. Radical surgeries are definitive procedures that preclude the possibility of future pregnancy, whereas linzagolix offers an approach that aligns with the goal of fertility preservation. 

As a result, the treatment goals and clinical outcomes of radical surgeries and linzagolix treatment are fundamentally different and not directly comparable. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 280 -->

**B 15.  Priority question: Page 127 of the CS mentions that “according to clinical experts, whether or not surgery could be considered a direct comparator to medical therapies is dependent on the type of endometriosis.” Please clarify for which types of endometriosis surgery can be seen as a direct comparator, and provide a subgroup analysis if there are indeed certain patients (depending on the type of endometriosis) for whom surgery is either a comparator or not.** 

According to expert clinical opinion,[2] surgery might be considered a direct comparator to pharmacological treatments, depending on the type of endometriosis, clinical management, and patient-specific characteristics and/or preferences. However, clinical experts lacked consensus regarding the types of endometrioses for which surgery could be considered a direct comparator. 

Concerning deep endometriosis, the complexity and high risk of complications were an indication to prioritise pharmacological therapies for some respondents. For others, surgical intervention might be prioritised to remove/shrink big deposits, i.e., treating clinicians reported different experiences and recommendations for clinical management. Patients also have different priorities and characteristics that may favour either pharmacological or surgical intervention. In summary, the definition of specific subgroups for which surgery could be seen as a direct comparator to pharmacological therapies (and specifically linzagolix 200mg +ABT) is not possible.

## _**Clinical effectiveness parameters**_ 

**B 17.  Priority question: On page 127, the company reports that “the principal source of data used to inform the effectiveness of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is EDELWEISS 3”. Also, section B.3.3.1 mentions that “both sets are derived from patient responses to treatment and individual patient-level data from EDELWEISS 3.” However, on page 117 of the CS, it is reported that the “markov transitions during initial treatment at month 6 were based on EDELWEISS 6 data”. Please explain why these transitions were only informed from EDELWEISS 6 data and not EDELWEISS 3 or both. Please also explain why the transitions to the health states contingent upon the level of pain experienced by the patient are only informed from EDELWEISS 3 trial data and not EDELWEISS 6 data. On the other hand, Table 40 of the CS also presents the probabilities of transitioning among pain-related health states, and these were informed from EDELWEISS 6. Please describe in detail the inputs that are informed from EDELWEISS 3 and the inputs that are informed from EDELWEISS 6 trial data. Please also explain in short, the rationale behind using a certain trial population for each of the (set) of inputs.** 

In the CS document, section B.3.3.1 contains an error and should be written as follows: 

Two sets of health states are used in the model to address patient response to treatment. The first set, applied during the initial decision tree, includes three possible response states: no response, partial response and complete response. The second set, based on EAP levels, is used after the first six months of treatment and consists of three overall pelvic pain states (no pain/mild, moderate, and severe). **Both sets are derived from patient responses to treatment and individual patient-level data. Response-based health-states and transitions are informed by the EDELWEISS 3 study, while pain-based health-states and transitions are informed by the EDELWEISS 6 study.** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 282 -->

The selection of data from EDELWEISS 3 and its extension, EDELWEISS 6, in the economic model was guided by the specific context of each transition and the relevance of the trial populations. Transitions in the initial decision tree were based on EDELWEISS 3, as its co-primary endpoint at three months provided the foundation for response-based health-states. Moreover, the EDELWEISS 3 population closely mirrors the modelled cohort at this stage—patients initiating GnRH antagonist therapy after a diagnosis of endometriosis and with a history of prior treatment. Transitions between response-related health states and pain-related health states at the sixth month, as well as subsequent transitions between painrelated states in the Markov chain beyond the sixth month, were informed by EDELWEISS 6 data, as the EDELWEISS 6 population more accurately represents patients who have already undergone six months of linzagolix treatment. The use of EDELWEISS 6 data enabled the representation of transitions between pain-related health states during ongoing GnRH antagonist therapy.

- **B 19.  Priority question: On page 134 it is noted that the percentage of women discontinuing treatment due to pregnancy was estimated from the live birth rate in the UK. Please comment on the validity of this assumption. In your response, please explain why the birth rate of the general population would be applicable to a population with endometriosis.** 

The assumption to estimate the percentage of women discontinuing treatment due to pregnancy based on the live birth rate in the general UK population was made due to the absence of data on pregnancy rates for women with symptomatic endometriosis undergoing GnRH antagonist therapy. While the live birth rate in the general population may not fully reflect the population with symptomatic endometriosis, it serves as a proxy to address this parameter conservatively (the pregnancy rate is expected to be lower as compared with the percentage of women trying to get pregnant). 

**B 20.  It is noted that some clinical parameters such as the response rate for laparoscopic surgery (informed from Johnson et al. 2004), the pain recurrence following surgery (informed from Vercellini et al. 2003), and disutility value for patients with infertility (informed from Relugolix NICE committee papers with the original source published in the 1990) are based on some relatively old studies. Please explain if there is a reason these studies were considered more appropriate over more recent ones.** 

Based on the SLR described in the Appendix M of the CS we have identified four studies that could potentially be used to inform response rates for laparoscopic surgery: Johnson et al. 2004, Sutton et al. 1994, Lalchandani et al. 2005 and Abbot et al. 2004 (Table 12).[16–19] All four studies were incorporated into the costeffectiveness model of the CS. The SLR did not identify more recent studies. Johnson et al. 2004 were selected as the patient population, and the definition of response was most in line with the population and response rate considered for GnRH analogues. Based on Johnson et al. 2004 we utilised values for visual analogue scale (VAS) ≥50% reduction in NMPP, as it was the highest value from all response endpoints reported in this study (which varied between 31.5–50%), 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 285 -->

reflecting a conservative approach. In scenario analyses, we tested the response rate from Sutton et al. 1994, which was less preferred as the definition of response was based on any improvement on VAS (0–10), and the study population comprised women with pain _suggestive_ of endometriosis. Lalchandani et al. 2005 was not selected as this study included women with minimal to moderate endometriosis and reported symptom-free outcomes. Abbot et al. 2004 was not selected as the response in this study was defined as any improvement in pain. 

The response rates utilised in base case and scenario analysis also align with the expert’s opinion.[2,3]

Three studies were considered to inform pain recurrence following surgery: Vercellini et al. 2003, Shakiba et al. 2008 (found via SLR described in the Appendix M of the CS) and Soliman 2017 (found via SLR described in the Appendix G).[15,20,21] Vercellini et al. was selected for a base case as the study population and reported outcomes were most comparable with the study population and outcomes applied for linzagolix. In addition, it was possible to digitise data from Kaplan–Meier curves presented in this study. Vercellini et al. reported a probability of recurrence of moderate to severe dysmenorrhea in patients who were undergoing first-line operative laparoscopy for symptomatic minimal to severe endometriosis and who reported pelvic pain of more than 6 months duration. The other studies reported reoperation free survival (Shakiba et al. 2008) or reoperation free survival or retreatment free survival (Soliman et al. 2017). We found these endpoints less accurate and incorporated data from Shakiba et al. 2008 for scenario analysis as it was possible to digitise it more accurately (in Soliman et al. 2017, curves are already smoothed, which makes it difficult to digitise and reconstruct properly). 

We used the disutility value for patients with infertility based on the WHO report (2024[22] ) to maintain consistency with the relugolix STA. In the SLR described in Appendix H of the CS, we have found only one alternative source to inform this parameter, but due to a possible typographical error we have not used values presented in that source in the base case (Aubry et al. 2017[23] ). We tried to contact the authors for a second time but did not receive any response.
