- **B 21.  Section 3.4.4. focuses on the adverse events (AEs), also referred to as adverse reactions, associated with linzagolix and its comparator, which were included in the scenario analyses. As shown in Table 61, the incidence of these AEs (depression, headache, hot flushes, and increased blood pressure) was set to 0.0% for linzagolix, based on data from the EDELWEISS 3 trial. Please clarify the rationale for this assumption, as information in the clinical effectiveness section (Section B.2.10) suggests that these adverse reactions do indeed occur in patients treated with linzagolix. For that matter, while depression and increased blood pressure were among the adverse reactions included in the cost-effectiveness model, they appear not to be recorded as adverse reactions in the clinical effectiveness section of the CS (which does mention “mood swings”).** 

In accordance with the applied methodology (Section B.3.4.3 of CS), the costeffectiveness model included only severe adverse events (grade 3 or higher). As mentioned in Section B.2.10.2 of the CS, most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) during the EDELWEISS 3 study were mild or moderate in intensity, and the incidence of severe TEAEs was low and comparable between groups (Placebo: 1 severe TEAE; linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: 2 severe TEAE). For this reason, it was decided to use data on adverse events from the NICE STA for relugolix and include them in the model exclusively for scenario analysis, in which probabilities of such events for linzagolix were set to be 0. Due to generally low instances of severe AEs during endometriosis treatment with GnRH analogues, its inclusion has a very limited influence on the cost-effectiveness model results.

## _**Health-related quality of life**_ 

- **B 23.  Priority question: It is stated that since HRQoL data were extracted from EDELWEISS 3 rather than EDELWEISS 6 (due to the possible attrition bias), and therefore the values obtained from EDELWEISS 6 were not described.** 

   - **a) Please provide a detailed explanation of the “possible attrition bias” argument.**

## Response B23a 

Patients who completed the six-month treatment period in the EDELWEISS 3 study were invited to enter the EDELWEISS 6 extension study. The primary objective of EDELWEISS 6 was to assess the maintenance of efficacy of linzagolix for up to an additional six months (up to 12 months of treatment in total) in women who had already completed six months of linzagolix treatment at a dose of 75 mg alone or 200 mg plus ABT in EDELWEISS 3. As a result, the population of EDELWEISS 6 consisted of patients who had already experienced six months of treatment with linzagolix and chose to continue. Specifically, there is a potential risk, that patients who did not perceive therapeutic benefits or who experienced the AEs during the initial six months were less likely to enroll in the extension study. Consequently, EDELWEISS 6 might represent a population with more favourable responses to linzagolix, leading to an overestimation of its impact on health-related quality of life. Examining the HRQoL data from EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 underscores the potential impact of attrition bias in the extension study. The mean changes from

To mitigate the influence of attrition bias on our CE model, we adopted a conservative approach by utilising HRQoL data from EDELWEISS 3. This study includes the broader initial patient population, encompassing both responders and non-responders to the treatment, thereby providing a more balanced and unbiased dataset. By using data from EDELWEISS 3, we aim to ensure that our regression model accurately reflects the real-world effectiveness of linzagolix without the skewing effects that could arise from the selective continuation of patients in EDELWEISS 6.

**would be expected the change for the severe pain health state to go in the same direction. Please justify why the scenario analysis led to an increase in the utility of patients in the severe health state, while led to a decrease in the utility value for the non-response health state.** 

## Response 26a 

Baseline data contain data from day 1. 

## Response B26b 

Scenarios were built based on methodological consistency. The base case scenario includes two regression models that do not include baseline observations, as they are irrelevant for treatment outcomes (patients at month 3 or 6 are assumed to be different vs patients at baseline). The second scenario includes two regression models which do include baseline observations as relevant for the analysis outcomes (only response status or severity is relevant). The difference can be explained with the following justification: 

- In the response model in the base case we utilised 3 and 6 months data only, where the patients’ response status was known. In scenario analysis, we additionally assumed that all patients at baseline were non-responders. It is possible that some of these patients had relatively high utility values at baseline and these patients also responded to treatment and subsequently transferred to response health (as baseline utility was found predictive of the future utility value under response). 

- In the pain model in base case we utilised data set with sixmonths observations only. It is possible that only the most severe and resistant patients remained in this health-state after the treatment with linzagolix, as compared with the full data set utilised in the scenario analysis; 

## **B 27.  Priority question: On page 158 of the CS, it is noted that according to clinical expert opinion, patients wanting to conceive can stop medical** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 294 -->

**therapy at any time. For this reason, there was no disutility assumed due to infertility whilst on therapy.** 

- **a) Please comment if this approach may be neglecting the trade-off in quality of life that some patients may encounter when they must decide on the management of endometriosis symptoms as compared to their child wish, which is inhibited by the medical treatment.** 

- **b) Please add a scenario to the model that includes a disutility for infertility whilst on therapy.** 

## Response B27a 

The potential trade-off in quality of life for patients managing endometriosis symptoms while considering their fertility aspiration is an important consideration. However, in the case of medical therapy, which is often the therapy of choice, alternative options for patients who wish to conceive (i.e., laparoscopic surgery) are available and may mitigate this trade-off. 

This trade-off in quality of life particularly affects patients with a long treatment history, for whom subsequent therapies may no longer represent a treatment of choice but rather the only remaining option. However, such patients are generally not treated with medical therapy but are instead referred for radical surgical interventions. 

The model accounts for the disutilities experienced by patients most significantly affected by this trade-off. The first group, considered in the base case, comprising patients who have undergone radical surgeries, experiences a reduction in quality of life due to the inability to conceive following such procedures. The second group, consisting of patients in more pretreated health-states with limited remaining treatment options (post-laparoscopy states and other medical treatment) who must decide between managing endometriosis symptoms and preserving their fertility aspirations, was represented in one of the scenarios where infertility-related disutility was incorporated into the quality of life for patients undergoing medical therapies. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 295 -->

## Response B27b 

As utility values were calculated on the data set from the linzagolix study EDELWEISS 3, adding additional infertility disutilities to patients in health states where pharmacological treatment is used (especially while patients are on linzagolix therapy) does not feel justifiable. 

We suggest another scenario be considered to address remaining uncertainties, where no infertility disutility is applied in any health-state. The results for such a scenario are presented in Table 15 and Table 16.

- **B 31.  Please provide a justification for the calculation of the utility scores for the other medical treatment and surgery treatment health states. How valid is the use the average utility scores of health states from which patients can transition to those states? Patients transition to another health state because the symptoms deteriorates or don’t improve, wouldn’t that mean that the quality of life utility also deteriorates?** 

The calculations of utility scores for other medical treatment and surgical treatment health states were designed to capture the quality of life implications for patients undergoing specific medical interventions while aligning well with data from the literature. The use of average utility scores of health-states from which patients transition to other medical treatment and surgery treatment states reflects the range of symptom severity and outcomes experienced by patients on subsequent therapy. Although transitions often occur due to symptom deterioration or lack of therapeutic effect, the methodology accounts for this by incorporating lower utility values from severe and no-response health states into the average. This approach aligns with established frameworks, such as the one described by Wang et al., 2019.[25] Applying this approach, patients who are more pretreated have lower quality of life as compared to patients responding to initial treatments.

Please provide more details on the source used to inform these inputs. What are the remaining procedures that were not considered in this analysis?**

for the distribution of laparoscopic procedures, and Theramex Data on File: Endometriosis Market Research Survey for Yselty[®] (Linzagolix)[14] for radical (hysterectomy and oophorectomy) surgeries. The percentages in this table represent the proportions of patients who underwent specific surgical procedures and are used as inputs in the model. The calculation formula for the costs of these surgeries is divided by the sum of the proportions, meaning that the proportions do not need to sum to 100%. No additional procedures for either conservative or radical surgeries were included in the analysis beyond those mentioned in Table 45 of CS.

## _**Electronic model**_ 

## **B 36.  On sheet ‘Controls’, rows 67, 68, 72 and 73, changing the user defined** 

## **value has no impact on the results. What setting in the model needs to be changed in order to use the user defined values for the calculation of the results?** 

In the electronic model, user-defined values are entered in dedicated tabs, while the Controls tab only displays these values. Specifically: 

1) Infertility disutility (Controls, row 67) is defined by entering a value in the Utility values tab (cell C29); 

2). The percentage of patients affected by infertility disutility (Controls, row 68) is defined by entering a value in the Utility values tab (cell C32); 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 302 -->

3). Laparoscopy complications disutility (Controls, row 72) is defined by entering a value in the Utility values tab (cell C39); 

4) Hysterectomy/bilateral oophorectomy complications disutility is defined in the Utility values tab (cell C36). 

We acknowledge that this setup may not feel entirely intuitive. However, it reflects the principle of keeping user-defined values related to utility in the Utility values tab, thereby maintaining the Controls tab in a more streamlined and readable format. 

## **Section C : Textual clarification and additional points** 

**C 1. Table 46 of the CS presents the discontinuation rates that were used in the electronic model for the alternative health states. The rate for the no Pain/mild and moderate health-states is set at 3.03%. However, on the “efficacy” sheet of the electronic model this value was set at 6.45% for in the leuprorelin, while the value of 3.03% is used for other GnRH agonists. Please comment if this an error in the electronic model or the CS** 

**document. Please correct the error if that pertains to the electronic model and provide updated results.** 

The values presented in Table 46 of the CS document are correct. However, a technical error was identified in the electronic model, specifically in the "efficacy" sheet, where the discontinuation rate for leuprorelin was erroneously displayed as 6.45%. Despite this, the correct value of 3.03% was applied in the calculations throughout the model. The error has been corrected, and the results were recalculated to confirm consistency. As expected, the corrected model produced identical results, and therefore no updates to the CS document were necessary. The revised model has been provided.

**C 4. Table 61 of the CS presents an overview of the frequencies of adverse reactions. Table 61 has been also corrected (depression: changed for 0.40% and hot flushes changed for 0.47%). ## **1 Clinical effectiveness** 

## _**1.1 Indirect treatment comparisons vs. relugolix combination therapy**_ 

In the absence of head-to-head data, an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) was performed using the Bucher analysis method to compare the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus add-back therapy (ABT) with relugolix 40 mg plus ABT (relugolix combination therapy [relugolix-oestradiol-norethisterone acetate] [relugolix CT]), a pharmacological comparator of relevance to the decision problem using published evidence from the clinical systematic literature review (SLR; see Section B.2.1 and Appendix D; an ITC comparing linzagolix and leuprorelin was presented in the company submission, section B2.9). The efficacy outcomes analysed in the ITC (Table 1) were based on those specified in the final scope issued by NICE and the availability of data reported in the literature. 

**Table 1: Outcomes assessed in the ITC for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT vs. relugolix CT** 

|**Outcome**|**Analyses**|**Output statistics**|

## **1.1.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies from the clinical SLR** 

As described in Section B.2.1 and Appendix D, an SLR was conducted in September 2024. Of the 22 studies identified for the intervention (n=2) and comparators (n=20), only two studies relating to linzagolix and relugolix CT were eligible according to the 

Addendum to clarification response – linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 317 -->

scope for this submission. The population, intervention, outcomes, study design (PICOS) criteria used for the ITC are presented in Appendix D. 

## **1.1.2 Risk of bias** 

The methodological quality of each trial was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Collaboration’s revised risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2).[1] Disagreements were resolved by consensus. The risk of bias was defined as low for all the trials included in the Bucher analysis. Further details can be found in Appendix D. 

## **1.1.3 Overview of the selected studies** 

The SLR identified the EDELWEISS[2] and EDELWEISS 3[3] studies for linzagolix in endometriosis-associated pain (EAP) and 20 comparator trials (described in 18 publications). The studies considered to be suitable for inclusion in the ITC Bucher analysis are presented in Table 2. 

The SLR for the comparators searched for trials that could be compared with the trials found in the review for the intervention (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT). Therefore, only studies with 12 or 24 weeks of follow-up were included in the ITC for the efficacy analysis. Safety was assessed using the longest available follow-up period of 24 weeks. 

Although two linzagolix studies (EDELWEISS 3, EDELWEISS) were identified from the SLR, only the EDELWEISS 3 trial was included in the ITC. The EDELWEISS study[2] was a dose-ranging phase 2b study that included a dose of linzagolix 200 mg alone (without ABT) and was not included in the ITC for the efficacy analysis due to a lack of alignment of clinically relevant endpoints for inclusion in the treatment comparison. In addition, safety in the EDELWEISS study was only assessed for 12 weeks, so this study could not be included in the ITC for the safety analysis. 

Reasons for exclusion of other studies from the ITC included: comparator therapy not relevant to the scope of this submission; no placebo group for comparison with the

<!-- page 318 -->

intervention arm; data displayed only graphically, without detailed breakdown for analysis; outcomes data did not include standard deviation/standard error; lack of clarity of scale used. Further details regarding the rationale for inclusion/exclusion of individual comparator trials on the basis of heterogeneity can be found in Appendix D.

## **1.1.4 Heterogeneity assessment of trials included** 

Consistently reported inclusion/exclusion criteria were age, diagnosis of endometriosis, menstrual cycle, presence of dysmenorrhoea and pelvic pain, history of surgery, and need for treatment. 

No trials were excluded from the Bucher analysis because of their inclusion/ exclusion criteria. The effect of different inclusion/exclusion criteria was assessed by reviewing the baseline characteristics. The included trials used similar inclusion criteria for age, endometriosis diagnosis and interval between menstrual cycles. Although the trials all included adult premenopausal women with moderate to severe endometriosisassociated pain (EAP) as measured by dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP), the scales used to measure dysmenorrhoea and NMPP scores differed between trials. The heterogeneity assessment confirmed the feasibility of an ITC 

Addendum to clarification response – linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 319 -->

between linzagolix vs. relugolix CT. Further details regarding heterogeneity are presented in Appendix D. 

## **1.1.5 Methods** 

An ITC was conducted using the Bucher method performed in R version 4.3.2. The Bucher method can only be applied to two-arm trials. The main assumption is that the relative efficacy of a treatment is the same in all trials included in the ITC to allow the indirect comparison of A vs. C when direct evidence of A vs. B and B vs. C is available. 

The results of the included trials were analysed to determine whether it was possible to construct a network of relationships between the different arms of the trials. The methodology of each study and patient baseline characteristics were also analysed to identify differences between the trials that might impact the health outcomes. SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 were two replicate, phase 3 studies which evaluated similar endpoints over the same observation periods, had the same study design and included patients with similar baseline characteristics. It was, therefore, possible to perform a metaanalysis of the SPIRIT 1/SPIRIT 2 studies and to include the results of the meta-analysis in the ITC. 

The EDELWEISS 3 linzagolix study and the relugolix CT studies SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 differed in their definitions of the co-primary efficacy endpoints dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, in terms of the rating scale used for the pain assessment (verbal rating scale vs. numeric rating scale), magnitude of significant clinical change and the assessment timepoint. Of note, the primary endpoint of EDELWEISS 3 was assessed at 3 months [week 12], whereas the primary endpoint of SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 was assessed at 6 months [week 24]; early pain control in patients is of utmost importance, hence the 3- month assessment was prioritised in the EDELWEISS studies. As patient-level data were available from the EDELWEISS 3 study, reconstruction of the endpoints was performed according to the definitions from the SPIRIT studies to reduce these differences and increase the ITC's validity. Logistic regression modelling was performed using the reconstructed endpoints to obtain outcomes (risk differences) to compare linzagolix with relugolix in an anchored ITC. As the SPIRIT and EDELWEISS 3 studies were generally well-balanced in terms of characteristics, an additional match-adjusted 

Addendum to clarification response – linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 320 -->

indirect comparison (MAIC) was performed using the reconstructed endpoints as a sensitivity analysis. Non-inferiority was defined based on p-values of >0.05 for the ITC and >0.1 for the MAIC (to select prognostic factors or treatment effect modifiers), indicating no statistically significant difference between the treatments. 

Detailed methods for the ITC are presented in Appendix D.

## **1.1.6.2 Safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT vs. relugolix CT** 

The safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT was comparable to relugolix CT (Table 5). Although the ITC results indicate that adverse changes in lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD) were statistically significantly increased with linzagolix vs. relugolix (Table 5), there was no significant difference between treatments for total hip BMD and the difference for lumbar spine BMD was not considered large enough to be clinically meaningful.[5–9] It is likely that the lumbar spine BMD result was affected by differences in the placebo arms across both trials, which served as a reference point for the ITC. The least squares mean percentage change from baseline to month 6 (measured by dualenergy X-ray absorptiometry) in lumbar spine BMD was comparable for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT (−0.80 in EDELWEISS 3[10] ; Section B.10.8) and relugolix CT (−0.70 in 

Addendum to clarification response – linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 322 -->

SPIRIT1, −0.78 in SPIRIT2[4] ), however results for the placebo groups differed between the EDELWEISS 3 and SPIRIT studies (0.78 in EDELWEISS 3; 0.21 in SPIRIT1, 0.02 in SPIRIT2). 

BMD was also assessed using Z-scores, which provide information on the BMD of the study population by comparing it with a reference group of women of the same age. In pre-menopausal women, Z-scores below −2.0 indicate a BMD ‘below the expected range for age’ and Z-scores above −2.0 indicate a BMD ‘within the expected range for age’.[5–9] In EDELWEISS 3, there was a greater numerical difference between mean lumbar spine Z-score at baseline in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT arm vs the placebo arm (0.25 vs 0.49, respectively; Section B.2.4.4), compared with smaller differences for relugolix CT vs. placebo groups in the SPIRIT1 and SPIRIT2 studies (0.17 vs 0.18, and 0.23 vs 0.35 for lumbar spine in SPIRIT1 and SPIRIT2, respectively).[4] 

Further reassurance that the lumbar spine BMD changes observed under treatment with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT are not clinically meaningful was provided from longer-term follow-up data after 12 months of treatment in EDELWEISS 6 which indicated that small fluctuations in the median Z-score values between baseline and month 12 were observed in all groups, with no defined pattern, and that minimum Z-scores at month 12 did not decrease below −2.0 at the lumbar spine, −1.4 at the femoral neck, and −1.5 at the total hip, femoral neck, and total hip (Section B.2.10.8). BMD Z-scores, therefore, remained ‘within the expected range for age’ despite 12 months of exposure to linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. Median Z-scores at month 12 for the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group were 0.09 at the lumbar spine, −0.03 at the femoral neck and 0.03 at the total hip.

## **2 Cost effectiveness** 

## _**2.1 Economic analysis**_ 

The patient population, model structure and features are identical to that described in the company submission, sections B3.2.1, B3.2.2 and B3.2.3. 

## **2.1.1 Intervention and comparators** 

The intervention evaluated in the model is linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, administered orally once daily. Linzagolix 200 mg is designed to address endometriosis symptoms by reducing EAP, while adding ABT preserves BMD. As a result, this regimen can be used continuously without a predefined treatment duration, except for cessation at the onset of menopause. 

The comparators in the model are: 

- Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists; with the licensed agents in the UK of leuprorelin acetate, goserelin, and triptorelin. All are administered via intramuscular or subcutaneous injection and are available monthly and threemonthly formulations. All GnRH agonists were assumed to have equal efficacy and safety [see company submission section B.2.9.7] 

- Laparoscopic surgery (excision and ablation) 

- Relugolix CT (40 mg relugolix, 1 mg oestradiol, and 0.5 mg norethisterone acetate), administered orally, once daily 

## _**2.2 Clinical parameters and variables**_ 

The clinical parameters are identical to those described in the company submission, section B3.3. Based on the results of the ITC, the efficacy of linzagolix and relugolix are assumed to be the same, therefore the probabilities used for relugolix in the model for response after 3 and 6 months, and transitions to and between pain-related health states are identical to those used for linzagolix and GnRH agonists (Table 6 to Table 8).

## _**2.4 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation**_ 

A cost and resources SLR was conducted to identify any relevant cost or healthcare resource use data relevant to the model. Full details of the SLR and results are presented in the company submission Appendix I. 

The model includes several cost categories to reflect the key cost components related to drug therapies, surgical procedures, disease management, the natural course of pregnancy, and management of fertility issues in patients with endometriosis. These remain the same in the model, including relugolix, except the addition of drug acquisition costs for relugolix CT, as detailed below. 

## **2.4.1.1 Drug acquisition costs** 

The costs of medical therapy (linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, relugolix CT and GnRH agonists) were applied in model cycles relating to patients on treatment, i.e., within a decision tree in the initial response states and whilst in No pain/mild or Moderate pain states thereafter. The duration of therapy for the intervention and comparator was assumed to be fixed (1.5 years for GnRH agonists) or without restriction (linzagolix and 

Addendum to clarification response – linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 329 -->

relugolix CT). Drug acquisition costs were not applied for treatment breaks (in the Offtreatment, No pain/mild and Pregnancy health-states). 

A 50:50 split was assumed between patients treated with the short- (1-month) and long(3-month) acting GnRH agonists - leuprorelin acetate, goserelin and triptorelin. This assumption was based on the equivalent parameter in the NICE STA for relugolix and indicated by expert opinion.[11,12] 

No wastage or compliance was considered in the base case analysis. However, compliance for linzagolix, relugolix CT and ABT for linzagolix was used in the scenario analysis, based on data from the EDELWEISS 6 study and relugolix CT long-term study.[13,14]

## _**2.7 Exploring uncertainty**_ 

Sensitivity analyses explored the underlying uncertainty in the base-case cost- 

effectiveness results. These include deterministic sensitivity analyses, probabilistic sensitivity analyses, and scenario analyses. The results for net marginal benefit are presented only for the base-case scenario but are available within the cost-effectiveness model. For comparison with laparoscopic surgery, no probabilistic or deterministic cost- 

Addendum to clarification response – linzagolix in endometriosis © Theramex (2024). All rights reserved. 




<!-- page 332 -->

effectiveness analyses were conducted as this is an additional comparator only. However, two alternative scenarios on surgery efficacy were performed. 

## **2.7.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

A probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was conducted to explore the uncertainty around key model parameters. PSA was conducted by varying these parameters using their upper and lower bound values based on an assigned distribution. 1,000 simulations were run for the PSA, by which time the incremental results converged to a stable mean, represented by the probabilistic incremental costs. The probabilistic result (£822) is close to the base case (£835), indicating that the cost-effectiveness results are robust (see Table 13 and Table 15). 

Output from the PSA iterations is presented as scatter points on the cost-effectiveness plane for linzagolix vs. relugolix (Figure 1). All scatter points representing the simulated incremental costs and QALYs are in the northeast quadrant for linzagolix vs. relugolix. This indicates that linzagolix plus ABT is associated with higher costs compared to relugolix and has comparable QALY. 

The PSA results were not plotted as a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC), as the QALY difference between compared therapies is equal to 0 or close to 0 in all iterations.

## **2.7.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

One-way deterministic sensitivity analyses (OWSAs) were conducted to examine the sensitivity of the model result to lower and upper estimates of parameter values. 

The results from the OWSA are presented in the form of a tornado diagram where the ten parameters with the largest influence on the ICER are presented in Figure 2 for linzagolix vs. relugolix. 

The tornado diagram below shows that the maximum age of patients with endometriosis has the largest impact on the incremental costs. Overall, the results appear robust, and none of the parameters considerably impact the incremental costs, as all results are within the range of £650 – £950 in any of the OWSAs.

## **2.7.3 Scenario analysis** 

The sensitivity of the model results to changes in key assumptions or parameters was explored through several scenario analyses. The scenario analysis results are presented below, with pairwise ICERs presented (Table 16). The most impactful scenarios are related to the time horizon parameters: different time horizons, or alternative starting age of patients with the disease. Other significant scenarios included treatment discontinuation assumptions, alternative rules for continuing initial treatment (i.e., minimum health benefit required to continue therapy), and discount rates for costs. 

The overall conclusion did not change for any of the alternative scenarios. 

Alternative approaches to obtaining health state transitions in the model remained the same as outlined in the company submission, section B.3.11.3.

## _**2.8 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence**_ 

Compared with the potential future second-line medical treatment (relugolix CT), linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is associated with incremental costs of £835. The results are stable across all types of sensitivity analyses. 

The limitations remained the same as outlined in the company submission, section B.3.15.

## Response A13C 

An in-depth analysis of the GnRH agonist trials excluded due to missing variability measures, or the data being presented graphically (with no numerical values provided) revealed that only one additional study could potentially be included in a comparison (Acs et al. 2015). However, the process has further limitations, and we believe the study should not be included in a hypothetical NMA. With limitations, it could be tested in a simple ITC by comparing the results from Acs et al. 2015 with those from the EDELWEISS 3 study. The analysis is presented in a dedicated paragraph below. The list of studies presenting data graphically and the reasons for not including them in the comparison are specified below. 

**Table 1: Studies presenting data in graphs and the reasons for not including them in an ITC and/or NMA** 

|**Study**|**Reasons for not including the study in ITC and/or NMA**|
|---|---|
|Acs 2015|The baseline characteristics presented in the publication are limited, encompassing<br>only mean age, BMI, mean time since diagnosis, and race. While it<br>is feasible to derive the mean values for dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, the standard<br>errors of the mean cannot be derived from the graphs, and the imputation of<br>variability measures would be necessary. Implementing data extraction from graphs<br>and the imputation of variability measures poses a considerable risk of bias.<br>Aside from the data presented on dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, data for<br>endometriosis-associated pelvic pain assessed on a numerical rating scale (NRS) is<br>available. ## **Indirect treatment comparison of the results from Acs et al. (2015) with those from the EDELWEISS 3 study** 

To compare results reported by Acs (2015) for leuprorelin with those from the EDELWEISS 3 study, it was assumed that dysmenorrhea and non-menstrual pelvic pain (NMPP) scores measured using the verbal rating scale (VRS) could be compared with those assessed using the

In addition to deriving confidence intervals for leuprorelin 3.75 mg versus placebo mean differences using the method described above, an approach based on scaling the standard deviation (SD) of linzagolix 200 mg versus placebo MDs was also applied ( **method 2** )[5] . This scaling utilised the relationship between variance and sample size, adjusting linzagolix SDs using the effective sample size (neff)[6] ratio for the Acs et al. 2015 study. A significant limitation of this comparison is the substantially lower baseline values reported by Acs et al. 2015 for the leuprorelin 3.75 mg and placebo arms compared to those observed in the EDELWEISS 3 study. Specifically, baseline dysmenorrhea scores for the leuprorelin and placebo arms were 1.29 and 1.40, respectively, as reported by Acs (2015), whereas, in the EDELWEISS 3 study, both arms recorded baseline dysmenorrhoea scores of 2.29. Similarly, baseline NMPP scores were markedly lower in the Acs (2015) study, with values of 0.94 and 0.96 for the leuprorelin and placebo arms, respectively, compared to 1.80 and 1.78 in the 



<!-- page 344 -->

EDELWEISS 3 study. These pronounced differences in baseline values limit the comparability of the results and must be carefully considered when interpreting the findings. 

The supplemented results do not change conclusions regarding the relative efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT vs leuprorelin 3.75 mg, as presented in the company submission Section B2.

**High risk of bias:** The study is judged to be at high risk of bias in at least one domain for this result or the study is judged to have some concerns for multiple domains in a way that substantially lowers confidence in the result.

## **B.25 Priority question: On page 143 of the CS, it is stated that the baseline** 

**observations were excluded from response regression models because patients in the no-response state showed higher utility values at the 3-month mark compared with baseline. At the other hand, it is shown in Table 50 of the CS that base EQ-5D-5L is associated with higher utility score.** 

**a) Please reflect on the validity of excluding base EQ-5D-3L although it is associated with a better HRQoL at later time points** 

**b) Please also include base EQ-5D-3L as covariate in the quality of life regression models and allow the use of these regression models in the estimation of healthrelated quality of life utilities.** 



<!-- page 354 -->

## Response B25a 

For the pain regression model, only 6-month observations were included, while for the response regression model, 3- and 6-month data were deemed suitable. During the early feasibility process, we considered the impact of baseline EQ-5D-3L as potentially significant, but due to potential autocorrelation, these baseline data were not included in favour of baseline pain scores (avoiding a potential collinearity problem). In both models, with and without baseline EQ-5D-3L, the covariates related to model states were statistically significant, thus supporting the conclusion that there is minimal impact on regression outputs and conclusions. 

## Response B25b 

We acknowledged the request of NICE and included the base EQ-5D-3L as a covariate for selecting the best fitted models. We built two requested regression models: 

1. pain-based for health states: no pain/mild, moderate, severe. 

2. response-based for health states: no response, partial response, complete response. 

Predictions of the newly developed regression models can be used in the costeffectiveness model (see Response B.24b) and have also been integrated into an additional scenario analysis (see response B.28). 

## **1) Pain-based model with base EQ-5D covariate** 

A utility regression model was developed for pain-related health states, incorporating baseline EQ-5D-3L as a binary covariate (1 for patients with baseline EQ-5D-3L below the median and 0 for those above the median). The model’s performance was assessed using the AIC and BIC criteria. (see Table B.25.1 below).

## Conclusions 

Utilising different regression models based on data from the EDELWEISS 3 study does not yield different QALY or ICER outputs, regardless of the comparator. Similarly, the 



<!-- page 363 -->

results generated with observed mean utility estimates (no regression modelling) from the EDELWEISS 3 study are close to the base case. 

The only utility scenario with markedly different results is based on the relugolix STA utility estimates, where the linzagolix QALY gain is lower, and the ICER is higher. In such a scenario, linzagolix remains cost-effective with an ICER below the defined threshold of £20,000 per QALY. The difference arises because the relugolix model and utility analysis did not define pain states; instead, they only defined response states. Additionally, it was assumed that all patients would experience the marginal benefits of treatment with initial GnRH analogues, even after the therapy had ended.

## **Single Technology Appraisal** 

## **Linzagolix for treating symptoms of endometriosis** 

## **Clinical expert response** 

1. We understand that relugolix CT is a combination therapy and linzagolix can be used with or without add-back therapy. For people with endometriosis, would you expect them to always take linzagolix with add-back therapy? 

Theoretically, studies indicate Linzagolix can be taken safely without add-back therapy (Edelweiss 3 study). If taken alone, patients can have significant reduction in dysmenorrhoea and are beneficial for patients not wishing to take hormonal medications or have contraindications such as thromboembolic and cerebrovascular diseases. Studies have shown only up to 3 months. 

Having to administer Linzagolix without add-back therapy is largely related to the dose and time duration in taking Linzagolix. 

Linzagolix doses between 75mg and 125mg in Caucasian women were safe enough to keep oestrogen levels between 20-50pg/ml. This was deemed the best balance between a reduction in endometriosis symptoms and safety end points.  If these levels are maintained and patient symptom-free, then there will be no need for add-back therapy. However it would be prudent to check bone mineral density levels. 

Beyond these doses, levels of oestrogen will drop to levels which will increase the risk of bone mineral density reduction and increase in menopausal symptoms such as hot-flushes. 

If women fail to respond to the lower dose then higher doses of Linzagolix (up to 200mg) may be warranted as a suggested  management plan.  This will inevitably reduce oestrogen levels beyond safety endpoints in which case addback therapy would be recommended to avoid safety risks. 

But whether Linzagolix can always be taken with add-back therapy will largely depend on if they have symptoms, if they have significant risk factors against add-back therapy and medical history. 

2. What, if any, are substantial differences in the administration and monitoring between relugolix CT use and linzagolix ABT for symptoms of endometriosis? 

The administration of Linzagolix with ABT and Relugolix-CT will be the same.  They both have similar pharmacokinetics and can safely be taken orally and given once a day.  They both come in tablet form with Linzagolix being manufactured for studies in the 50mg, 75mg, 100mg and 200mg dosages but commercially come in 100 and 200mg tablets. Linzagolix would need to be taken with a separate ABT tablets in the form of estradiol 1mg and norethisterone 0.5mg. 

Clinical expert response Linzagolix for treating symptoms of endometriosis 




<!-- page 373 -->

Monitoring patients while on either Relugolix CT or Linzagolix ABT would be more or less the same.  These would include bone mineral density assessments, blood pressure monitoring as both require hormone replacement.  If however there is any doubt on adherence that Linzagolix is being taken without ABT then there is more risk of a drop in BMD, in which closer monitoring may be required. 

3. What, if any, are substantial differences in the safety and tolerability profiles between relugolix CT or linzagolix ABT for symptoms of endometriosis? 

Measurements for parameters of safety have largely been in relation to its pharmacokinetics, vasomotor side-effects, and its anti-oestrogen effects. Its effects in its metabolism and blocking GnRH receptors with ABT will lead to a less dose-dependent hypooestrogenic state with menopausal symptoms and a reduction in bone mineral density. 

Studies show that Linzagolix-ABT can have a small increase in lipid profile with a 15% rise in total cholesterol and 20% increase in LDL. These changes were not seen with Relugolix-CT. So patients with hypercholesterolaemia taking LinzagolixABT may require lipid profile monitoring.   There was also an initial transient increase in AST but this level normalised whilst participants were still on treatment within the 52 week extended study. 

For menopausal side-effects, the most common was hot-flushes which were reported in both studies with Relugolix CT and Linzagolix ABT.  Both were of similar rates but neither higher than 15% of patients.  (Relugolix-CT up to 11% and Linzagolix-ABT up to 13%). 

BMD levels decline for Relugolix CT, Linzagolix ABT 100mg and Linzagolix ABT 200mg when given up to 52 weeks to -0.8%, -1.5% and -2% from their baseline respectively. So use beyond 1 year could suggest levels will continue to decline with continued use. 

I reiterate that Relugolix studies, Linzagolix-ABT extension studies do not exceed beyond 52 weeks so long term effects of these symptoms cannot yet be objectively determined. 

4. In terms of clinical outcomes, do you consider relugolix CT and linzagolix ABT to be comparable treatments for the symptoms of endometriosis? 

There are no direct studies comparing both together Relugolix-CT and LinzagolixABT for the treatment of endometriosis however, in terms of their pharmacokinetics, mechanism of action and tolerability they compare.   There is comparisons in the LIBERTY and ELARIS extension studies showing that significant reduction in blood loss (less than 80mls) were seen in 77% in Relugolix CT and between 76% and 94% in patients who received 200mg Linzagolix amenorrhoea was established.  This could be extrapolated for dysmenorrhoea (as no menstrual bleeding means no dysmenorrhoea) . The 200mg Linzagolix-ABT showed complete amenorrhoea in as high as 81% of patients after 52 weeks of the trial drug. However both treatments reduce to similar degrees endometriosis associated pains and non menstrual pelvic pains. 

5.  Do you have any other comments on the comparison of relugolix CT and linzagolix ABT for symptoms of endometriosis? 

Clinical expert response Linzagolix for treating symptoms of endometriosis 

2 of 3 



<!-- page 374 -->

Comparative studies for these two drugs were mainly in women at the average age being in their mid thirties to mid forties. Many of the studies were for management of uterine fibroid and heavy menstrual bleeding. Consideration for treatment for endometriosis may be for patients at a younger cohort with fertility considerations. 

Quality of life, Visual Analogue Scores (VAS) and Endometriosis Health Profile 30 (EHP-30)  data for Relugolix, Relugolix CT Linzagolix and Linzagolix ABT all show a comparable improvement in scores when given over the selected period of time. 

Lastly, deciding whether relugolix CT or Linzagolix ABT would largely be patient specific and patients who may require treatment without hormone replacement may initially benefit with Linzagolix only. 

Clinical expert response Linzagolix for treating symptoms of endometriosis

## **1. Executive summary** 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the Evidence Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. If possible, it also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 presents the key model outcomes. Section 1.3 discusses the decision problem, Section 1.4 issues relate to the clinical effectiveness, and Section 1.5 issues related to the cost-effectiveness (CE). A summary is presented in Section 1.6. 

Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on key as well as non-key issues are in the main EAG report, see Sections 2 (decision problem [DP]), 3 (clinical effectiveness) and 4 (CE) for more details. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

## **1.2 Overview of key model outcomes** 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

14 



<!-- page 389 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

Overall, linzagolix 200 mg + ABT is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Increasing the number of QALYs in the no pain/mild state on initial treatment because treatment can be continued until menopause (when compared with leuprorelin) or because a larger proportion of patients experiences no pain/mild symptoms (when compared with surgery). 

- Decreasing the number of QALYs in the no response state (when compared with surgery) because surgery patients wait 18 months in no response before they receive the surgery. 

- Decreasing the number of QALYs in the health states associated with other medical treatment or surgery as fewer patients need these other treatment options. 

Overall, linzagolix 200 mg + ABT is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Increasing the drug acquisition costs on initial treatment due to the higher unit costs and the longer treatment duration 

- Increasing the resource use costs on initial treatment (in comparison with leuprorelin) due to the longer treatment duration 

- Increasing the treatment costs for other medical treatment, laparoscopic waiting and postlaparoscopic treatment (in comparison with leuprorelin), because GnRH agonists, which are more expensive, are part of the treatment baskets for other medical treatment after linzagolix. 

- Decreasing the treatment costs for the surgery states as fewer patients need surgery in the linzagolix arm. 

- Decreasing the resource use costs for the other medical treatment and surgery states as fewer patients enter these health states. 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- The transition probabilities between health states after patients have stopped their initial treatment; 

- Excluding the disutility for infertility (weighted for percentage of women with a child wish) after a radical surgery or including the disutility for infertility (weighted for percentage of women with a child wish)  also in other health states; 

- Using an alternative data source for estimates relating to infertility and pregnancy (Soliman et al. 2017);[1] 

- The utility values for the health states after the initial treatment; 

- Only continuing treatment in complete responders after 6 months. 

## **1.3 The decision problem: summary of the EAG’s key issues** 

The decision problem addressed in the company submission (CS) is broadly in line with the final scope issued by NICE. However, there was uncertainty as to the precise nature of the population in terms of treatment history and line of therapy (Table 1.2). It should be noted that the effectiveness of linzagolix 200 mg plus add-back therapy (ABT) as estimated from the trial might not be applicable to clinical practice due variation in ABT (Table 1.3). There was also a lack of justification for the exclusion of comparators (Table 1.4).

## **1.6 Summary of the EAG’s view** 

The company’s base-case deterministic results for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT compared to leuprorelin and surgery showed ICERs of £5,554 and £693 per QALY gained, respectively. Linzagolix was around £835 more expensive than relugolix, whilst yielding the same number of QALYs. 

20 



<!-- page 395 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

After implementing the EAG preferred assumptions and estimates, these ICERs increased to £8,638 (linzagolix compared to leuprorelin) and £1,082 per QALY gained (linzagolix compared to surgery,) respectively. The incremental costs for linzagolix versus relugolix remained the same as in the company base case.(see Table 1.10). 

The probabilistic results both for the company and the EAG base case were very similar to the deterministic results. The PSA results show for both base cases that the probability of linzagolix being cost-effective at thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000 per QALY gained is 100% compared to leuprorelin and 100% compared to surgery. In the comparison between linzagolix and relugolix, linzagolix is more expensive yielding the same QALYs in all iterations. 

The company defined a large range of scenarios, with were also applied to the EAG preferred base case. In the comparison between linzagolix versus leuprorelin the ICER did not go above £13,000, with various scenarios yielding an ICER around £10,000. In the comparison between linzagolix and surgery the highest ICER was almost £10,000, when a time horizon of 1.5 years was applied. For all other scenarios the ICER remained below £3,000. 

Of the EAG defined exploratory scenario analyses, most had little impact on the results, only using the health state utilities as reported by Wang et al. led to a small increase in the ICERs versus leuprorelin and surgery.[3] In all scenarios considered, linzagolix remained more expensive and equally effectiveas relugolix, as was the case in the EAG base-case analysis.

## **2.1 Population** 

The population in the Scope is “ _Adults with symptoms of endometriosis_ ”, but in the decision problem (DP) it is described as: _“Symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in women with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis”_ (see Table 1).[4] It is also referred to as “second-line” in Table 1, which would seem to be more limited. Figure 2 of the company submission (CS) shows that first-line treatment can be any of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)/analgesics, hormonal treatment or surgery.[4] 

**EAG comment:** The Evidence Assessment Group (EAG) requested clarification as to the precise nature of the medical and surgical treatments mentioned in Table 1 to which the company responded that the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) reported that EDELWEISS 3 _“…previous medical treatments consisted of analgesics for pelvic pain, including opioids. The most frequently reported other pharmacotherapies for endometriosis treatment included dienogest, hormonal oral contraceptives and GnRH agonists."_[5] They went on to state that these prior therapies are those that would be received in United Kingdom (UK) clinical practice prior to receiving linzagolix 200 mg plus add-back therapy (ABT), according to clinical expert opinion and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)/European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) guidelines. 

The EAG also requested clarification as to whether patients where the comparator would be leuprorelin would have a different treatment history and/or be considered to form a different subgroup to those where the comparator would be some form of surgery. The company responded that this was not the case: _“For patients treated with leuprorelin, other GnRH agonists or conservative surgery at this point in the treatment pathway, a similar mix of previous treatments to linzagolix would be expected.”_[5] They went on to state that women who had already undergone surgery might also be eligible for further surgery. 

In conclusion, it seems that the company is not ruling out any treatment history in the DP population, whether medical or surgical, or in terms of line of therapy, which is at least second, and that all patients in this population might be eligible for either medical or surgical treatments. This creates substantial uncertainty as to the precise nature of this population in clinical practice and is therefore a key issue. 

It is also worth noting that there is no age limit nor any mention of menopause in the population description. Although the anticipated marketing authorisation (MA)[6] and the key trial of linzagolix, EDELWEISS 3, limits eligibility to those of reproductive age (see Section 3.2.2), endometriosis can still require management post-menopause.[7] This therefore increases the uncertainty associated with the population, as well as one regarding the applicability of the trial data if the population is broader than women of reproductive age. 

## **2.2 Intervention** 

The intervention in the DP is linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, which is as in the NICE scope.[4] 

**EAG comment:** The precise nature of ABT was not found in the CS, so the EAG requested that this be provided as would be received in clinical practice in the National Health Service (NHS), to which the company responded that for EDELWEISS 3, ABT comprised oestradiol (E2) 1 mg/norethisterone acetate 0.5 mg.[5] They went on to state that in clinical practice there is large array of different forms of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) that could be used as ABT, providing a large table listing many doses of oestradiol and progesterone either as monotherapy or in combination. There is therefore a 

27 



<!-- page 402 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

concern that the effectiveness of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT as estimated from the trial might not be the same as in clinical practice, which implies that this is a key issue. 

## **2.3 Comparators** 

The comparators in the NICE scope were: 

Where HRT is suitable, established clinical management without linzagolix plus ABT, including: 

- analgesics or NSAID alone or in combination 

- neuromodulators 

- relugolix-oestradiol-norethisterone acetate (relugolix combination therapy [CT]; subject to NICE evaluation) 

- other hormonal treatment such as combined hormonal contraception (off-label for some combined hormonal contraceptives), oral progestogens, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists 

- surgery such as excision/ablation with or without hysterectomy 

Where hormone-based therapy is not suitable, stablished clinical management without linzagolix plus ABT, including: 

- analgesics or NSAID alone or in combination 

- neuromodulators 

- surgery such as excision/ablation with or without hysterectomy 

Those in the DP were only:[4] 

- leuprorelin, as a representative of all GnRH agonists 

- surgery, limited to minimally invasive procedures only, excluding hysterectomy 

Relugolix was excluded on the basis that it is not currently part of NHS clinical practice, given that is it currently subject to a NICE appraisal.[4] 

**EAG comment:** Only one type of GnRH agonist, leuprorelin, was included in the DP and the clinical effectiveness section, but three types were included in the costing (see Table 65, CS). Table 65 also refers to short- (1-month) and long- (3- month) acting GnRH agonists, but no such distinction was made in the indirect treatment comparison (ITC). Therefore, the EAG requested that the company include all GnRH agonists that might be used in clinical practice, differentiating between short- and long- acting forms of leuprorelin as required, as comparators in both analysis of clinical effectiveness and CE. The EAG also noted that, although surgery was included in the DP and the cost effectiveness analysis (CEA), it was not included in the clinical effectiveness evidence. The EAG therefore requested adequate justification for the exclusion of comparators including surgery other than minimally invasive, and the inclusion of all comparators in the NICE scope, including in the clinical effectiveness section and the ITC and the CEA. The company responded that: _“Based on clinical expert opinion in the UK, and in line with European clinical guidelines, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists (including linzagolix) will be used as second-line hormonal treatment options, as an alternative to GnRH agonists.”_[5] On this basis they rule out analgesics, neuromodulators and any hormonal contraception, stating that the latter are only used first-line. They emphasise this by stating: _“GnRH agonists are reserved as second-line hormonal treatment, and are therefore considered to be_ 

28 



<!-- page 403 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

_appropriate comparators. The following GnRH agonists are indicated for the treatment of endometriosis: goserelin (depot injection), leuprorelin (depot injection), nafarelin (nasal spray), buserelin (nasal spray), and triptorelin (depot injection). Intranasal GnRH agonists (nafarelin and buserelin) are rarely prescribed, with all surveyed clinical experts reporting a preference for intramuscular or subcutaneous formulations, therefore only leuprorelin acetate, goserelin, and triptorelin were considered comparators in the model. Leuprorelin, as a representative of all GnRH agonists, is included in the base case…”_ However, the EAG notes that it is misleading to state that more than one GnRH was included in the CEA: inclusion of the costs for more than one is not the same as including each of several as separate comparators given that there might be variation in the effectiveness between these comparators. Note that the company did not provide any other types of GnRH agonist in the ITC, which could have shed light on this. Indeed, the EAG clinical expert stated that there were several options for the population as described in the DP: “ _GnRH agonists are a common choice for this group. It depends on what is available in the formulary ranging from Prostap_ [leuprorelin] _, Decapeptyl_ [triptorelin] _, Zoladex_ [goserelin] _. Generally, im or subcutaneous preparations are used and not nasal.”_ 

In relation to surgery, the company stated:[5] _“Surgery is not considered to be a direct comparator to linzagolix because:_ 

- _1) Linzagolix would be used in situations where GnRH agonists are currently prescribed, and where medical therapy is preferred over surgical intervention._ 

- _2) Treatment decisions are guided by the need to balance treatment priorities regarding fertility and pain management. Women who do not wish to take hormonal therapy due to priorities regarding fertility would not be suitable for linzagolix treatment and would be prioritised for surgical treatment._ 

- _3) Clinical experts suggest that when included in the overall pathway, GnRH analogues impact when and how surgery might be used. GnRH analogues may be used as a complementary treatment to reduce the risk of symptom recurrence post-surgery or to provide symptom relief whilst women are waiting for surgery, and in this case, do not directly replace surgical treatment.”_ 

The company seem to be suggesting that the population in the DP and for those eligible for linzagolix would rule out surgery as a comparator, according to some preference (point 1), according to fertility priorities (point 2), and because GnRH analogues in some way accompany surgery (either before or after). However, the population as expressed in the DP and subject to clarification, as described in Section 2.1, does not explicitly recognised a population that precludes surgery. It is also not expressed in relation to the timing of surgery, either before or after. In addition, the company have provided a comparison with surgery in the CS. This means that unless the population is redefined in a more precise way, surgery, both less and more invasive might still be a comparator or comparators. Indeed, for the population as currently described in the DP, the EAG clinical expert stated: _“The commonly used treatments for this group is GnRH agonist with add back HRT, alternative hormonal treatment that they may not have tried, Dienogest or repeat surgery.”_ With regards to the nature of the surgery, the clinical expert went on to state: _“The options include both repeat laparoscopic surgery to excise/ablate endometriosis or hysterectomy depending on patients wishes, future desire for fertility, coexisting symptoms or pathology such as heavy menstrual bleeding or adenomyosis.”_ Given that the population as currently described in the DP would be subdivided into those eligible for surgery and those not eligible for surgery, the EAG asked how patients might differ, to which the clinical expert stated: _“This is largely governed by informed choice and patient preference. In the group that is trying to conceive,_ 

29 



<!-- page 404 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

_surgery is the preferred option as all other hormonal treatments are contraceptive in nature. GnRHa may also be prescribed to those who have multiple co-morbidities and are not fit for surgery or repetitive surgery has not been particularly beneficial.”_ The EAG concludes from this that it might be reasonable to define a population for the DP i.e. those eligible for linzagolix in terms of eligibility for surgery i.e. those who either: 

- express a preference to not have surgery 

- are not fit for surgery 

- have not benefited previously from laparoscopic surgery 

However, this would need to be explicitly acknowledged if surgery were to be ruled out as a comparator. 

With regards to forms of pharmacological treatment other than GnRH agonists and specifically analgesics or neuromodulators, the EAG clinical expert stated: _“Yes, this is in conjunction with analgesics and neuromodulators for pain management where required.”_ The EAG interprets this response as indicating that analgesics and neuromodulators would not be an alternative to GnRH agonists or surgery but used adjunctively. 

The company also did not include relugolix CT as a comparator on the basis that it is still the subject of a NICE appraisal. However, the NICE technical team asked the company to consider its inclusion on the basis that it might soon receive a positive recommendation by NICE. The company have responded by providing an addendum with an ITC, both an unadjusted Bucher and a matching adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC), and a CEA of a comparison with relugolix CT (see Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 4). 

Lack of justification for the exclusion of pharmacological comparators, particularly GnRH agonists other than leuprorelin, and the lack of presentation of clinical effectiveness evidence for surgery unless surgery can be ruled out, implies a key issue. 

## **2.4 Outcomes** 

The company included the following outcomes, which were specified in the NICE scope:[4] 

- Pain 

- Opioid use 

- Analgesic use 

- Adverse effects of treatment 

- Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) 

They excluded: 

- Recurrence, progression and regression of endometriosis 

- Admission to hospital 

- Subsequent surgical treatment 

- Fertility 

- Complications of treatment 

**EAG comment:** The EAG considers that admission to hospital should have been included even if only occurring in 2% of patients. Also, the EAG considers that it might be reasonable to exclude

## **3.1 Critique of the methods of review(s)** 

## _**3.1.1 Searches**_ 

The following paragraphs contain summaries and critiques of the searches related to clinical effectiveness presented in the CS.[4] The Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH) evidence-based checklist for the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) was used to inform this critique.[9, 10] The EAG has presented only the major limitations of each search strategy in the report.

## **EAG comment:** 

- Searches were undertaken in two stages in order to identify clinical evidence on safety and efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg (the intervention) and other therapies (comparators) for the treatment of endometriosis. The searches were conducted in December 2023 and updated in September 2024. Initially the search searches were presented in two tables which combined results of the three databases (MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library) and provided the hits for each resource in separate columns. This approach hindered the EAG’s ability to fully critique the search methods therefore the EAG requested that the company supply the search strategies in their original format as recommended by best practice “ _… bibliographic database search strategies should be copied and pasted into an appendix exactly as run and in full, together with the search set numbers and the total number of records retrieved by each search strategy. The search strategies should not be re-typed, because this can introduce errors._ ”[12] The EAG was grateful to the company for their prompt response and the revised searches combined with the company’s response to clarification provided sufficient details for the EAG to appraise the literature searches.[5, 13] 

- The revised searches were well structured, transparent and reproducible. 

- Whilst searches were performed on an adequate number of bibliographic databases, other than reference checking, no grey literature searching was conducted. Best practice recommends the searching of grey literature in order to minimise publication bias.[14] Without running their own searches, the EAG is unable to say what impact this may have had on the overall recall of results. 

- The EAG noticed that whilst the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR) was mentioned in Section D2.2.1 (Appendix D) line #35 of the comparators search in the Cochrane Library appeared to remove all Cochrane records except for those in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL).[13] The company confirmed that whilst CDSR was searched, the records were not screened due to the scope of the SLR.[5] For this reason, the EAG have removed CDSR from the list of searched resources above. 

- The first search for the intervention used a broad search strategy combining facets for endometriosis and linzagolix, no limits were applied. The second search for comparators combined facets for endometriosis and named GnRH analogues. In the Embase and MEDLINE searches, this was then combined with a study design filter for clinical trials. 

- At the time of requesting the revised searches, the EAG also queried if the strategies had included both subject headings and free text terms. The company confirmed that whilst Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and Emtree had been consulted to identify relevant synonyms, they had not been included in the strategies. The company went on to say “ _Not all databases have indexing terms and some contain records that have not yet been indexed. It was decided that a search strategy based on free-terms and synonyms would be sufficient to cover relevant publications_ .”[13] The EAG would point out that in this case all three resources searched in the clinical effectiveness SLR contained subject headings and that Cochrane best practice states that “ _Both free-text and subject headings (e.g. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and Emtree) should be used._ ”[12] A brief comparison of the company’s own search facets for endometriosis in PubMed demonstrate the potential impact: 

Intervention Search facet for endometriosis (All fields including MeSH) = 131,507 

Comparators Search facet for endometriosis (limited to free text in title and abstract) = 121,040 

Although the difference displayed in final numbers when combined with the other facets will be much smaller, and key papers with the relevant terms in their title and abstracts where available, should have been retrieved, the EAG feels it possible that relevant studies may have been missed.

**EAG comment:** The EAG noted that the DP includes a broad set of comparators representing established clinical management without linzagolix. However, the company’s SLR appears to limit the scope of comparators in several areas. The company was asked to provide a detailed justification when comparators deviate from the NICE scope e.g. are listed in the NICE scope but were not used in the CS and provide clarification on the following points:[5] 

- a. The scope includes a variety of hormone-based treatments, such as combined hormonal contraception and oral progestogens, as potential comparators. The company were asked to clarify why these additional hormonal treatments were not included in the GnRH analogue SLR. The company responded that, _“As described in response to question A2a, combined hormonal contraception and oral progestogens are used as first line hormonal therapies in UK practice and were therefore not considered to be comparators in the submission.”_ 

- b. The scope specifies surgical comparators as _“excision/ablation with or without hysterectomy.”_ The company were asked to explain the rationale for limiting surgical comparators in the surgical SLR to minimally invasive procedures only, excluding hysterectomy. The company responded that, _“In the NICE endometriosis guideline (published in 2017 and updated in 2024)_ 

36 



<!-- page 411 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

_the suggested surgical approaches involve laparoscopic excision or ablation plus adhesiolysis and laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy, depending on the location of the lesions. Hysterectomy is advised only if other surgical options have been offered, failed or are inappropriate, and research with clinical experts indicated that hysterectomy tends to be a last resort rather than considered early in the treatment pathway. Additionally, hysterectomy is indicated if treatmentresistant adenomyosis or heavy menstrual bleeding is present. Linzagolix is a treatment indicated for the treatment of adult women of reproductive age - in this population it might be a priority to maintain fertility. When performing a hysterectomy, the fertility is not maintained. Therefore, it was decided not to include it in the feasibility analysis.”_ 

- b. The scope lists analgesics, NSAIDs, and neuromodulators as part of established clinical management without linzagolix. The company were asked to clarify why these treatments were not included as comparators in the SLRs. The company responded that, _“Analgesics and NSAIDs are routinely prescribed as first-line therapies in endometriosis (often before a formal diagnosis has been made). Expert elicitation revealed an expectation that once GnRH agonists (or antagonists) are introduced, there is a clinical expectation that the need for such treatments should reduce or cease. Neuromodulators are reserved for patients with exceptionally difficultto-manage pain secondary to endometriosis. Prescription would be started after referral to a specialist pain service rather than as part of routine supportive care. As such, the proportion of patients prescribed neuromodulators is limited and not part of routine practice.”_ 

In conclusion, the EAG eligibility criteria might be appropriate if either GnRH agonists and minimally invasive (laparoscopic) surgery are the only comparators (see Section 2.3). 

## _**3.1.3 Critique of data extraction**_ 

According to the CS, two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts for eligibility based on the predefined selection criteria. Any disagreements were resolved in consultation with a third reviewer.[4] 

No details of the process of data extraction were provided. 

**EAG comment:** The EAG asked the company to describe the process used for data extraction and risk of bias assessment of the included studies (for intervention and comparator data). The company responded that, “ _Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and quality-checked by the other reviewer. The extraction was performed in tables. Additionally, if available in the identified publications, graphs were provided. Data from graphs was not extracted if specific values were not provided, due to the possibility of introducing bias to the analysis.”_ The EAG is satisfied with this response. 

## _**3.1.4 Quality assessment**_ 

The Company conducted the quality assessment of trials included in the Bucher analysis. The assessment covers six key domains of methodological quality, including randomisation, blinding, and the handling of missing data.

## _**3.2.2.1 EDELWEISS 3 overview**_ 

EDELWEISS 3 was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 trial of linzagolix in women of reproductive age with Moderate to Severe EAP[4] . 

The trail comprised a 3-month screening period, a 6-month treatment period, a 6-month extension and a 6-month drug-free follow-up period.[4] Please see Figure 3.2 for an overview of EDELWEISS 3 trial process. 

The CS[4] clarifies that the EDELWEISS 3 co-primary efficacy endpoints were a clinically meaningful reduction from baseline of dysmenorrhoea (reduction of ≥1.10 points on the verbal rating scale [VRS]) and NMPP (reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. Secondary endpoints were changes from baseline to month 6 in dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia, overall pelvic pain, interference of pain with the ability to perform daily activities (using the Endometriosis health profile 30 [EHP-30] pain dimension) and dyspareunia, and no analgesic/no opiate use for EAP during the preceding 4-week period at month 6. Other secondary endpoints included analgesic and opioid use for EAP, number of days in hospital, Physician Surgery Intention Question (PSIQ)/Subject Surgery Intention Question (SSIQ) and HRQoL.

## _3.2.2.1.1 EDELWEISS 3 Eligibility criteria_ 

The following criteria applied for inclusion of participants in the study:[4] 

- Women of reproductive age with surgically confirmed endometriosis in the past 10 years 

40

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

- Moderate to Severe EAP over the month prior to screening and over two menstrual cycles during screening 

- Body mass index (BMI) ≥18 kg/m2 

- Practice birth control if of childbearing potential 

The following criteria applied for exclusion of participants in the study:[4] 

- Liver enzyme anomalies 

- Osteoporosis or other metabolic bone disease 

- Use of certain medications (e.g. COC, GnRH agonists or systemic glucocorticoids) within a specified wash-out period

## _**3.2.2.2 EDELWEISS 6 overview**_ 

Patients who completed the 6-month treatment period in the EDELWEISS 3 study were invited to enter the EDELWEISS 6 extension study. In EDELWEISS 6, patients who received placebo in EDELWEISS 3 were randomised 1:1 to linzagolix 75 mg or linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. Patients who received active treatment in EDELWEISS 3 continued with the same treatment.[4] Please see Figure 3.2 above for an overview of EDELWEISS 6 trial process. 

In line with EDELWEISS 3, the co-primary endpoints of EDELWEISS 6 were clinically meaningful reduction of dysmenorrhoea (reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) and NMPP (reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days preceding the month 12 visit, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. Secondary endpoints of EDELWEISS 6 included changes from baseline to month 12 in dysmenorrhoea, NMPP, dyschezia, OPP, interference of pain with the ability to perform daily activities (using the EHP-30 pain dimension) and dyspareunia. Other secondary 

42

endpoints included analgesic and opioid use for EAP, number of days in hospital, PSIQ/SSIQ and HRQoL[4] . 

## _3.2.2.2.1 EDELWEISS 6 Eligibility criteria_ 

The following criteria applied for inclusion of participants in the study:[4] 

- Patients who completed the 6-month treatment period in EDELWEISS 3 

The following criteria applied for exclusion of participants in the study:[4] 

- Liver enzyme anomalies reaching discontinuation levels 

- BMD decrease of >8% from EDELWEISS 3 baseline or a Z-score ≤2.5 at either the femoral neck, hip or spine at EDELWEISS 3 month 6

## _**3.2.5 Efficacy results of the EDELWEISS 3**_ 

## _**3.2.5.1 Co-primary endpoints of EDELWEISS 3**_ 

According to the CS[4] , the co-primary endpoint for the group of patients receiving a daily dose of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT shown that at month 3, the estimated percentage of responders for dysmenorrhoea was 72.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 65.3–79.4) in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group versus 23.5% (95% CI: 17.5–30.7) in the placebo group (odds ratio [OR] 8.80 [97.5% CI: 4.86–15.91]; p<0.001); the proportions for NMPP were 47.3% (95% CI: 39.5–55.3) with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus 30.9% (95% CI: 24.1–38.6) with placebo (OR 2.01 [97.5% CI: 1.18–3.42]; p=0.007). Further details can be found in the Figure 3.3 below. 

The company noticed that the linzagolix 75 mg alone dose demonstrated a clinically meaningful and statistically significant reduction in dysmenorrhoea versus placebo at month 3, but the reduction in NMPP at month 3 versus placebo was not statistically significant.[4]

The company observed improvements from baseline in the EHP-30 dimensions of pain, control and powerlessness, emotional wellbeing, social support, self-image and sexual relationship and European Quality of Life-5 dimensions 5 levels (EQ-5D-5L) index and visual analogue scale (VAS) scores with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT up to month 12 in EDELWEISS 6[4] . 

**EAG comment:** There was a continued improvement with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT in all outcomes during the 6-month extension to the 6-month double blind randomised period, with plateauing towards the end of the 12-month follow-up period.

The company also mentioned that _“Treatment compliance was high in EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 2, with a median in all treatment groups of 100% in EDELWEISS 3 and >90% in EDELWEISS 2. Approximately 75% of patients in EDELWEISS 3 had a compliance of ≥98%.”_[4]
