## _**3.2.7.5 Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events**_ 

## _3.2.7.5.1 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 2_ 

In EDELWEISS 3, the treatment discontinuation rate due to TEAEs in the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT group (3.1%) was similar to that for the placebo group (2.5%), although the rate was slightly higher for the linzagolix 75 mg group (5.6%); While, in EDELWEISS 2, treatment discontinuation rates due to TEAEs were comparable between the placebo and linzagolix groups.[4] 

## _3.2.7.5.2 EDELWEISS 6_ 

Nine patients discontinued treatment due to TEAEs from month 6 to month 12, with rates comparable across treatment groups (placebo/linzagolix 75 mg: 3.4%; placebo/linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: 3.5%; linzagolix 75 mg: 2.5%; linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: 1.6%).[4] 

70 



<!-- page 445 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

## _**3.2.7.6 Serious adverse events**_ 

## _3.2.7.6.1 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 2_ 

Serious adverse events (SAEs) were comparable across all groups in EDELWEISS 3, with none reported in EDELWEISS 2, indicating good tolerability for linzagolix. In EDELWEISS 3, serious TEAEs included pneumonia and abdominal pain (n=1 each) in the 200 mg group, and peritonitis and endometriosis (in the same patient) in the 75 mg group, none of which were treatment-related.[4] 

## _3.2.7.6.2 EDELWEISS 6_ 

Four patients experienced serious TEAEs from month 6 to 12, none related to linzagolix. These included genital tract bleeding (n=1, placebo/linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT), exacerbation of cholelithiasis (n=1, placebo/linzagolix 75 mg), acute anxiety (n=1, linzagolix 75 mg), and vaginal bleeding (n=1, linzagolix 75 mg). The vaginal bleeding was linked to ABT, though this patient received an ABT placebo.[4] 

## _**3.2.7.7 EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6 | Bone mineral density**_ 

Bone mineral density (BMD) was largely unaffected by linzagolix treatment at month 6 (EDELWEISS 3) and month 12 (EDELWEISS 6). Some BMD increases were noted at 6 months after end of treatment (EDELWEISS 6 month 6 ExFU), indicating partial recovery.[4] 

Most patients in the linzagolix groups had either an increase, no change or ≤3% decrease in BMD at month 6 in the lumbar spine (84.5%), femoral neck (88.2%) and total hip (94.3%).[4] Further details can be found in Table 3.29.[4]

## **3.3 Critique of trials identified and included in the indirect comparison and/or multiple treatment comparison** 

An ITC was carried out to compare the safety and efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT with other GnRH analogues. A SLR was used to select appropriate studies for inclusion in the analysis. Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the intervention treatment (linzagolix) are provided as Table 3.4, and for the comparator treatments (other GnRH analogues) as Table 3.5. The review considered efficacy, safety and quality of life (QoL) outcomes in patients with diagnosed endometriosis. For linzagolix, eligible studies were randomised or non-RCTs, single arm studies, observational studies, and long-term follow up to RCTs; for GnRH analogues only RCTs were included. For linzagolix, included comparators were placebo or any pharmacological intervention; for GnRH analogues included comparators were placebo or any other GnRH analogue. Only studies written in the English language were included in the review. 

One study (EDELWEISS 3[18] ) was identified for inclusion as a part of the intervention SLR. As no headto-head trials comparing linzagolix to comparators were identified, the SLR for comparators was narrowed down to only include studies that could be compared to the intervention as part of an anchored ITC. This limited studies to those with 12- and 24- week follow-up for efficacy outcomes, and 24 weeks of follow-up for safety and QoL outcomes. Studies were also excluded from the SLR for other reasons, listed in Appendix D of the CS, Section 3.2.1, page 28: 

_“It should be noted that the studies D'Hooghe 2019, Harada 2021, Bergqvist 2000 were not included in the indirect comparison for the following reasons:_ 

_D'Hooghe 2019 – no comparison of leuprorelin vs placebo, study includes results for comparison of opigolix vs placebo;_ 

_Harada 2021_ [relugolix versus leuprorelin] _and Bergqvist 2000_ [goserelin versus nafarelin] _– no placebo group in the study._ 

_Other studies included as a result of the systematic review for the comparator were not included in the analysis because the relevant outcomes/endpoints were not matched to the EDELWEISS 3 study:_ 

- _studies with data on graph: Acs 2015 (for NMPP and DYS)_ [elagolix versus leuprorelin versus placebo] _, Elaris EM1 (for EHP-30 pain dimension only)_ [elagolix versus placebo] _, Elaris EM2 (for EHP-30 pain dimension only)_ [elagolix versus placebo] 

- _studies with data without standard deviation/standard error (SD/SE): Dlugi 1990_ [leuprorelin versus placebo] _, Ling 1999_ [leuprorelin versus placebo] _; Elaris EM1 (for lumbar spine only), Elaris EM2 (for lumbar spine only)_ [elagolix versus placebo] 

- _studies with unreadable data: Acs 2015 (for dyspareunia – unclear which scale was used)_ [elagolix versus leuprorelin versus placebo] _.”_ 

Three studies were identified for the comparator; the SPIRIT 1 and 2 studies, and Osuga 2021a[19] /2021b[20] . The SPIRIT studies compare relugolix CT with placebo; Appendix D of the CS (page 28) includes data for these studies, but states that: 

_“Relugolix plus ABT has been included in this report, since it was listed in the final scope for this submission (subject to NICE evaluation). However, since it has not yet been approved by NICE, results comparing linzagolix to relugolix have not been presented in the company submission (Document B)”_ 

Therefore, the ITC for linzagolix and relugolix was not included in Document B of the CS. 

76

Osuga 2021a/2021b also included treatment arms for varying doses of relugolix; as this is not being used as a comparator, this data was not included in the ITC. However, it is worth noting, as this affects the context of the study. 

The studies vary from each other in several respects. The number of participants is higher in EDELWEISS 3 than in Osuga 2021a/2021b (162 in either arm for EDELWEISS 3, 82 and 99 for treatment and placebo groups in Osuga 2021a/2021b, respectively). The placebo used in each study also differs; EDELWEISS 3 uses an oral placebo, whereas Osuga 2021a/2021b administered two placebos concurrently: an oral placebo and an injected placebo. This was due to the different administration methods of the study drugs; relugolix was given orally, and leuprorelin as a subcutaneous injection. In order to maintain blinding, all participants received a daily oral tablet (relugolix or placebo), and a subcutaneous injection (leuprorelin or placebo) every 4 weeks. 

**EAG comment:** Given that only one trial of one comparator was included, the EAG requested that consideration be given to the inclusion of more studies. Specifically, the EAG recommended a network meta-analysis (NMA) in order to include non-placebo-controlled trials, as well as including data from graphs and imputing measures of variance, which potentially could have permitted the inclusion of further studies, and more comparators i.e. opigolix and elagolix. Note that in the factual inaccuracy check (FAC) the company have informed the EAG that neither of these comparators is licensed in the UK, but the EAG understand that they might still be used in clinical practice.[21] The company restated reasons that included heterogeneity, and stated that: _“…many studies are outdated, methodology and population descriptions are not provided in certain instances and are unclear when reported, with some results only presented graphically (with no numerical values provided) and/or without variability measures (like standard deviation).”_[5] They also cited a lack of common comparators as a reason: _“Finally, as we were only able to link linzagolix with leuprorelin (EDELWEISS 3 and Osuga studies), it can be assumed that including trials comparing GnRH agonists vs active treatments would not offer any benefits to the ITC. To address this, studies comparing different GnRH agonists with placebo, and studies linking different GnRH agonists vs other GnRH agonists, directly or indirectly, are required. We have only one GnRH agonist which we can compare with linzagolix via placebo.”_ The company stated that: _“Introducing any additional studies would result in further limitations, making conclusions more difficult to interpret and results more prone to bias… Building an NMA would not be credible in_ 

77 



<!-- page 452 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

_this therapeutic area for the reasons already mentioned above.”_ However, none of the studies listed above were excluded explicitly because of heterogeneity, and the only study that could not be connected in an NMA using common comparators of either placebo, leuprorelin or relugolix CT seems to be Bergqvist 2000 (goserelin versus nafarelin). Not that the company stated in the FAC that one of the studies, D’Hooghe 2019, was excluded erroneously and one, Harada 2021, was excluded for reasons that were incorrectly reported in the CS.[21] D’Hooghe 2019 could therefore be included in any ITC or NMA. Harada 2021 should have been excluded because of the lack of accompanying ABT in the relugolix arm, which the EAG considers to be reasonable. The company did include an additional ITC (EDELWEISS 3 versus Ács 2015), using imputed 95% CIs in answer to Question A13c.[22] Efficacy outcomes (dysmenorrhoea and NMPP) were reported in this study and were compared in the ITC. A consideration of clinical heterogeneity is reported in Section 3.4.1 and the results are reported in Sections 3.4.2 and 3.4.3. 

The company also provided an addendum with an ITC versus relugolix.[23] A consideration of clinical heterogeneity is reported in Section 3.4.1 and the results are reported in Section 3.4.2.

## _**3.4.1 Assessment of clinical heterogeneity**_ 

An analysis of heterogeneity was carried out by comparing the baseline characteristics for each study. Comparisons were made using data from the Osuga 2021a paper, as it has a longer observation period than Osuga 2021b, but as the 2021a paper is a long term extension of Osuga 2021b, refer to the same population.[4] A summary of baseline characteristics recorded for EDELWEISS 3 and Osuga 2021a is presented in Table 3.33. 

**EAG comment:** Table 3.28 also contains the trials for the two additional ITCs provided in response to clarification.[22, 23] 

## _**3.4.1.1 Age**_ 

The mean age of participants in the two trials from the original CS was similar, varying between 34.6 years (linzagolix plus ABT, EDELWEISS 3) and 36.6 years (placebo, Osuga 2021a). 

The mean age of participants differed between the two trials in the response to clarification; 31.4 for both treatment arms in the Ács 2015 trial, and 34.6 and 34.9 for the linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and placebo arms in the EDELWEISS 3 trial, respectively. Age in the relugolix trials was somewhere in the middle. 

## _**3.4.1.2 Ethnicity**_ 

The vast majority of participants in the EDELWEISS 3 study were White (98.1 and 98.8% of participants in the linzagolix plus ABT and placebo arms, respectively. This was similar to the populations in Ács 2015 (100% White, both arms), SPIRIT 1 (91.5 and 91.0% White for relugolix plus ABT and placebo, respectively) and SPIRIT 2 (90.3 and 89.7% white for relugolix plus ABT and placebo, respectively). 

Osuga 2021a was markedly different to the other studies; all participants in the trial were Asian. This is acknowledged in Appendix D, page 51: “ _Significant heterogeneity was observed in Osuga 2021a. This study included only Japanese women, whereas the remaining studies included mostly Caucasian women.”_ 

## _**3.4.1.3 Body Mass Index**_ 

Mean body mass index (BMI) differs between participants in each study. The mean BMI for participants in EDELWEISS 3 was 24.1 for both treatment arms. Osuga 2021a and Ács 2015 were lower; 21.7 in the leuprorelin arm, and 21.2 in the placebo arm for Osuga 2021a, and 22.6 for all participants in Ács 2015 (BMI for each treatment arm was not recorded). Mean BMI was higher in SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2, ranging from 25.6 (SPIRIT 1, relugolix plus ABT arm) to 26.1 (SPIRIT 1, placebo arm and SPIRIT 2, relugolix plus ABT arm). 

## _**3.4.1.4 Pain assessment**_ 

Baseline pain scale scores were provided for all studies except Ács 2015. 

79 



<!-- page 454 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

## _3.4.1.4.1 EHP-30 scores_ 

EHP-30 pain scale scores were provided in EDELWEISS 3, Osuga 2021a, SPIRT 1 and SPIRIT 2. EHP-30 scores were slightly higher in SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 than in EDELWEISS 3, ranging from 51.8 (EDELWEISS 3, placebo arm) to 58.3 (SPIRIT 1, relugolix plus ABT). 

Baseline pain scores were far lower in Osuga 2021a (27.0 for the leuprorelin arm, 23.7 for the placebo arm) than in EDELWEISS 3 (52.4 for the linzagolix plus ABT arm, 51.8 for the placebo arm). This is addressed on page 47 of Appendix D, where the CS postulates that differences in baseline pain measures are due to differences in pain tolerance between different ethnicities: 

_“Therefore, the difference in mean pain scores between Osuga 2021a and other studies may be due to differences in pain tolerance between the Asian and Caucasian populations”_ 

The authors also note that: _“No studies were identified on perception of endometriosis-related pain in relation to race”._ 

## _3.4.1.4.2 VRS pain scale scores_ 

VRS pain scale scores for dysmenorrhoea and NMPP were reported in EDELWEISS 3 and Osuga 2021a. Measures were lower in Osuga 2021a for both dysmenorrhoea (1.2 for both treatment arms) and NMPP (0.7 for both treatment arms) than in EDELWEISS 3 (dysmenorrhoea = 2.29 and NMPP = 1.2 for both treatment arms).

## _3.4.1.4.3 NRS pain scale scores_ 

Numeric rating scale (NRS) pain scale scores were reported for EDELWEISS 3, SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 for dysmenorrhoea and NMPP. Dysmenorrhoea scores were similar between studies, ranging from 7.1 (SPIRT 2, placebo arm) to 7.2 (EDELWEISS 3, placebo and SPIRIT 1, relugolix plus ABT). Baseline NMPP scores were also similar, ranging from 5.5 (SPIRIT 2 placebo arm) to 5.9 (SPIRIT 1, relugolix plus ABT arm). 

## _**3.4.1.5 Lipid profile**_ 

Blood lipid profile measures were reported in EDELWEISS 3, SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2. LDL cholesterol was slightly lower in SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2, ranging from 98.9 mg/dL (SPIRIT 2, placebo arm) to 101.9 mg/dL (SPIRIT 1, placebo arm) than in EDELWEISS 3 (115.4 mg/dL for placebo, 114.3 mg/dL for linzagolix plus BT). 

A broader range of values for baseline triglyceride values was seen between SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2, ranging from 89.7 mg/dL (SPIRIT 1, relugolix plus ABT) to 102.8 mg/dL (SPIRIT 2, placebo); mean triglyceride values for EDELWEISS 3 were 90.0 mg/dL and 91.9 mg/dL for linzagolix plus ABT and placebo arms, respectively. 

## _**3.4.1.6 Bone mineral density**_ 

Bone mineral density (BMD) z-scores were reported in EDELWEISS 3, SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 for total hip and lumbar spine. Scores for total hip were slightly lower in SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 than EDELWEISS 3; the range of values for SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 was -0.01 (SPIRIT 1, relugolix plus ABT arm) to 0.12 (SPIRIT 2, placebo arm), whereas values for EDELWEISS 3 were 0.30 and 0.40 for the linzagolix plus ABT arm and placebo arm, respectively. 

Scores for lumbar spine were similar across the studies, ranging from 0.20 (EDELWEISS 3, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT) to 0.50 (EDELWEISS 3, placebo arm). 

## _**3.4.1.7 Time since surgical diagnosis of endometriosis**_ 

Mean time since surgical diagnosis of endometriosis was similar in EDELWEISS 3, Osuga 2021a, SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2, ranging from 3.1 years in Osuga 2021a (leuprorelin arm) to 4.1 years in SPIRIT 2 (relugolix plus ABT arm). Ács 2015 was markedly different to the other studies, with a mean of 1.82 years for all participants (mean time since surgical diagnosis of endometriosis by treatment arm was not recorded). 

Definitions of duration of disease also varied between the studies; Osuga 2021a reports mean disease duration, EDELWEISS 3 reports time since first surgical diagnosis. 

_“Due to the lack of a definition of disease duration in Osuga 2021a, it is difficult to determine the timeframe for this variable, although the mean is similar across the included studies.”_ (Appendix D of the CS, Section 3.3.3.4, page 45). 

Inclusion criteria for Osuga 2021a state: _“a diagnosis of endometriosis in the previous 5 years (confirmed by laparotomy, laparoscopy, or magnetic resonance imaging detection of ovarian chocolate cyst[s])”_[20] 

83 



<!-- page 458 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

## _**3.4.1.8 Use of analgesic agents**_ 

Use of analgesic agents at baseline is reported in EDELWEISS 3, SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2. Overall analgesic use was similar across the studies, ranging from 89.2% of participants (SPIRIT 1, placebo arm) to 96.9% of participants (EDELWEISS 3, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT). 

Use of opioids differs markedly between studies; the lowest opioid usage is in EDELWEISS 3 (12.3 and 5.6% of participants in the linzagolix plus ABT and placebo arms, respectively), then SPIRIT 1 (30.2 and 24.5% of participants, relugolix plus ABT and placebo arms, respectively), with the highest usage in SPIRIT 2 (48.5 and 36.6% of participants, relugolix plus ABT and placebo arms, respectively).

## _**3.4.2.3 Linzagolix plus ABT (EDELWEISS 3) and relugolix plus ABT (SPIRIT 1/SPIRIT 2)**_ 

A Bucher ITC was carried out to compare the efficacy of linzagolix plus ABT versus relugolix plus ABT. In order to compare EDELWEISS 3, SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 by this method, a meta-analysis of the SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 trials was carried out. Justification for this decision is provided in the addendum to clarification response: 

_“SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 were two replicate, phase 3 studies which evaluated similar endpoints over the same observation periods, had the same study design and included patients with similar baseline characteristics. It was, therefore, possible to perform a meta-analysis of the SPIRIT 1/SPIRIT 2 studies and to include the results of the meta-analysis in the ITC.”[23]_ 

This allowed the results of the meta-analysis to be compared to EDELWEISS 3; results of the Bucher ITC are presented as Table 3.36.  No significant differences were found between linzagolix plus ABT and relugolix plus ABT for any of the outcomes.

The addendum to clarification response acknowledges that differences were present between the SPIRIT studies and EDELWEISS 3: 

_“The EDELWEISS 3 linzagolix study and the relugolix CT studies SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 differed in their definitions of the co-primary efficacy endpoints dysmenorrhoea and NMPP, in terms of the rating scale used for the pain assessment (verbal rating scale vs. numeric rating scale), magnitude of significant clinical change and the assessment timepoint. Of note, the primary endpoint of EDELWEISS 3 was assessed at 3 months [week 12], whereas the primary endpoint of SPIRIT 1 and SPIRIT 2 was assessed at 6 months [week 24]; early pain control in patients is of utmost importance, hence the 3- month assessment was prioritised in the EDELWEISS studies.”[23]_ 

Due to the availability of patient-level data in the EDELWEISS 3 study, reconstructed endpoints were generated based upon the definitions in the SPIRIT studies. Risk differences were calculated by logistic regression modelling of these reconstructed endpoints, and a MAIC was carried out. The results of this MAIC are presented as Table 3.37. According to the addendum to clarification response: 

_“As the SPIRIT and EDELWEISS 3 studies were generally well-balanced in terms of characteristics, an additional match-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) was performed using the reconstructed endpoints as a sensitivity analysis. Non-inferiority was defined based on p-values of >0.05 for the ITC and >0.1 for the MAIC (to select prognostic factors or treatment effect modifiers), indicating no statistically significant difference between the treatments.”[23]_

## _**3.4.3 Safety outcomes**_ 

## _**3.4.3.1 Linzagolix plus ABT (EDELWEISS 3) and leuprorelin (Osuga 2020a)**_ 

The safety outcomes from the ITC comparing the EDELWEISS 3 and Osuga 2020a studies are shown in Table 3.38. 

Significant differences were found between lumbar spine BMD (p<0.001), rate of serious treatmentemergent adverse events (TEAEs) (p=0.03) and incidence of hot flushes (p<0.001). Loss of BMD at the lumbar spine and incidence of hot flushes were higher for leuprorelin compared to linzagolix plus ABT (MD: 4.18, 95% CI: -3.56, 4.80 for lumbar spine BMD; MD: -0.34, 95% CI: -0.47, -0.31 for hot flushes). It is likely that this difference is due to the use of ABT with linzagolix. 

Serious TEAEs were found to be significantly more prevalent for linzagolix plus ABT compared to leuprorelin (MD: 0.06, 95% CI: 0.01, 0.11). The serious TEAEs reported were xxxxxxxxx xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx; these were not considered by investigators to be related to linzagolix or ABT.

**EAG comment:** It does appear to be the case that there is little difference between linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT and leuprorelin in efficacy using the CS ITC with Osuga 2020a. This was to some extent confirmed using the ITC provided in response to clarification i.e. with Ács 2015. However, for dysmenorrhoea this depends on the method used to impute the missing CIs with methods 1 and 2 showing a statistically significant difference in favour of linzagolix. The EAG questions the validity of method 1, which assumes that each CI limit (upper or lower) is proportional to the point estimate, providing no evidence for this assumption. The EAG also questions the validity of method 2 given that the paper cited for the methodology does not seem to describe a method of imputing CIs, but instead how to estimate the precision of indirect comparisons. Finally, method 3 simply assumes that the CIs (and, by implication, the same standard errors (SEs) in both trials are identical, but this seems unlikely given that the sample size of EDELWEISS is about four times that of Ács 2015 (n=362 versus 87). The EAG considers that a more valid method would be one that assumes the same SD, as mentioned in the Cochrane Handbook. This means that the SE is calculated as SD/sqrt(n). The EAG does not have access to the original means for each arm from Ács 2015, but it seems clear that, if the sample size is approximately four times smaller then the SEs would be approximately twice as large and therefore the CI, which are proportional to SE, would also be twice as large. This is likely to increase the CI in the indirect estimate. 

89 



<!-- page 464 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

However, loss of BMD at the lumbar spine and incidence of hot flushes were higher for leuprorelin compared to linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. The EAG considers that this is probably related to the addition of ADT to linzagolix 200 mg. 

The same appears to be the case from the ITC with relugolix CT, in terms of efficacy i.e. little difference, whether using the Bucher method of the MAIC.  However, the greater loss in lumbar spine BMD with linzagolix 200 mg cannot be attributed to the use of ABT because it was combined with both interventions. The company argued that: _“…the difference was not considered large enough to be clinically meaningful.”_ (page 12).[23] However, no reference was cited to support this. It should also be noted that there was a lack of full details of the MAIC analysis: it was unclear about the number of important baseline characteristics, which were adjusted for in the MAIC analysis. Therefore, given that there was a lack of full details of the MAIC analysis, this issue may have introduced the uncertainty in the results of MAIC analysis. 

In conclusion, the EAG considers that it is reasonable on the basis of these ITCs to consider that the efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is similar to that of leuprorelin and relugolix CT. However, it still remains uncertain how it might compare to other GnRH agonists such as goserelin or triptorelin, as mentioned by the EAG clinical expert. 

## **3.5 Additional work on clinical effectiveness undertaken by the EAG** 

None. 

## **3.6 Conclusions of the clinical effectiveness Section** 

The CS[4, 11] and response to clarification[5] provided sufficient details for the EAG to appraise the literature searches conducted to identify relevant clinical evidence on safety and efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg (the intervention) and other therapies (comparators) for the treatment of endometriosis. Searches were conducted in December 2023 and updated in September 2024. The revised searches provided by the company were clear and reproducible.[13] The EAG noted some limitations regarding the lack of additional searches beyond key databases and the failure to include MeSH/Emtree terms. Without rerunning the searches, the EAG is unable to say what impact this may have had on the overall recall of results, but it is possible that some relevant papers may have been missed. 

There was one key trial, the Phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 study (N=484) and its extension study EDELWEISS 6 (N=353 for the treatment extension analysis set/356 in the extension safety analysis set) designed to access the efficacy and safety of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT for the treatment of Moderate to Severe EAP in women of reproductive age. The trial comprised a 3-month screening period, a 6-month treatment period and a 6-month extension. The EAG identified that limiting to reproductive age and lack of UK patients might limit the applicability of the trial to UK clinical practice. 

In EDELWEISS 3, there was a statistically significant advantage to linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT versus placebo in all outcomes, except for dyspareunia (VRS) and EHP-30 modular sexual relationship where there was only a numerical advantage. This advantage included the co-primary endpoints of clinically meaningful reduction of dysmenorrhoea (reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) and NMPP (reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days preceding the month 6 visit. In EDELWEISS 6, there was a continued improvement with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT in all outcomes during the 6-month extension to the 6-month double blind randomised period, with plateauing towards the end of the 12-month follow-up period. AE rates appear to have been similar between the placebo and linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT with higher rates for headache, hot flush and mood swings, which 

90 



<!-- page 465 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

were regarded as treatment related. Decrease in BMD, albeit appearing to be uncommon, was also more common with linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT. The treatment effect on the co-primary endpoints of dysmenorrhoea and NMPP seemed to be consistent across the subgroups that were examined. However, there seems to be a trend of increasing treatment effect with increasing age for both outcomes, which might indicate that linzagolix is more effective in older women at least amongst those of reproductive age, which might have implications for UK clinical practice, as stated above. 

An ITC using the Bucher method was carried out to compare the safety and efficacy of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT with other GnRH analogues. A SLR was used to select appropriate studies for inclusion in the analysis. Three studies were identified for the comparator: the SPIRIT 1 and 2 studies to compare with relugolix CT, and Osuga 2021a to compare with leuprorelin. Although an ITC with relugolix CT was not included in the CS because it had not been approved by NICE, it was included in response to a request by the NICE technical team in the clarification letter, and the company also performed a MAIC. The EAG requested a NMA to include all comparators, including all GnRH agonists and relugolix CT. However, the company did not comply with this request, citing heterogeneity, availably of data only graphically, lack of measures of variance and lack of common comparators to form a network as reasons. The EAG notes that none of the GnRH agonist trials were excluded explicitly because of heterogeneity. Lack of common comparator was cited as a reason for three trials: 

- D'Hooghe 2019 – opigolix versus placebo 

- Harada 2021 - relugolix versus leuprorelin 

- Bergqvist 2000 - goserelin versus nafarelin 

Data only available graphically was cited for: 

- Ács 2015 (for NMPP and dyspareunia) - elagolix versus leuprorelin versus placebo 

- Elaris EM1 (for EHP-30 pain dimension only) - elagolix versus placebo 

- Elaris EM2 (for EHP-30 pain dimension only) - elagolix versus placebo 

Lack of SD/SE was cited for: 

- Dlugi 1990 - leuprorelin versus placebo 

- Ling 1999 leuprorelin versus placebo 

- Elaris EM1 (for lumbar spine only) - elagolix versus placebo 

- Elaris EM2 (for lumbar spine only) - elagolix versus placebo 

Therefore, given that placebo, leuprorelin or relugolix CT were available as common comparators, it seems that only Bergqvist 2000 (goserelin versus nafarelin) could not be connected in a NMA. The company stated in the FAC that one of the studies, D’Hooghe 2019, was excluded erroneously and one, Harada 2021, was excluded for reasons that were incorrectly reported in the CS.[21] The latter should have been excluded due to lack of accompanying ABT in the relugolix arm, which the EAG considers to be reasonable, but D’Hooghe 2019 could have been included. The company did in fact include Ács 2015 for NMPP and dyspareunia, which also required an assumption regarding missing SD/SE. A comparison of baseline characteristics did in fact show women substantial clinical heterogeneity, most notably in that Osuga 2021a only included women who were Asian, and the company postulated that this might also explain lower pain scores.

## _**4.1.3 Findings of the CE review**_ 

The PRISMA flow diagram for the SLR of CE studies is presented in Figure 1 of Appendix G.[24] The search, conducted on 11 July 2024, identified 16 CE studies that were included in the final review (i.e., references 84 up to 99 of the CS),[4] all of which were published after 2011. These studies originated from different countries, including the UK, US, China, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil, Turkey and Russia, and consisted of seven full articles and nine conference abstracts. Among the 16 studies, two were costutility studies, four were cost-minimisation studies, and 10 were CE studies. They analysed a range of treatment options for endometriosis, including dienogest, (combined) oral contraceptives, goserelin, elagolix, leuprolide acetate, NSAIDs, short-acting reversible contraception (SARC), and long-acting reversible contraception (LARC). So, none of the studies focused on evaluating the CE of linzagolix. Most of the studies employed either a Markov model or a decision tree model (see Table 33 of the CS for an overview of the study characteristics). The SLR did not identify any previous NICE Technology Appraisals (TAs) for endometriosis treatment. 

Furthermore, the company did an SLR aimed to identify relevant studies on HRQoL in relation to endometriosis, with searches completed on 10 July 2024. As can be seen in Figure 1 of Appendix H, this review identified 11 studies. Publications reporting results from EQ-5D questionnaires were prioritised, as the SLR aimed to gather HRQoL data for an economic model and given the guidelines set forth by NICE. Consequently, all 11 included studies used the EQ-5D questionnaire to measure HRQoL. The studies assessed HRQoL in adults with endometriosis undergoing a variety of medical procedures (primarily surgical treatments), none of them with a specific focus on linzagolix. Selected studies were conducted in Australia (2), New Zealand (2), United Kingdom (2), United States (1), Ireland (1), France (1), Turkey (1), and Japan (1). 

Finally, an SLR conducted on 6 September 2024, aimed to identify relevant studies on resource use and/or costs in relation to endometriosis. This review identified 15 studies (Figure 1 of Appendix I). In addition, a search of grey literature identified three more studies, including the NICE STA for relugolix.[27] The selected studies originated from the UK (2), the US (10), Australia (1), Israel (1), and Spain (1). Again, the selected studies covered a wide range of medical procedures.

## _**4.2.2 Model structure**_ 

The company developed a de novo semi-Markov model in Microsoft Excel[®] to assess the CE of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT compared to alternative treatment options for UK adult pre-menopausal patients with Moderate to Severe EAP who have a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis. The model consists of 17 mutually exclusive health states that reflect the varied responses of patients to both medical therapies and surgical interventions. 

To capture clinically and economically significant aspects of managing symptomatic endometriosis, the company divided the model into two main components. The first component is a decision tree, wherein health states are determined by treatment response, defined as a meaningful reduction in pain levels. This part consists of two 3-month cycles followed by a 6-month period during which the decision to continue treatment is made. The 3-month cycles align with the EDELWEISS 3 primary endpoints, which include a clinically meaningful reduction of dysmenorrhoea and NMPP to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3. The 6-month period is consistent with clinical practice, where specialist consultations for treatment continuation typically occur biannually and allowed flexibility to build the tunnel-state pregnancy. Additionally, the Markov transitions during initial treatment at month 6 were based on EDELWEISS 6 data. Due to the relatively long cycle length, a half-cycle correction has been applied. 

The second component of the model focuses on health states contingent upon the level of pain experienced by the patient. The model structure is based on reviews of the study designs for EDELWEISS 3, as well as prior economic models for the treatment of symptomatic endometriosis identified through a targeted SLOR (see Section 4.1 of this report and Appendix G of the CS)[24] and established clinical practice guidelines.[2, 28] Additionally, the company had the model structure and patient pathway validated by clinical experts.[29, 30] The various conditions or stages through which the model can transition over time are presented in Figure 4.1. 

98 



<!-- page 473 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

**==> picture [452 x 204] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 4.1: Model structure** 

Based on Figure 4 of the response to the clarification letter[5] 

The first two cycles of the model last 3 months each. During this time, patients are categorised into one of three (relative) health-states based on their treatment responses: 

- No response: in this state, patients show no clinically relevant improvement in NMPP or dysmenorrhoea compared to baseline 

- Partial response: in this state, patients experience a clinically relevant reduction in NMPP or dysmenorrhoea, indicating a partial therapeutic effect 

- Complete response: in this state, patients exhibit a dual response, with clinically relevant reductions in both NMPP and dysmenorrhoea, reflecting an optimal treatment outcome 

After each of the two 3-month cycles of initial treatment, patients who do not respond to treatment (No Response) are transitioned to subsequent treatment options, which may include the Other Medical Treatment health state or the Laparoscopy #1 Waiting health state. Patients remain in the Laparoscopy #1 Waiting state for one cycle of the model (6 months) before progressing to the Laparoscopy #1 state. After the first 3 months, partial responders may move in the next 3 months to either No Response or Complete response or may remain in Partial response. Complete responders remain in that state in the next 3 months. 

Following the two initial cycles, a new phase in the model starts (Markov model), where treatment cycles extend to 6 months. Patients who responded to the treatment (Complete response and Partial response) are categorised into three pain-related health states based on OPP: No pain/mild, Moderate, or Severe. Patients can transition between pain states until they transition into the Severe state (dependent on treatment waning assumption applied), until the maximal duration of therapy is reached (in the case of GnRH agonists) or until moving to the Pregnancy tunnel state. 

- Patients entering the Severe pain state are transitioned to Other Medical Treatment or Laparoscopy #1 Waiting. 

- When the maximum therapy time is reached, patients remaining in No pain/mild are transitioned to Off-treatment No pain/mild, and those remaining in the Moderate pain state transition to Other Medical Treatment or Laparoscopy #1 Waiting. 

- Patients can enter the Pregnancy state from No pain/mild pain state (fixed probability per model cycle). 

99 



<!-- page 474 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

If symptoms recur whilst in the Other Medical Treatment state, patients transition to the Laparoscopy #1 Waiting state and subsequently to the Laparoscopy #1 state. Laparoscopy #1 is a temporary state, and patients remain in it for one cycle of the model. This pathway assumes timely surgical intervention for patients experiencing symptom resurgence. 

After conservative surgery is performed in Laparoscopy #1, patients enter a postoperative care phase in the Post-Laparoscopy #1 state, aimed at maintaining the benefits of the surgical procedure. From this state, they may proceed to another surgical intervention, either conservative surgery Laparoscopy #2 or a radical procedure - Radical surgery #1. Notably, patients who experience a recurrence of symptoms within three months of their initial surgery bypass the Post-Laparoscopy #1 state and move directly to the second surgical procedure. Following Laparoscopy #2, patients may enter the Post-Laparoscopy #2 state, analogous to the Post-Laparoscopy #1 state, or proceed to a radical surgical intervention, specifically Radical surgery #1. After this intervention, patients transition to the Post-Radical surgery state. Alternatively, if they still have disease symptoms, they undergo a second radical surgery, Radical surgery #2. Post Radical surgery #2 they will also transition to the Post-Radical surgery state (for a description of the treatment applied in this health-state see Section 4.2.9 or CS Section B.3.5.7).[4] 

Similar to Laparoscopy #1, the states Laparoscopy #2, Radical surgery #1, and Radical surgery #2 are temporary. Patients remain in these states for one model cycle, subsequently transitioning either to the next surgical intervention state or post-surgical intervention state. 

Patients can only enter the Pregnancy state from the No pain/mild pain state (fixed probability per model cycle). Pregnancy is a tunnel state with three sub-states, each with one cycle duration. It was assumed that 18 months would be the minimum time for conception, pregnancy and breastfeeding. After three cycles (18 months) spent in this health state, patients move back to the No pain/mild pain state (with active initial treatment) or to the Off-treatment, No pain/mild state if the maximal therapy time of the initial treatment has been reached. 

It is important to note that patients may transition to the "Dead" state from any health state within the model and the same mortality rate is applied across all states. 

**EAG comment:** The EAG is much in favour of the company’s approach to use response status only as health states in the first 2 cycles, and then after 6 months translating response status into pain health states, since response status is relative to starting situation of patient, i.e. patient may have Complete response but may still have more pain than a patient with Partial response who was in a better position at baseline. 

However, it is unfortunate that this classification based on pain state was not used for all other treatments after the initial treatment, such as Other Medical Treatment or the surgery health states. Instead, patients now enter for example into a post-surgery state without separating patients based on their pain levels. As a consequence, for instance, utilities for these surgical treatments were derived as some (weighted) average of utilities estimated for the No pain/mild, Moderate pain, and Severe pain health states. This means that implicitly some distribution over pain health states is assumed, but this approach lacks transparency. 

## _**4.2.3 Population**_ 

The patient population considered in the CEA consisted of adult pre-menopausal women with Moderate to Severe EAP and a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis (Section B.3.2.1 of the CS[4] ). The patient demographics used in the base-case model, which were taken from the

**EAG comment:** The EAG observed that the EDELWEISS 3 trial, which served as the basis for the patient characteristics in the model, did not include any patients from the UK. It can be questioned, therefore, to which extent the population demographics in the economic model are generalisable to the patient population in England and Wales. In their response to the clarification questions, the company argued that the EDELWEISS 3 trial population is generalisable to the patient population in England and Wales, based on the assumption that there are no clinically relevant differences between the overall patient populations in Europe and the US compared to the UK (apart from the underrepresentation of non-white ethnic groups in the EDELWEISS 3 population). The EAG agrees with this reasoning and considers that the absence of UK participants in the EDELWEISS 3 trial is unlikely to introduce significant bias. 

Furthermore, it appeared to the EAG that the population defined by the NICE scope was “adults with symptoms of endometriosis”, whereas the population considered in the CS was “women with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis” (see Table 1 of the CS[4] ). The company clarified this apparent discrepancy by explaining that the wording used for the population (i.e., “symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in women with a history of previous medical or surgical treatment for their endometriosis”) reflects the expected indication for linzagolix in the UK and its position in the treatment pathway. According to the expected indication, linzagolix would not be used as a first-line therapy in adults with symptoms of endometriosis and would only be indicated when other treatments (medical, surgical or both) have been tried. This means that linzagolix is intended for secondor later-line therapy after conventional hormone therapy. The company further explained that the majority of the EDELWEISS 3 study population had undergone previous surgeries/procedures for endometriosis treatment before inclusion into the study, including treatments such as analgesics for pelvic pain, dienogest, hormonal oral contraceptives, and GnRH agonists (see response B2d of the response to the clarification letter).[5] As indicated in Section 2.1 of this report, there appears to be substantial uncertainty as to the precise nature of this population in clinical practice and is therefore a key issue. 

## _**4.2.4 Interventions and comparators**_ 

The intervention evaluated in the model is linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT, administered orally once daily. In principle, this treatment can be used continuously without a predefined treatment duration, except for cessation at the onset of menopause. The comparators in the model are: 1) GnRH agonists, with the 

101 



<!-- page 476 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

licensed agents in the UK of leuprorelin acetate, goserelin, and triptorelin, and 2) laparoscopic surgery (Section B.3.2.4 of the CS[4] ). In the base-case analysis, leuprorelin acetate was selected as primary comparator, as all GnRH agonists are considered to have equivalent efficacy in this population, and leuprorelin acetate has the largest market share in the UK. Intranasal GnRH agonists (nafarelin and buserelin) were not included as comparator due to their limited clinical use. Laparoscopic surgery is an additional comparator included in the analysis, at the request of NICE and the EAG, as expressed during the decision problem meeting for linzagolix. 

Initially, relugolix (i.e., relugolix-oestradiol-norethisterone acetate, or relugolix combination therapy) was not included as a comparator, as it had not yet been approved by NICE. However, after the clarification phase, the company provided comparative data on relugolix at NICE’s request and incorporated it into the economic analysis.[5] 

**EAG comment:** The main EAG concerns related to the intervention and relevant comparators are discussed in Section 2.3 of this report. 

## _**4.2.5 Perspective, time horizon, and discounting**_ 

The CEA was performed from an NHS perspective. Therefore, the analysis accounted for expenses associated with the healthcare sector. In term of outcomes, the direct health effects experienced by the patients were included. Health effects on carers were excluded. 

The study’s time horizon in the base-case was 15.1 years, spanning the period from a starting age of 34.9 years (i.e., the mean age of women included in the EDELWEISS 3 study) to the average age of menopause in the UK, set at 50 years. 

Both costs and outcomes were discounted at an annual rate of 3.5%. 

**EAG comment:** The analysis was done from the perspective of the NHS, aligning with the NICE reference case. The decision to ignore health effects on carers can be justified in the context of this disease. 

The discount rates applied in the analysis were also consistent with the NICE reference case. 

The base-case analysis used a 15.1-year time horizon, reflecting the period between the expected age at initiation of linzagolix treatment and the age at which women typically reach menopause in the UK. The latter was sourced from the National Health Service website: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/menopause/. As such, a life-time horizon was not adopted. The question is whether the chosen time horizon is long enough to reflect all important differences in costs or outcomes between the technologies being compared, as required by the NICE reference case. In response to the clarification letter, the company argued that the selected time horizon was indeed sufficient to capture all significant differences in costs and outcomes between the compared technologies. The company further stated that extending the time horizon to account for cases of postmenopausal endometriosis would have a marginal impact and not affect the overall conclusions. This is because post-menopausal endometriosis affects only a small proportion of patients and because of the high discount rate after 15 years. Furthermore, the expected impact on the CE results of using a lifetime time horizon should be marginal, according to the company. 

The EAG agrees that only a small proportion of women (~2–5%) experience post-menopausal endometriosis (as mentioned in Section B.1.3.1.1 of the CS[4] ), and also supported by a report from the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) on the quality of care 

102 



<!-- page 477 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

provided to women diagnosed with endometriosis[31] ) and that, generally, adopting a life-time horizon is expected to have a minimal impact on the CE results. To confirm this expectation, the EAG performed an exploratory scenario analysis, extending the time horizon with 10 years (see Section 6.1.2). 

## _**4.2.6 Treatment effectiveness and extrapolation**_ 

As mentioned in Section 4.2.2, the company’s model consists of two parts, i.e. a part describing the initial 6 months of treatment through a response-based decision tree followed by a long-term Markov model with health states based on OPP. Event and transition probabilities were derived by the company from individual patient-level data from EDELWEISS 3.[18] These will be presented in Section 4.2.6.1 and 4.6.2.2, respectively. 

Then, the company’s approach to estimating the rate of treatment discontinuation is discussed in Section 4.2.6.3. When patients fail on the intervention or comparator, they will receive other medical treatment or surgery. The estimated proportions of patients for these events are presented in Section 4.2.6.4. Finally, Section 4.2.6.5 presents the data the company used for the comparator ‘laparoscopic surgery’. 

## _**4.2.6.1 Treatment response first 6 months**_ 

For the first part of the model, the company divided treatment response into Complete response, Partial response, and non-response, where response was assessed at 3 months and 6 months. 

Complete response was defined as a clinically meaningful reduction in both dysmenorrhoea (i.e., a reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) and NMPP (i.e., a reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS), from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

For Partial response, the company submission presents three different definitions: 

1. **Dysmenorrhoea- or NMPP-based definition** (company base-case): A clinically meaningful reduction in either dysmenorrhoea (as above) or NMPP (as above) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

2. **Dysmenorrhoea-based definition:** A clinically meaningful reduction in dysmenorrhoea (i.e., a reduction of ≥1.10 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

3. **NMPP-based definition** : A clinically meaningful reduction in NMPP (i.e., a reduction of ≥0.8 points on the VRS) from baseline to the last 28 days of randomised treatment up to month 3, along with stable or decreased use of analgesics for EAP. 

It is assumed that patients with No response at 3 months switch to a different treatment. 

Treatment continues for another 3 months for the complete and partial responders; those patients with a Partial response at 3 months may either lose their response, maintain a Partial response or achieve a Complete response (by month 6) whereas patients with Complete response retain that Complete response.  Patients who have moved from Partial response to No response at 6 months are assumed to switch to a different treatment. 

Based on the results of the ITC (Section 3.4.2) the company assumed that response rates for GnRH agonists are equal to those derived for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT.  Furthermore, at the request of NICE, the company also added relugolix to the model as a comparator. Based on an ITC the company 

103 



<!-- page 478 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED

## _**4.2.6.3 Treatment discontinuation**_ 

The company’s model includes for each cycle a probability that a patient will discontinue the initial treatment. 

In the model, treatment discontinuation is interpreted by the company as a loss of efficacy (i.e., patients moving to the Severe pain health-state), intolerability to treatment, a break in the state of No pain/mild symptoms, or due to pregnancy and breastfeeding. The percentage of women discontinuing treatment due to pregnancy was estimated from the live birth rate in the UK,[34] whereas the rate of patients who discontinue linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT due to loss of efficacy or intolerability to treatment was estimated based on EDELWEISS 3 and 6.[18, 32, 33] 

In the EDELWEISS 3 and 6 studies, discontinuation was primarily attributed to factors such as COVID19, political reasons, or the withdrawal of patient consent from the study. Such instances of discontinuation, which were clearly unrelated to the medical intervention, were excluded from the analysis. Following the exclusion of these cases, discontinuation rates were assessed at three and six months of treatment using individual patient-level data, and the resulting discontinuation coefficients were determined and are presented in Table 4.10. 

Note that again the assumption is made that patients receiving GnRH agonists and relugolix have the same discontinuation rates as those derived for patients receiving linzagolix plus ABT. Additionally,

## _**4.2.6.5 Clinical parameters for comparator laparoscopic surgery**_ 

For the comparison of linzagolix versus laparoscopic surgery, two additional parameters were required, i.e. the response rate for laparoscopic surgery and pain recurrence following surgery. These parameters were established by the company with studies found in the SLR described in Appendix M of the CS.[15] 

Response rate for laparoscopic surgery was set to 50% based on Johnson et al. 2004.[37] The response definition provided in this study (at least 50% reduction of pain on the VAS) was considered most consistent with the response definition applied for the pharmacological treatments. As different definitions of pain response and timepoints were available in this study, the company opted to select the most conservative (in favour of surgery versus linzagolix), i.e. the highest response rate. The response rate for surgical treatment was validated with clinical expert opinion.[2, 30] The split between complete and partial responders was assumed similar to the one observed at 3 months after start of pharmacological treatment (see Table 4.8). In the scenario analyses, the company explored the impact of using the higher response rate of 63% as reported by Sutton et al.[38] 

Pain recurrence following surgery was established based on the Kaplan-Meier (KM) curve for the recurrence of Moderate to Severe pain based on the Vercellini et al. 2003 (see Figure 4.2).[39]

**EAG comment:** The EAG encountered  major issues in the estimation of the various transition probabilities, leading to various EAG derived transition probabilities to correct some errors. Three additional, smaller, issues relate to a potential error in the estimation of the number of patients in each pain state after the first 6 months of treatment for the two alternative definitions of partial responders, the probability per cycle of becoming pregnant, and the wait time for a laparoscopy. 

## **Major issues** 

For the transition probabilities between the various surgery related health states, the company presented three different sets of estimates (see Table 4.10), all based on data collected in a market research survey among 47 gynaecologists.[2] 

The EAG was unable to understand the rationale for the base-case estimates, for example the transition from laparoscopy #1 to Radical surgery #1 is estimated as: 

(Laparoscopy as first surgical type) **x** (radical surgery as second surgical type) **x** (% patients in whom recurrence occurs within 0-3 months after unsuccessful surgery) = 50% * 25% * 16% = 2.04% 

It is unclear why this calculation starts with the 50% of all first surgeries being a laparoscopy, which is then multiplied by the 25% of all second surgeries being a radical surgery. This calculation estimates the probability that a woman who is referred for surgery will first have a laparoscopy and then a radical surgery. However, in the model we are interested in the probability of needing a radical surgery conditional of just having had a laparoscopy. In that regard the alternative defined by the company is more intuitive, i.e. 

(Annual recurrence rate after laparoscopic surgery) **x** (fraction immediate recurrence: 0-3 months of 1[st] year recurrence) **x** (treatment decision following recurrence is repeat surgery) **x** (adjusted % of radical surgery). 

Here it is clear for a woman to transition to radical surgery she 1) needs to have a recurrence of pain after her laparoscopy, 2) needs to decide with her doctor that a new surgery is the best option and 3) decide that radical surgery is a better option than a second laparoscopy. In addition, a correction is made to the recurrence rate since the recurrence needs to be in the first 3 months in order to transition immediately from laparoscopy to radical surgery, bypassing the post-laparoscopy state. 

However, some of the alternative probabilities also appear to be incorrect. For example, for the transitions from post-laparoscopy #1 to laparoscopy #2 and to radical surgery #1, the adjustment to the annual recurrence to exclude the 0–3-month recurrence also includes the probability that a repeat surgery is required, which is incorrect. 

Thus, the EAG has calculated alternative transition probabilities, where the simplifying assumption is made that the probability to go from laparoscopy to radical surgery is the same as from postlaparoscopy to radical surgery. This simplification is made as a) it is not clear why 0-3 months was chosen for the immediate transition to radical surgery after a laparoscopy instead of 0-6 months in line with the cycle length, b) if a distinction is made between 0-3 months versus 3-9 or 3-12 months, we should also consider differences between the first year and subsequent years (which is impossible given the Markov property of the model), and c) the distribution of recurrence over time is only based on expert opinion and thus subject to large uncertainty. 

We estimate the transition from any laparoscopy state to radical surgery based on the 6-month recurrence rate after laparoscopy * probability that the treatment decision after recurrence is a new 

112 



<!-- page 487 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

surgery * probability that the new surgery is a radical surgery, which yields a probability of 2.46%. Similarly, the transition from any laparoscopy state to a next laparoscopy is the 6-month recurrence rate after laparoscopy * probability that the treatment decision after recurrence is a new surgery * probability that the new surgery is a laparoscopy, yielding a probability of 3.54%. As for theprobability from first to second radical surgery, the company used the 6-months recurrence rate for this probability. However, the EAG considers this incorrect, as this should be multiplied by the probability of a surgery (45%) in case of recurrence. This adjustment leads to a probability of 1.26% to have a second radical surgery after having already had one. 

All these transition probabilities will be implemented in an EAG preferred base-case, which will be presented in Section 6 of this report. 

## **Additional issues** 

- Table 4.7 shows how the complete and partial responders are classified based on pain score. The percentages presented for the partial responders are based on the base-case definition of a partial responder as having either a dysmenorrhoea or a NMPP response. The electronic model also contains the pain classification when Partial response is 1) defined as patients with only a dysmenorrhoea response and 2) defined as patients with only an NMPP response, and the underlying patient numbers are reproduced in Table 4.14. The number of patients with such Partial response and their distribution over the pain states appear incorrect to the EAG, as for both alternative definitions of Partial response the number of patients should be lower than for the base case definition. The EAG considers it possible that the correct rows for only DYS responders and for only NMPP responders can be found by subtracting the values from the complete responders from the current rows for DYS responders and NMPP responders. However, this cannot be known for sure at this moment, as the EAG has no access to the patient level data. Thus, no corrections have been made, also because such changes would only lead to different results when running a scenario analysis changing the definition of Partial response, for the base-case the error and the corrections have no impact.

- In the model a probability of becoming pregnant is incorporated for women with no pain or mild pain. This probability is estimated from the live birth rate in the UK, and, according to the company it assumes that women with endometriosis have similar desires and probability of pursuing pregnancy as the general UK population, as there is no evidence to suggest otherwise. The company states that this approach ensures that the model reflects real-world reproductive intentions without introducing unnecessary bias. The problem however is that the UK live birth rate not only reflects real-world reproductive intentions, but also the success in becoming pregnant and delivering a baby. As the company explains in their submission (Section B.1.3.2.1), while women without endometriosis have a 10%–20% chance of getting pregnant each month, this is reduced to only a 1%–10% chance for patients with endometriosis.[40] Thus, 

113 



<!-- page 488 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

the EAG considers that it would be preferable to use a smaller pregnancy rate in the model. However, the company ran a scenario excluding pregnancy from the model which led to a rather modest increase in the ICER. In Section 6, we will apply the same scenario to the EAG basecase to assess the impact. 

- Another smaller issue concerns the waiting time for a laparoscopy. In the CS it is stated that the average wait time for a laparoscopy in the UK is 18 months. The company incorporated this into the model for the comparison of linzagolix versus surgery. This means that at the start of the model, the patients in the surgery arm will remain in the No response state for the first 18 month. However, in the modelling of laparoscopy as subsequent treatment, this wait time has been modelled for only 6 months. When queried about this during clarification, the company responded that “ _The waiting for laparoscopy health state one cycle of six months was implemented to maintain model simplicity and not introduce additional tunnel states within the CE model. As the health-state utility value of Laparoscopy #1 waiting is lower compared with Post-laparoscopy #1 (0.644 vs 0.758) the solution is conservative regarding impact on the ICER (as patients in comparator arms are assumed to progress quicker to laparoscopy healthstates.”_ . The EAG concurs with this conclusion. 

## _**4.2.7 Adverse events**_ 

The company included AEs in the scenario analysis but not in the base-case, due to an absence of significant (grade 3 or 4) AEs, such as depression, headache, hot flushes or increased blood pressure in the EDELWEISS 3 study. Surgical complications were included in the base-case analysis. The company’s approach to incorporate the influence of AEs and surgical complications on HRQoL (i.e., the disutilities associated with them) will be discussed in Section 4.2.8.3 below. The impact on resource use and costs will be discussed in Sections 4.2.9.4 (AEs) and 4.2.9.5 (surgical complications). 

**EAG comment:** Despite the absence of significant AEs for linzagolix, the EAG does not consider it appropriate to exclude AEs from the base-case analysis. Therefore, the AEs are included in the EAG base-case which is presented in Section 6. 

## _**4.2.8 Health-related quality of life**_ 

In the base-case analysis, the company mainly used HRQoL evidence from the EDELWEISS 3 trial. Only information about the disutility for infertility and surgical complications were taken from the literature as EDELWEISS 3 did not provide relevant HRQoL inputs for these parameters. The systematic literature search also provided alternative HRQoL utility values for some health states. The impact of the use of these HRQoL utilities was explored in the company’s scenario analyses. Both the evidence from the EDELWEISS 3 trial and the literature are described in detail in the subsections of this paragraph. 

## _**4.2.8.1 Health-related quality of life from clinical trials**_ 

In EDELWEISS 3, the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was administered to patients at day 1, month 1, month 3 and month 6. Patients had to choose between five levels of difficulty for five different domains (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression) resulting in a five-digit health state. The five-digit health states of the individual patient level-data were mapped to the EQ-5D3L UK utility score using the NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) mapping function according to the algorithm presented in Hernández‐Alava and Pudney et al. 2017.[41] EQ-5D-3L utilities were based upon the UK value set, which is in accordance with the current NICE guidance. 

114 



<!-- page 489 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

The EQ-5D-5L was also administered in EDELWEISS 6. However, the company did not incorporate the data from EDELWEISS 6 in the CEA due to possible attrition bias. In the response to the clarification letter, the company explained that patients who completed the 6-month treatment period of the EDELWEISS 3 study were invited to enter the EDELWEISS 6 extension study. Therefore, the patient population of the EDELWEISS 6 study consists of patients who already received 6 months of treatment with linzagolix and who choose to continue. The company state that there is potential risk, that patient who did not perceive therapeutic benefits or who experienced AEs during the initial 6 months were less likely to enrol in EDELWEISS 6. Therefore, EDELWEISS 6 might represent a patient population with more favourable responses to linzagolix, leading to an overestimation of its impact on HRQoL. This assumption of the company was supported by evidence from the EDELWEISS 6 study which showed a slightly larger increase in EQ-5D-5L utility at month 6 for the subgroup of patients who continued in EDELWEISS 6 (see Table 4.15)

## _4.2.8.1.1 Response-based regression model_ 

The response categories used in the response-based regression model were based upon to the response criteria used for the co-primary endpoints of EDELWEISS 3 and EDELWEISS 6. 

- Complete response = a patient meeting the response criteria for both dysmenorrhoea and NMPP endpoints, indicating a comprehensive improvement in pain management and overall wellbeing 

- Partial response = a patient achieving a response in either dysmenorrhoea or NMPP but not both, potentially reflecting a more limited benefit from the treatment 

- No response = a patient who did not meet the criteria for any of the endpoints, indicating a lack of therapeutic effect. 

Table 4.17 shows the observed EQ-5D-3L utility in the three response states at 3 months and 6 months for all treatment arms combined. The baseline HRQoL utility for all patients in EDELWEISS 3 was 0.631.

The company used two different datasets for the estimation of the regression model. The primary dataset consisted of all observations at month 3 and month 6 for patients who could be categorised to any of the response groups (n=862). The second dataset (n=1,325) included the baseline data and classified those observations to the No response category. In the primary dataset, the baseline data were excluded because it was shown that non-responders had a better HRQoL at 3 and 6 months compared to baseline. According to the company, this meant that non-responders had some improvement in overall health and a reduction in EAP was observed, despite the lack of a clinically relevant response. The company stated that the exclusion of baseline HRQoL ensured that the model accurately reflects the HRQoL in the three response states. 

Multiple linear mixed-effects regression models with different covariates were tested on the primary dataset for best fit to the data, with the selection based on AIC and BIC criteria. In the initial CS, none of these five models included baseline EQ-5D-3L utility as a covariate despite the significant association with 6-month EQ-5D utility. The EAG asked to perform this analysis as well to assess whether this would improve the statistical fit of the model. Furthermore, the EAG also asked to run a model that only includes the response-based health state and no other covariates. - No pain/mild: OPP, VRS scale <1 

- Moderate pain: 1 ≤ OPP, VRS scale ≤2 

- Severe pain: OPP, VRS scale >2

Two different datasets were used for the estimation of the pain-based regression models. The primary dataset consisted of the 6-month observations of all patients. Initially, the dataset was restricted to the 6- months observations of the patients with a partial or Complete response, because only these patients will continue linzagolix or the comparative treatment. However, only one of these patients could be classified in the Severe pain category, rendering the estimate highly unreliable. Therefore, the decision was made to develop the regression model on all 6-months observations instead. The second dataset included all available observations (baseline, 3- and 6-months). 

Similarly to the response-based models, a series of multiple models with varying covariates were tested to determine the most appropriate fit to the data. However, as only 6-months observations were included in the primary dataset, multivariate linear regression analyses were performed. In the initial company submission, the model was selected according to statistical fit based upon AIC and BIC. In the initial CS, the first model, which only includes the pain-based health states, showed to have the best statistical fit according to AIC and BIC. Therefore, this model was used to estimate the HRQoL utilities for the pain-based states. All coefficients were significant (p-value < 0.05). The same regression model was applied to the second dataset to explore the impact on the inclusion of baseline and 3-month data. For this analysis, a multivariate linear-mixed effects regression analysis was performed. The inclusion of baseline and 3-month data had limited impact on the estimation of the No pain/mild or Moderate pain state, but increased the HRQoL utility for patients with Severe pain. In the response to the clarification letter, the inclusion of EQ-5D-3L baseline utility was applied to the primary dataset. Furthermore, a scenario was included in which the utility values from the relugolix STA were used as inputs for the pain-based states as well,[27] assuming that No pain/mild had a similar utility value a as Complete response, Moderate pain as Partial response and Severe pain as No response.
