## **EAG comment:** 

## **Major concerns** 

The EAG has two major concerns with respect to the selected models for the response-based and painbased model. 

First, the inclusion of covariates in addition to the health-states complicates the estimation of the utility scores. The covariates are dichotomised on the median and have therefore a limited generalisability to other studies. In other studies, the median could be different. Furthermore, the uncertainty in the distribution among the different categories is difficult to incorporate in a probabilistic sensitivity analysis. For the response-based health states, the simple model (without any covariates in addition to health states) has a higher AIC, but a lower BIC than the model that was selected by the company. There is thus no clear consensus which of these models has the best statistical fit. The EAG acknowledge that the inclusion of baseline EQ-5D leads to a substantial lower AIC and BIC, but the challenges regarding the inclusion of the dichotomized covariates are also applicable to this model. Furthermore, the estimated HRQoL utility only marginally differ between the model selected by the company, the model without any additional covariates, and the model that includes baseline EQ-5D as a covariate (see Table 4.21). Therefore, the EAG prefers to use the model without any covariates in the EAG base-case. 

The second major concern of the EAG is the exclusion of baseline data in the estimation of the utilities for the pain-based models. The company excluded the baseline utilities to be consistent with the method used for the estimation of the response-based model. However, the EAG does not consider this a valid argumentation as the nature of the classification of the health states differs between the response-based and the pain-based health states, which makes consistency between the two model types irrelevant. The response classification is based upon the observed change from baseline to 3 or 6 months, while the pain classification is based on the severity of pain at that specific moment. The EAG agrees with the company to exclude baseline utilities for the response-based health states. It is invalid to classify all baseline values in the No response states, because these patients have not yet received treatment and can therefore not be a responder of non-responder. However, as the classification for the pain-based states is derived from the reported severity of pain at certain time points, there is no reason to exclude the baseline data. The inclusion of that data would even improve the validity of the estimated utility for Severe pain as much more patients experience Severe pain at baseline. Therefore, baseline data is included in the models that are used for the estimation of HRQoL utilities for pain-based health states in the EAG base-case. 

122 



<!-- page 497 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

The changes in the model selection for the response-based and model-based model also have consequences for the utility values for the other health states (see Section 4.2.8.2). Table 4.26 reports all the utility values that are used in the EAG base case. 

## **Additional concerns** 

The EAG agrees with the company that EDELWEISS 6 might consist of a relatively more favourable patient population as it is likely that mainly patients who experienced benefits from linzagolix choose to continue treatment. Nevertheless, data from month 9 and month 12 in EDELWEISS 6 could have been used in addition to month 6 data in the estimation of the utility scores for the pain-based utility model to increase the sample size and include longer follow-up data. For those health states, the utilities are categorized based on the pain level which might be less influenced by the attrition bias of EDELWEISS 6. The EAG could not explore the impact of the inclusion of that information as this data was not available. 

Furthermore, the EAG also identified some aspects which were either not clarified in the response to the clarification letter or were unclear in the company’s response. First, it is unclear whether the 1- month HRQoL were also included in the baseline data or not. The EAG assumes that these measurements are included in the baseline data as the company responded that baseline data contains data from day 1. Second, in the response to question 25 of the clarification letter,[42] the company mention the AIC and BIC of a model that not only includes pain states and baseline EQ-5D-3L, but also base pain level and dyschezia. These two additional variables are not reported in the regression output in the electronic model. Therefore, the EAG considers it possible that a typing error is made in Table 25.1 of the response to the clarification letter with regard to the model structure. 

Finally, in Section 4.2.6, the company presented three potential definitions of Partial response, with the base-case definition a response in either dysmenorrhoea or NMPP but not both, and two alternatives based on 1) a clinically relevant response on only dysmenorrhea or 2) a clinically relevant response on only NMPP, with the latter two options explored in scenario analyses. However, in these scenario analyses no re-estimated utilities are used for Partial response and No response, rendering these scenario analyses incomplete. It is not clear how much this would influence the outcomes of these scenario analyses. 

## _**4.2.8.2 HRQoL used in CEA**_ 

The utilities that have been estimated through the regression analyses for the response-based health states and the pain-based health states (see Section 4.2.8.1) were used as HRQoL input for the health states No response, Partial response, Complete response, No pain/mild, Moderate pain, or Severe pain. In the company base-case, no disutilities for AEs were applied to these health states, as the company assumed that these were already captured within the QoL measurements of EDELWEISS 3. Additionally, no infertility disutilities were assumed during linzagolix treatment (and conservatively, any other medical therapy) because the half-life of linzagolix is approximately 15 hours and ovarian activity may recover within days of treatment cessation.[43] The company stated that according to clinical expert opinion, patients wanting to conceive can stop medical therapy at any time, which would justify not applying any disutility for infertility in these health states. 

The HRQoL for the other health states were estimated utilising the results of the regression models from EDELWEISS 3. The following algorithm was employed for the estimation of the remaining health states: 

123 



<!-- page 498 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

- Health states to which patients transition from the No pain/mild health state (i.e. off-treatment, No pain/mild, off-treatment during washing period and conceive, different phases of conception and breastfeeding) were assigned the HRQoL values corresponding to the No pain/mild state as it was assumed that they experience the same (low) level of pain. The assumption regarding the maintenance of treatment effects is derived from EDELWEISS 6. 

- Other medical treatments: the mean value of No response, No pain/mild, Moderate and Severe was used. In the response to the clarification letter[5] this choice was motivated by stating that the use of the average utility from these health states reflects the range of symptom severity and outcomes experienced by patients on subsequent therapy. By applying this approach, patients who are more pretreated have lower QoL as compared to patients responding to initial treatments (because the average also includes lower utility values for No response and Severe). The company state that this algorithm is in line with Wang et al.[3] 

- Waiting period for laparoscopy: the mean value of No response, Moderate and Severe. The company stated that the HRQoL of No pain/mild was not included in this calculation, because these patients typically do not require surgical intervention. The company considered this approach conservative, because these patients were already heavily pretreated (with surgery and a multitude of pharmacological therapies, including GnRH analogues). It is assumed that most patients receive sub-optimal treatment whilst waiting for the next surgical treatment. 

- Laparoscopy #1 and #2: The company assumed that during and shortly after surgery, patients had a utility of 0 for 3 days due to the invasive nature of the surgery. This duration of zero utility was taken from Wang et al.[3] For the remaining period of the 6-month cycle, the utility was assumed to be the average of No response, No pain/mild, Moderate and Severe. Furthermore, a disutility for surgical complications was added for the proportion of patient experiencing complications. This disutility was taken from literature (see Section 4.2.8.3). A conservative approach was taken to assume similar HRQoL in both laparoscopic health states, although clinical experts indicated that subsequent surgical procedures tend to be more invasive, leading to more complications.[30] 

- Utilities for post-laparoscopy health states #1 and #2 were derived from HRQoL values assigned to other medical treatments and the off-treatment state. It was assumed that 32% of the patients had a utility similar to other medical treatments, because these patients still experience symptoms after surgery and require additional treatment and 68% had a utility score similar to off-treatment state. The company motivated this distribution by stating that this allocation was proportionally to the transitions from these states to the post-laparoscopy state. 

- For radical surgery, it was assumed that patients have a zero utility for 7 days. For the remaining days of the 6-months period, it was assumed that the utility value was the average of the utility in the No response, Moderate and Severe pain. Furthermore, disutilities were applied for the proportion of patients experiencing surgical complications (see Section 4.2.8.3). 

- The HRQoL for post-radical surgery was assumed to align with the No pain/mild health state, with an additional infertility-related disutility applied to the proportion of patients who wish to preserve fertility. This value is higher than the utility value of the post-laparoscopic states, which is, according to the company, in line with literature.[44] This could be because most patients are assumed to be cured from endometriosis after radical surgery, whereas some patients would still experience EAP after laparoscopic surgery. 

A summary of the HRQoL utility values in the company’s CE model can be found in Table 4.26.

## **EAG comment:** 

## **Major concerns:** 

The estimation of the HRQoL in the other health states rely heavily on assumptions and are mainly based upon estimations from the 6-months HRQoL measurements in the EDELWEISS 3 utility values. It is hard to validate these assumptions as long-term HRQoL information is limited available in the literature (see also Section 4.2.8.3). The EAG has two major concerns with regards to the assumptions of the company. 

First, for the ‘other medical treatment’ state the company uses an average utility of the patients in the No pain/mild, Moderate, Severe and No response health state. The EAG agrees with the company that the use of an average HRQoL takes into account that patients respond differently to other medical treatments and have different pain levels. However, the EAG considers it more appropriate to exclude the utility value of non-responders in this estimation of the average utility as these non-responders were already reclassified to the Severe and Moderate pain state. Therefore, in the EAG base-case, the utility values of the ‘other medical treatment’ and surgery states were recalculated by excluding the nonresponse health state from the estimation (see Table 4.26). 

Secondly, the company used the transition probability from ‘other medical treatment’ to laparoscopic surgery (32%) as the probability of patients who experience symptoms after a laparoscopic surgery and need additional medical treatment. The EAG considers this to be incorrect and prefers to use the distribution of patients in No pain/mild (32%), Moderate (18%) and other medical treatments (32%) after laparoscopic surgery (see Sections 4.2.6.2, 4.2.6.4 and 4.2.6.5) to estimate weights for the utility for No pain/mild, Moderate and ‘other medical treatment’ respectively. This results in a utility value of 0.784 for post-laparoscopic surgery #1 and #2. 

The EAG doubts whether it is appropriate to only include a disutility for infertility after radical surgery. The company motivates this choice by stating that this disutility was captured by the EQ-5D values collected during the trials as patients were aware of the fact that they could not get pregnant while receiving treatment. The EAG considers that even if this utility decrement would have been captured, it should be emphasised that GnRH agonists are only administered for a maximum of 1.5 year, whereas in the model women can remain on linzagolix treatment until the start of menopause (16 years). Therefore, the impact of the utility decrement due to infertility would be much longer for women on linzagolix compared to those on GnRH agonists. It is unknown whether this longer time of infertility is fully captured by the EQ-5D values in the first 6 months. In the response to the clarification letter, the company provided two additional scenarios in which either infertility was applied to none of the health states or to all health states. According to the EAG, both scenarios are incorrect representations of the reality. However, the evidence is missing to accurately reflect infertility in any of the other health states. 

## **Minor concern:** 

The company justifies their assumptions by stating that these are in line with Wang et al.[3] However, this is not completely true as in Wang et al. the utility for other medical treatment is estimated from a placebo-arm of a clinical trial. Furthermore, the utility for the laparoscopic surgery and radical surgery state in Wang et al. is based upon a reduction in QoL of respectively 12.5% and 15.4% relative to the utility value of No pain/mild off-treatment. The EAG has used this calculation in an EAG scenario analysis. Furthermore, the EAG also run a scenario in which the published values from Wang et al. were used as HRQoL input.[3] 

128 



<!-- page 503 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

The EAG is uncertain about the company’s expectation that women can conceive right after stopping treatment, without consideration of the time on treatment. In the expert elicitation report (set 2) it is noted that “ _Whilst respondents have limited or no experience prescribing linzagolix plus ABT, the majority expect ovulation to resume within 1-3 months, especially if the treatment duration is short (i.e., less than six months). It was noted that it might take up to six months if the treatment duration was longer than six months_ .”[30] 

However, the EAG considers it likely that adding a ‘waiting time’ before being able to conceive would only marginally affect the ICER. 

## _**4.2.8.3 HRQoL from literature**_ 

The SLR for HRQoL identified 11 studies which were potentially relevant to the DP. Out of these studies, two studies were especially relevant as these studies included health states with similar definition as defined by the company. 

Aubry et al. 2017[45] reported EQ-5D scores for a cohort of patients experiencing symptoms which were not captured by the clinical trial data from EDELWEISS, specifically focusing on infertility. A discrepancy was noticed regarding the disutility for infertility in this study, because the utility for patients with infertility (0.66) was higher than the utility for patients without infertility. The authors of the publications were contacted by the company to clarify this discrepancy. However, No response was received at time of submission. The company decided to interchange the utility scores for patients with fertility and without fertility (i.e. higher utility score for patients without infertility) resulting in a disutility of 0.10 for infertility. Although the company aimed to use this estimate in a scenario analysis, this scenario was not run in the electronic model. 

Kent et al. 2016[44] provided QoL (utility) values for patients with Severe endometriosis undergoing various treatments, including GnRH agonists, conservative surgery and pelvic clearance. EQ-5D was measured before the surgery, and 2, 6 and 12 months after surgery. Kent et al. 2016 presented the EQ5D scores on a scale from 0–100 (see Table 4.27).

## **EAG comment:** 

## **Major concern** 

The disutility for infertility was informed from the World Health Organization (WHO) report on the Global Burden of Disease which was published in 2004 with the original source for this input being the Global Burden of Disease report published in 1990. Therefore, the EAG is uncertain if this value is still representative. In the response to the clarification letter, the company motivated their choice to be consistent with the relugolix STA and the fact that no adequate alternative value was found in the systematic literature search. The EAG explored the impact of using this alternative source (Aubry et al. 2017[45] ) in an EAG scenario. 

The company did not provide a rationale for not using the utility estimates from Kent et al. 2016 in the base-case analysis. However, the EAG agrees with the company’s choice to use these estimates in the scenario analysis because Kent et al. 2016 report median scores on a scale from a 0-100 which is not line with the NICE reference case. As Kent et al. 2016 did not report the use of a tariff, we suspect the use of the VAS score. 

There is no rationale given for choosing the value of Roberts et al. for the disutility of surgery complications in the base-case analysis. Furthermore, the alternative disutility values have not been explored in scenario analyses performed by the company. It is expected that these alternative sources will lead to slightly higher ICER, but this will be explored in EAG scenario analyses.

## _**4.2.9 Resources and costs**_ 

The analysis considered healthcare use and costs related to: 

- Drug acquisition and drug administration (for linzagolix and the comparator drug) 

- ABT, consisting of Kliovance (for patients on linzagolix and GnRH agonists and for patients who had radical surgery) 

- Laparoscopic surgery 

- Radical surgeries (i.e., hysterectomy and oophorectomy) 

- AEs/adverse reactions associated with linzagolix and the comparator drug 

- Complications following laparoscopic surgery 

- Complications following radical surgeries 

- Other medical therapies (e.g., analgesics and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems) 

- Disease management and regular monitoring 

Certain other costs were ignored, including pregnancy costs (assumed to be similar between the intervention and the comparators) and costs of diagnostic tests (as it was assumed that all patients had already been diagnosed). In general, cost prices were taken from UK sources, such as the British National Formulary (BNF) and the ‘National Schedule of NHS costs 2021/2022’, where feasible.[49] 

**EAG comment:** Overall, the approach used to assess resource use and costs seems appropriate. For example, a wide range of costs was included, and cost prices were based on UK sources. Nevertheless, several comments can be made. These are detailed in Sections 4.2.9.1 to 4.2.9.7 below, which explain how resource use and unit cost prices were determined for each cost category. 

## _**4.2.9.1 Drug acquisition and drug administration**_ 

Linzagolix was assumed to be used continuously, without a predefined treatment duration, until menopause. Based on clinical expert opinion, the treatment duration of the comparator, leuprorelin, was set at 18 months to align with clinical practice. The base-case analysis did not consider drug wastage or treatment compliance. 

The cost price for the intervention was the price provided by the company. Those of the comparators were derived from the BNF, assuming a 50:50 split between patients treated with the short-acting (1month) and long-acting (3-month) formulations (Table 4.30). Leuprorelin acetate was used as the primary base-case comparator. However, other GnRH agonists (goserelin and triptorelin) were also included as potential comparators in the model, which is why they are included in the table. Based on the cost per pack provided in the table, ‘drug costs per cycle’ were calculated, where a distinction is made between cycle 1 and 2, each 3 months, and the subsequent cycles which are 6 months. 

The costs of treatment administration were excluded for the intervention therapy and ABT (as these are administered orally), while for the comparators (administered via subcutaneous or intramuscular injection) these were calculated at the costs of administration by a nurse at a General Practitioners (GP’s) office during a 30-minute visit (£26.50, as mentioned in Table 67 of the CS[4] ).

## _**4.2.9.3 Laparoscopic and radical surgeries**_ 

The distributions of specific procedures for patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery (excision or ablation) or radical surgery (hysterectomy or oophorectomy) (Table 4.32) were derived from a 2024 report by the NCEPOD on the quality of care provided to women diagnosed with endometriosis[31] and from the Endometriosis Market Research Survey.[2] These weights were combined with unit costs of laparoscopic and radical surgeries, which were primarily derived from NHS data (the ‘National Schedule of NHS Costs 2021/2022’), to arrive at costs of surgical procedures per health state (Table 4.32). As there was no unit cost for oophorectomy, the cost of this procedure was estimated as 61% of the cost of a hysterectomy, as was also done in the NICE STA for relugolix.[27]

## _**4.2.9.4 AEs**_ 

The frequencies of AEs (i.e., headache, hot flush, depression, and increased blood pressure), which were included only in a scenario analysis, and their costs are highlighted in Table 4.33. Resource use for the AEs included in the CEA was assumed to consist of one 10-minute consultation with a GP, as shown in Table 77 of the CS.[4] The cost of this consultation was taken from cost estimates published by the Personal Social Services Research Unit (PSSRU) at the University of Kent.[50]

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

**EAG comment:** The incidence of AEs (depression, headache, hot flushes, and increased blood pressure) was based on the EDELWEISS 3 study (linzagolix) and the NICE STA for relugolix (comparators).[27] 

For linzagolix, the incidence of these AEs was set to 0.0%, based on data from the EDELWEISS 3 trial. However, the clinical effectiveness section of the CS (Section B.2.10) suggests that these adverse reactions do occur in patients treated with linzagolix. In its response to the clarification questions, the company explained that the CE model included only Severe AEs (Grade 3 or higher), that most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) during the EDELWEISS 3 study were mild or Moderate in intensity, and that the incidence of Severe TEAEs was low and comparable between groups (placebo: 1 Severe TEAE; linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT: 2 Severe TEAE). For this reason, the company opted to use data on AEs in the model exclusively for scenario analysis, and to set the probabilities of such events for linzagolix at 0. The EAG, however, feels that it would have been appropriate to include AEs in the base-case analysis and to exclude them in a scenario analysis (rather than the other way around), despite their low incidence. This is why the EAG included AEs in the EAG base-case (Section 6.1.1). Furthermore, given the uncertainty surrounding AEs associated with linzagolix treatment, the EAG adjusted their incidences in a EAG scenario analysis (Section 6.1.2). 

For GnRH agonists, the frequencies of AEs were reported as 0.47%, 1.71%, 0.40%, and 0.24%, for depression, headache, hot flushes, and increased blood pressure, respectively (Table 61 of the CS).[4] However, the corresponding probabilities included in the electronic model were 0.40%, 0.47%, 1.71%, and 0.24% for the same AEs. In its response to the clarification questions, the company provided the correct values: 0.40%, 1.71%, 0.47%, and 0.24%, for depression, headache, hot flushes, and increased blood pressure, respectively (as shown in Table 4.34). The company also provided a corrected model. Since the costs associated with the AEs which frequencies were erroneously switched in the model were identical, correcting these frequencies had no impact on the results. 

The costs of all these AEs, which were included in the scenario analysis, were set at £49.00, based on the assumption that they resulted in one 10-minute consultation with a healthcare professional. According to the EAG, this seems quite a low estimate of the healthcare resource use resulting from (some of) these AEs. In the response to the clarification questions, the company substantiated this assumption, stating that changing the resource use and costs for AEs, occurring at low rates during endometriosis treatment with GnRH analogues, would have a very limited influence on the CE model results. The EAG agrees that setting the costs of the AEs to higher, more realistic, values will likely have a negligible impact on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER).

## _**4.2.9.6 Other medical therapies**_ 

Other medical therapies, considered the first subsequent treatment following the failure of the intervention or comparator therapy, were modelled as a weighted basket of potential therapeutic options (Table 42 of the CS).[4] This resulted in the distribution of medical therapies, differentiated by health state, presented in Table 4.35. This distribution was based on the so-called ‘Endometriosis Market Research Survey 2024’ and, for NSAIDs/painkillers, on literature representative of the UK population. Notably, analgesics, included in this basket of therapies, were also included for patients on the initial treatment (the intervention or comparator drug). 

Table 4.35 also provides the costs of these therapies calculated per model cycle and categorised into acquisition and administration costs. As mentioned in the electronic model, the cost prices used for

## _**4.2.9.7 Disease management and regular monitoring**_ 

The CEA assumed that resource use (e.g., visits to healthcare professionals) was necessary to monitor patients undergoing medical therapy and to follow-up patients during treatment breaks. For example, patients on initial therapy and those on other medical therapies were assumed to require regular monitoring by a nurse at a frequency of four visits per year, while patients on a treatment break with no or mild pain were assumed to require one nurse visit per year. This resource use related to ‘disease management and regular monitoring’, which was based on expert opinion, is summarised in Table 4.36. As the CS did not include a table on this subject, the information presented in Table 4.36 was derived from the Excel file containing the model. 

Unit costs for ‘disease management and regular monitoring’ were based on NHS data (the ‘National Schedule of NHS costs 2021/2022’) and on PSSRU cost estimates (Table 73 of the CS).[49, 50] These unit costs were used to calculate the costs for each health state, as presented in Table 4.36.

## _**4.2.10 Severity**_ 

The company stated in their submission that in assessing the proportional and absolute QALY shortfall, it is not anticipated that the treatment of linzagolix 200mg plus ABT for endometriosis will be applicable for any form of severity weighting. 

Based on the estimated proportional (0.09) and absolute (1.86) shortfall using the DSU severity shortfall calculator, the EAG concurs with this assessment.[51]

## **5. Cost effectiveness (CE) results** 

## **5.1 Company’s CE results** 

## _**5.1.1 Original company’s CE results**_ 

Table 5.1 shows the company’s base-case deterministic CE results for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT compared to leuprorelin and surgery. Compared with leuprorelin, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is associated with incremental costs of £2,252 and incremental QALYs of 0.41, resulting in an ICER of £5,554 per QALY. The comparison of linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT with surgery reports incremental cost of £421 and an incremental QALY of 0.61, resulting in an ICER of £693.

Overall, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Increasing the number of QALYs in the No pain/mild on initial treatment because treatment can be continued until menopause (when compared with leuprorelin) or because a larger proportion of patients experiences No pain/mild symptoms (when compared with surgery). 

- Decreasing the number of QALYs in the No response state (when compared with surgery) because surgery patients wait 18 months in No response before they receive the surgery. 

- Decreasing the number of QALYs in the health states associated with other medical treatment or surgery as fewer patients need these other treatment options. 

Overall, linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Increasing the drug acquisition costs on initial treatment due to the higher unit costs and the longer treatment duration 

- Increasing the resource use costs on initial treatment (in comparison with leuprorelin) due to the longer treatment duration 

- Increasing the treatment costs for other medical treatment, laparoscopic waiting and postlaparoscopic treatment (in comparison with leuprorelin), because GnRH agonists, which are more expensive, are part of the treatment baskets for other medical treatment after linzagolix. 

- Decreasing the treatment costs for the surgery states as fewer patients need surgery in the linzagolix arm. 

- Decreasing the resource use costs for the other medical treatment and surgery states as fewer patients enter these health states.

## **5.2 Company’s sensitivity analyses** 

## _**5.2.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA)**_ 

In the initial CS, the company only performed a probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) for linzagolix in comparison with leuprorelin. In the response to the clarification letter, a PSA was also performed for linzagolix in comparison with surgery and relugolix. The company performed pair-wise comparisons with each individual comparator. For each PSA, the key model parameters were sampled simultaneously from their corresponding probability distributions over 1,000 iterations. The input parameters and the probability distributions used in the PSA can be found in the “Parameters” sheet of the electronic model. The average PSA results are summarised in Table 5.5 and are overall in line with the deterministic ones shown in Table 5.2.

The company also plotted the PSA outcomes on the CE plane, as shown in Figures 5.1 to 5.3. In the comparison with leuprorelin, all simulation outcomes were in the northeast quadrant where linzagolix is both more costly and more effective than leuprorelin. In the comparison with laparoscopic surgery, most simulation outcomes were also in the northeast quadrant, whilst a very small proportion of outcomes were in the southwest quadrant indicating lower costs for linzagolix in comparison with laparoscopic surgery. The comparison with relugolix shows an equal distribution of outcomes in the northwest and northeast quadrant indicating, but with very small differences in QALYs between linzagolix and relugolix indicating higher costs for linzagolix and comparable QALYs.

## _**5.2.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA)**_ 

The company also conducted deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSAs) were input parameters were varied using lower and upper estimates of parameter values. These lower and upper values were based on the 95% CI around each base-case value, where the SE was either based on observations (mostly transition probabilities and utility regression equations derived from patient level data) or assumed to be 10% of the mean value. Figures 5.6 to 5.8 present the 10 most influential parameters on the ICER of linzagolix versus leuprorelin, laparoscopic surgery, and relugolix, respectively. The tornado diagrams shows that the maximum age of patients with endometriosis has the largest impact on the ICER for all three comparators. The company indicated that none of the input parameters have a considerable impact upon the ICER, as it does not exceed £7,000 per QALY in any of the DSAs.

## **5.3 Model validation and face validity check** 

Some of the validation efforts conducted on the economic model were briefly discussed in the validation Section of the CS (B.3.14).[4] These validation efforts refer to an internal validation conducted by the developers. For example, black box testing was done to ensure technical validity.  The model structure and clinical assumptions were discussed and ratified through interviews with clinical experts (gynaecologists) in two rounds, the first with six experts and the second with 10 experts. 

In the first round the focus was on 1) the treatment pathway(s) in UK clinical practice, 2) where linzagolix would fit in the treatment pathway, if adopted, 3) commonly used outcomes to determine treatment success/failure, and 4) key considerations for treatment-related adverse effects. In the second round of interviews the focus was on 1) validating the model logic and ensure it makes sense from a clinical perspective, 2) validating key data inputs for the CE model, and 3) elicit key model inputs for which values are currently unknown. The company has included full reports of both rounds of interviews with their submission.[29, 30] 

In the remaining of this Section, the validation efforts performed on the model, as presented by the company,  are categorised according to the types of validation used in the Assessment of the Validation Status of Health-Economic decision models (AdViSHE) tool.[52]

## _**5.3.1.1 Face validity testing (conceptual model)**_ 

On page 191 of the CS, the company indicated that the model structure, including e.g. treatment pathway, model health-states, and the most impactful assumptions, was validated with clinical experts.

## **6. Evidence Assessment Group’s additional analyses** 

## **6.1 Exploratory and sensitivity analyses undertaken by the EAG** 

## _**6.1.1 Explanation of the EAG adjustments for the EAG base-case**_ 

Based on all considerations in the preceding sections of this EAG report, the EAG defined a new basecase. This base-case included multiple adjustments to the original base-case presented in the previous sections. These adjustments made by the EAG, which together form the ‘EAG base-case’, were subdivided into three categories (derived from Kaltenthaler et al., 2016):[53] 

- Fixing errors, i.e. correcting the model where the company’s submitted model was unequivocally wrong. 

- Fixing violations, i.e. correcting the model where the EAG considered that the NICE reference case, scope or best practice had not been adhered to. 

- Matters of judgement, i.e. amending the model where the EAG considers that reasonable alternative assumptions are preferred. 

No unequivocal errors or violations were identified in the company’s model, however, at various points the EAG prefers alternative assumptions. This led to the following changes to the company base-case analysis: 

1. In Section 4.2.6, it was explained that for the transition probabilities between the various surgery related health states, the company had presented three different sets of, all based on data collected in a market research survey among 47 gynaecologists.[2] However, the EAG was unable to understand the logic of calculations of the base-case estimates. On the other hand, the alternative approaches defined by the company are more intuitive, but some of the alternative probabilities also appear to be incorrect. Thus, the EAG has calculated alternative transition probabilities, where the simplifying assumption is made that the probability to go from laparoscopy to radical surgery is the same as from post-laparoscopy to radical surgery. This simplification is made as a) it is not clear why 0-3 months was chosen for the immediate transition to radical surgery after a laparoscopy instead of 0-6 months in line with the cycle length, b) if a distinction is made between 0-3 months versus 3-9 or 3-12 months, we should also consider differences between the first year and subsequent years (which is impossible given the Markov property of the model), and c) the distribution of recurrence over time is only based on expert opinion and thus subject to large uncertainty. 

2. In Section 4.2.8.1.1 it was discussed that the EAG has some difficulties with the use of covariates dichotomised at the median as the median will differ from population to population. It is also difficult to incorporate uncertainty surrounding these distributions in a probabilistic sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, there was no conclusive evidence that the model with the covariates had the best statistical fit as the model without additional covariates had a higher AIC, but a lower BIC than the model selected by the company. In the end, the estimated HRQoL utilities only marginally deviate from each other. Therefore, the EAG prefers a simpler regression model without any covariates except for the response states. 

3. As described in Section 4.2.8.1, the EAG does not agree with the company that because of consistency a similar regression model should be selected for the pain-based model as for the regression-based model. The response-based health states are defined based on the improvement in relation to baseline, while the pain-based health states are defined according to 

164 



<!-- page 539 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

absolute pain level at a specific moment. Thus, for the regression model for the pain-based health states the EAG believes that there is no reason to exclude baseline data from the regression analysis as pain categories could be adequately identified at baseline. Furthermore, the inclusion of baseline data increases the number of patients with Severe pain and therefore reduces uncertainty about the estimate. Therefore, the EAG prefers to use regression model 2 (including baseline and 3-month data) for the estimation of the utility values for the pain-based health states in the EAG base-case. 

4. For the EAG, there is no reason to include the No response health state in the estimation of the average utility for other medical treatment and surgery health states. Therefore, the utility of non-responders is excluded from the estimation of utility values for other medical treatment and surgery health states in the EAG base case. 

5. The HRQoL utility for the post-laparoscopic health states is estimated in a different way, as the EAG considered the approach by the company incorrect. The EAG applied weights for No pain/mild, Moderate and other medical treatments. The weights were derived from the proportion of patients who were classified as No pain/mild, Moderate or other medical treatment in the (laparoscopic) surgery comparator arm. 

6. In the CS, AEs (i.e., headache, hot flush, depression, and increased blood pressure) were excluded from the base-case analysis and included only in a scenario analysis. In their response to the clarification questions,[5] the company explained that the reason for this approach was the generally low incidence of Severe AEs during endometriosis treatment with GnRH analogues. Consequently, the company argued that including AEs in the base-case analysis would have a very limited influence on the CE model results. However, the EAG considers that the low incidence of AEs is not a sufficient reason for excluding them from the base-case and feels that it would be more appropriate to include them (as they do entail additional resource use and costs, regardless of their low incidence). 

An overview of the EAG changes is presented in Table 6.1.

## **Scenario 5: AEs following linzagolix (Section 4.2.8.7)** 

The incidence of AEs (depression, headache, hot flushes, and increased blood pressure) following linzagolix was set to 0.0%, based on data from the EDELWEISS 3 trial. However, the clinical effectiveness section of the CS (Section B.2.10) suggests that AEs do occur in patients treated with linzagolix. Therefore, the EAG ran a scenario in which the incidence of AEs for linzagolix treatment was equated to the incidence of AEs following treatment with the primary base-case comparator (i.e., leuprorelin acetate). 

## **6.2 Impact on the ICER of additional clinical and economic analyses undertaken by the EAG** 

## _**6.2.1 Results of the EAG preferred base-case scenario**_ 

Table 6.3 shows the results of the deterministic EAG’s base-case (discounted). These indicate that linzagolix is more costly but also more effective than leuprorelin and surgery, accruing 0.33 and 0.57 incremental QALYs at £2,810 and £615 additional costs compared to leuprorelin and surgery respectively. These incremental QALYs and costs results in ICERs of £8,638 and £1,082 per QALY gained **.** Linzagolix is more costly than relugolix with similar effects. Therefore, linzagolix is dominated by relugolix. 

When compared to the company base-case (see Table 5.2), we observe that for all treatment strategies the total costs become lower, though the incremental costs of linzagolix versus leuprorelin and versus surgery increase. At the same time, for all treatment strategies the total QALYs increase, whilst the incremental QALYs decrease, which leads to an increase in the ICER compared to leuprorelin from £5,554 to £8,638 and compared to surgery from £693 to £1,082. The incremental costs for linzagolix versus relugolix remains the same as in the company base-case.

## **6.4 Conclusions of the CE Section** 

The company provided a model that was based on previous models for treatment of endometriosis and appeared to reflect the current treatment practice, with highly individualised treatment pathways, appropriately. The company’s CEA complied with the NICE reference case. In order to compare the various treatment strategies, indirect comparisons had been done, suggesting that there was no reason to assume a difference in effectiveness between linzagolix, leuprorelin, and relugolix. 

The model consists of two parts, first a decision tree, modelling treatment response in 2 cycles of 3 months and then a Markov model where patients are assigned health states based on their pain level with regard to OPP. Treatment response, transitions between health states and treatment discontinuation were estimated based on the EDELWEISS 3 and 6 RCTs. 

Transitions between the various surgery health states were estimated based on expert elicitation in a market research survey among 47 gynaecologists.[2] However, the EAG was unable to understand the rationale for the way the base-case estimates were calculated. The same was, to a lesser extent, true for alternative estimates that the company estimated based on the same information from the market research survey. The EAG finds it unsettling that based on the same underlying data two very distinct estimators are constructed to estimate the transition probabilities, which produce quite different estimations. Using some of the logic of the alternative approach from the company, the EAG calculated alternative transition probabilities, which have been implemented in an EAG preferred base case. 

Health state utilities for the three response states and the three pain states were derived from regression models using EQ-5D data from the EDELWEISS 3 study. The utilities for subsequent states were derived using some combination of these six ‘core’ utilities. The EAG did not agree with the model 

177 



<!-- page 552 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

selection for the regression models and believes that other models explored by the company should be preferred. For the model for response state utilities, the EAG preferred the model without dichotomised (at the median) covariates. For the model for the pain state utilities, the EAG preferred the model that included baseline data, as it decreases the standard error around the utility estimates, and the EAG does not think there is a compelling reason not to include base line utilities based on the patient’s (absolute) pain status at base line. 

For the estimation of the average utility for other medical treatment and surgery health states, the EAG does not see a reason to include the No response health state in their estimation. Therefore, the utility of non-responders is excluded from the estimation of utility values for other medical treatment and surgery health states in the EAG base-case. Furthermore, the EAG considered the approach by which the company estimated the HRQoL utility for the post-laparoscopic health states incorrect. The EAG applied weights for No pain/mild, Moderate and other medical treatments. The weights were derived from the proportion of patients who were classified as No pain/mild, Moderate or other medical treatment in the (laparoscopic) surgery comparator arm. This leads to a small increase in this utility. 

The EAG had no major comments on the company’s methods for estimating resource use and costs, except for a few concerns. First, the methods partly relied on expert opinion (for example, resource use related to disease management and regular monitoring). Second, they also partly relied on assumptions (for example, resource use for the AEs included in the analysis was assumed to consist of one 10-minute consultation with a general practitioner). Finally, some data used in the analysis came from a single, small-scale investigation (e.g., the distribution of procedures for patients having laparoscopic or radical surgery, and the distribution of ‘other medical therapies’ following the failure of the intervention or comparator therapy). Finally, the EAG decided to include AE in the model as a matter of principle, whilst at the same time acknowledging that this addition is likely to have a negligible impact on the results. 

In general, the EAG considered the (reporting on the) model validation efforts rather limited. 

The company’s base-case deterministic results for linzagolix 200 mg plus ABT compared to leuprorelin and surgery showed ICERs of £5,554 and £693 per QALY gained, respectively. Linzagolix was around £835 more expensive than relugolix, whilst yielding the same number of QALYs. 

After implementing the EAG preferred assumptions and estimates, these ICERs increased to £8,638 (linzagolix compared to leuprorelin) and £1,082 per QALY gained (linzagolix compared to surgery,) respectively. The incremental costs for linzagolix versus relugolix remained the same as in the company base-case. 

When considering how the individual changes to the company’s base-case impact the results using the alternative transition probabilities for the transitions between the various surgery health states has the largest impact, with a smaller impact of changes in the utilities for the health states after the initial treatments. The impact of using different regression models for the utilities of the response states and the pain states was negligible, as was the impact of including adverse effects in the model. However, an accurate estimation of the pain-based health states is in fact important as the HRQoL utilities of the other health states currently depend upon these health states. Furthermore, the HRQoL in these subsequent health states is a driving factor for the difference in QALYs between the treatment alternatives as the proportion of patients who need subsequent treatment differ between linzagolix and leuprorelin or surgery. Unfortunately, empirical evidence is missing with respect to the health-related quality of life in these health states. Therefore, there is a large uncertainty regarding these input parameters. 

178 



<!-- page 553 -->

CONFIDENTIAL UNTIL PUBLISHED 

When accounting for parameter uncertainty, both for the company base-case as for the EAG preferred base case the probability that the ICERs are below the common NICE threshold of £20,000 is 100%. 

The company defined a large range of scenarios, with were applied to the EAG preferred base-case. In the comparison between linzagolix versus leuprorelin the ICER did not go above £13,000, with various scenarios yielding an ICER around £10,000. In the comparison between linzagolix and surgery the highest ICER was almost £10,000, when a time horizon of 1.5 years was applied. For all other scenarios the ICER remained below £3,000. 

Of the EAG defined exploratory scenario analyses, most had little impact on the results, only using the health state utilities as reported by Wang et al. led to a small increase in the ICERs versus leuprorelin and surgery.[3] In all scenarios considered, linzagolix remained more expensive and equally effective as relugolix, as was the case in the EAG base-case analysis.
